#### EXCERPTS FROM FRANCESCA ALBANESE’S SPEECH TO THE UN GENERAL ASSEMBLY, OCTOBER 30, 2024

#### *For the first time, I’m really upset. I’m upset at people’s indifference.*

#### *The intensity of this genocide and the way it enters into our lives and the fact that some people are not affected by it while others are devastated.*

#### *To think that I find myself once again in front of the people who represent most of the countries that, either all together or some smaller group, could stop this. Really, at the stroke of a pen.*

#### *I always experience a sense of shock and disappointment when I come to this room because many of you recited the same script from last year.*

#### *Of course, we condemn Hamas’s attack. Of course, we express solidarity with the Israeli victims. Of course, we demand the release of the hostages.*

#### *But is it possible that after forty-two thousand people have been killed, you cannot empathize with the Palestinians?*

#### *Those of you who have not uttered a word about what is happening in Gaza demonstrate that empathy has evaporated from this room. Empathy is the glue that makes us stand united as humanity. This is not about charity toward the Palestinians. This is about your obligations. Your obligations include ensuring the full implementation of the conventions to prevent the crime of genocide.*

#### *And therefore, today, if you really want to comply with international law, there is no other way than by imposing sanctions on Israel and revising the diplomatic, economic, political, military, and strategic ties you have with it.*

#### *And may this be the last genocide in human history.*

# PREFACE

#### I AM WRITING THESE WORDS at a strange moment in my life: I have just been sanctioned by the United States. As of July 9, 2025, I have been named a “specially designated national” by the Department of the Treasury, barring all US nationals, including my own daughter, and corporations from engaging with me and causing the freezing of my assets in the United States.

#### I am the first UN official in history to receive such a sanction — one I share with Vladimir Putin, Bashar al-Assad, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and Nicolás Maduro — for the absurd “crime” of allegedly working with the International Criminal Court. In reality, I have been targeted for reporting on Israel’s violations of Palestinian human rights — or, as the United States chooses to frame it, “anti-Semitism.” This label does a grave disservice to Jewish people worldwide and risks trivializing the history and reality of hatred against Jews. These sanctions are punishment for my insistence on fulfilling my UN mandate under the harshest circumstances, when the people of Gaza and the Occupied Palestinian Territory were enduring unspeakable suffering.

#### I did not set out, at the start of my life, to confront power in this way. I was born and raised in a small mountain town in southern Italy — a place few leave and even fewer move to. My adolescence was shaped by a visceral rejection of injustice. At that time, the Mafia’s violence — its assassinations of judges, lawyers, and journalists — left an indelible mark on me. After the anti-Mafia prosecutors Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino were murdered in 1992, Sicily found the strength to erupt in outrage. Ordinary people began to stand together against organized crime, joined in solidarity by Italians from other regions.

#### From this, I learned that unity and courage are the most powerful forces for change. At eighteen, after my father passed away, I sought refuge in the rationality of law. Although a sense of social justice had long been in my veins, the order, structure, and logic of legal disciplines offered reassurance. I was also lucky to have a strong and supportive mother always by my side, graciously holding my hand or with her arm on my shoulder, at every moment of need.

#### At university, I started to find my path. I joined a collective of critically engaged students, animating the cultural life of the law school and representing my peers in academic institutions. My political conscience started to manifest. For example, I took it personally when my department sought to honor Giovanni Gentile, Mussolini’s minister of education who signed the 1938 racial laws that condemned thousands of Italian Jews to death. I helped mount a protest, and we won: The commemorative plaque to honor the memory of Gentile was not placed in the law school.

#### To support myself, I worked one, two, sometimes three jobs at the same time, and still graduated with the highest honors. Those years allowed me to travel, study English abroad, and glimpse horizons far wider than my small town. Becoming a practicing attorney-at-law was never my calling. I did complete my law degree but had no interest in the bar; I wanted to be a human rights lawyer, using the law to defend those whose rights had been denied, beyond the courtroom — an idea that scarcely existed in Italy then. (While in the United States “lawyer” is tied to bar admission, internationally the title is widely used for specialists in law in both academic and professional *settings. That is where I belong: me voilà.)*

#### For a brief moment, I even entertained the idea of becoming a journalist, but it faded when a generous scholarship — and the chance to study in the charming city of Lecce, in my beloved southern Italy — drew me back to international law and development.

#### It was during one of my many student jobs that I first stepped into the world of international affairs, with an internship at Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. That experience opened the door to my first missions abroad, to

#### Pakistan, Guinea-Bissau, and more fundamentally to a UN scholarship, which took me to Morocco for two years, where I both enjoyed traveling and worked as an unwilling chronicler of injustices and human rights abuses. This led me to want to further pursue postgraduate studies in human rights law, so I decided to enroll in an LLM program at the University of London School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS).

#### SOAS played a decisive role in shaping my intellectual trajectory. As a postgraduate student, I first encountered critical approaches to international law and development studies, and it was a total epiphany, though not pain free of *course. This is where I met Edward Said — not in person but through his writings. Orientalism and his other works* offered me the language and framework to understand the politics of representation, the construction of “the Other,” and the distortions embedded in Eurocentric legal narratives and development approaches. These ideas were not always comfortable, but they were irresistible in their power to unveil the world as it is. Said, along with Antonio Gramsci — another of my intellectual lighthouses — helped me grasp how culture sustains power, and how resistance begins by questioning the stories power tells.

#### These influences left a profound mark on my work and the choices I made from that point forward. What followed was four years with the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, when I was based in Geneva but traveled across the Arab world and Southeast Asia. Eventually, I moved to Palestine to work with the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), fulfilling what had since SOAS become my “dream” of going to Palestine. In London I had studied the question of Palestine through a legal lens and was left with a sense of insurmountable and enduring injustice that, with my good intentions and hard work, I felt totally equipped to help resolve! (Not to be missed is how much my good intentions were tinged with white-savior illusions, which would soon be shattered by reality.)

#### As a UN lawyer in occupied Jerusalem, often traveling across Gaza, the West Bank, and the neighboring countries where millions of Palestinian refugees still lived, I wrestled daily with the dissonance between the principles of international law — equality, justice, dignity — and the realities of power politics. Nowhere was this gap more visible than in Palestine, where the international community’s inaction made a mockery of the law it claimed to uphold. This contradiction ultimately led me to leave the United Nations, first to pursue other job opportunities and then independent research.

#### After Palestine I moved to Washington, DC, where my husband had joined the World Bank and where we welcomed our first daughter, Leila. To celebrate her US citizenship, we decided to make the first and biggest investment of our lives: a small but lovely condo in Adams Morgan. Unlike my husband, who didn’t particularly love DC life, I slowly fell into a pleasant relationship with the city. Yes, there were the lobbyists, but there were also lovely parks: the first huge green spaces I truly experienced in a city. I still remember what I call the “green, red, and yellow baptism”: the first rain of leaves I encountered during one of my early walks in town, while, with my relatively small eight-month belly, I toured potential condos with a Realtor, searching for the nest where I would give birth. I also traveled across the racial contradictions that survive, often painfully, under the skin of the city and are reflected in its urban geometries and demography.

#### As a new mom to a wonderful girl, I began exploring the city and, slowly, the United States. I used my maternity leave to step away from human rights work for a while and trained to become a yoga teacher, which was the most spirituality I could absorb at the time. But the continuous bombing of Gaza — in 2012 and 2014 — pulled me back in. With Leila tied to my chest, I began attending protests, trying to assuage the guilt I felt for being away from my UNRWA colleagues and the people of Gaza who were mourning their loved ones. The sense of impotence was suffocating. I remember joining a sit-in in front of Target on Columbia Road in the summer of 2014 and crying on the shoulders of volunteers from Jewish Voice for Peace. That was the beginning of my friendship with many DC-based peace activists. I also began volunteering as a yoga teacher for disadvantaged communities, from Columbia Road to Anacostia.

#### It did not take long before, despite a well-paid but emotionally unfulfilling job as a “technical expert” with an American NGO, my heart and mind returned to Palestine. This time, it was for research, which I conducted while an external researcher affiliated with Georgetown University’s Institute for the Study of International Migration.

#### Four years later, after another international move — this time to Indonesia — and the birth of my son, Giordano, my research culminated in a book on Palestinian refugees in international law, published by Oxford University Press in 2020. For Palestinian refugees, “refugee status” is more than a legal label; it is the lived experience of exile from a homeland that once existed. Their plight made clear to me that any resolution must address the collective right of the Palestinian people to self-determination. This became the focus of my first report as a UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, a role I assumed in 2022.

#### Professor Michael Lynk, my predecessor, had first sparked my curiosity eighteen months earlier. After attending several of my online book talks, he asked whether I had considered expressing interest in the position. “You have stellar UN experience, academic credentials, a kind spirit, and you’re a great communicator…” I still remember my

#### *husband’s gaze from the back of the room as I Zoomed with Michael: This is so not going to happen, Franci.* But it did. From an extraordinary pool of candidates, the Human Rights Council chose me for this voluntary

#### position, created in 1993 to document and report to the UN on violations committed by Israel as the occupying power in Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem — territories under military occupation for twenty-six years by then. I am the eighth person, and first woman, to serve as the UN Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in the Palestinian territory occupied by Israel since 1967. Though the work is pro bono, the mandate is demanding.

#### In this role, as one among more than fifty UN independent experts (the crown jewel of the UN, as late UN secretary-general Kofi Annan used to call us), I strive to embody what Said modeled: a truthful witness. Impartiality does not mean indifference; it means investigating rigorously, judging facts against the law, and speaking truth to power — even when it’s inconvenient. In Palestine, this entails exposing the deep asymmetry between occupier and occupied, colonizer and colonized, and showing how decades of dispossession have been normalized by an international community that is unwilling to act.

#### The journey from a small southern Italian town to the heart of international law has been marked by restlessness, conviction, and an irrevocable intolerance for injustice. If there is one lesson I carry with me, it is this: Standing together with courage, even against entrenched power, makes change not only possible but inevitable.

#### —

#### THIS BOOK was originally written for an Italian audience, and in its first few months, it was an absolute success. At every stop on the Italian book tour, I was met by thousands of people, all eager to learn more about the situation in Palestine and how they could contribute. This enthusiasm is unusual for an essay, all the more so for a book written by a jurist on a topic that has been systematically erased from the public agenda by a subservient press and the ideology of those in power.

#### Given the impact this book has had in Italy, I was glad to hear that a US publisher was interested in bringing it out in English. All the more as the United States remains the main obstacle to a peaceful resolution of the situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory because of unconditional US support for Israel. By shielding Israel from the proper consequences for its actions in front of the international community — whether diplomatically through its veto in the Security Council or materially through billions of dollars of arms shipments to Israel that allow it to maintain the status quo of occupation, or the sanctioning of people and institutions critical of Israel, as has happened to me and many others working for justice, from the International Criminal Court to Palestinian human rights organizations — the United States has fostered a culture of impunity for Israel that has allowed it to commit the worst of crimes.

#### At the time this book is being translated, the Gaza genocide is a part of our history: a blemish on humanity for which our grandchildren will hold us to account. This is said and done; now the task at hand is to stop the genocide and find a way forward. This book is a small effort toward that end. In presenting the ten stories that follow, I aim to grapple with the past and present of Palestine, with the hope of imagining a better future for all who share the land. I don’t aim to sugarcoat the gruesome reality in which we live today; make no mistake, these stories are brutal, devastating, and heart-wrenching, many of them told straight from ground zero of genocide, others from the unimaginable position of those who have been forced to watch the atrocities unfold from afar.

#### Yet even as these stories present a picture of pain and despair, it is my hope that they will also bring an understanding that peace in Palestine and in the entire region is possible — that this land can be a home for Jews, Christians, Muslims, and anyone who calls the Holy Land home, regardless of whatever name the land goes by — through a grounding in universal justice and accountability for all. Each story offers a different, complementary lens from which to view the ongoing genocide and the global missteps that brought us to this point, and presents the raw human experiences from which we might fashion an alternative, shared future for Israelis and Palestinians alike.

#### What might that future look like? Though any long-term solution will need to be decided upon by Israelis and Palestinians themselves, I can say with confidence that a lasting peace will require sacrifice from everyone, most of all from Israelis — not of their rights as human beings, to live in peace, security, and dignity with their neighbors, but of their privileges as citizens of a settler colony built on the denial of indigenous self-determination. True peace can only be built on equality and freedom for all, grounded in a vision of universal justice that affords equal rights and responsibilities to all, regardless of their race or nationality.

#### Not to betray Said’s message, I resolutely include the Israelis in this rehumanizing discourse. Like the Palestinians, they are part of an anachronistic settler-colonial endeavor, of course with unequal responsibilities and suffering. Ending Jewish Israeli domination will be a rehumanizing act. No one can oppress and brutalize others without themselves experiencing a loss of humanity in the process.

#### And meanwhile, one thing is for certain: This future will be made possible only by the work we do today. What

#### matters now is that the current injustice is stopped immediately and further injustice is prevented; it is up to us, international civil society, lawyers, students, and citizens of the world, to take responsibility and use our voices to demand our governments meet their obligations and protect the multilateral international order that is threatened now more than ever.

#### When the world sleeps, it falls on us, we the people, to wake it up — and now more than ever the world needs an awakening.

# INTRODUCTION

#### *Is solidarity a political form of love?*

#### I became a refugee at the age of ten. What stands clearly in my child’s mind was the identity of the invisible enemy who destroyed my life. What did he look like? Was he a human or a beast? Why did he make me a refugee? What had I done to him? Where did he come from? What language does he speak? *— SALMAN ABU SITTA, Mapping My Return*

#### IN RECENT TIMES I have found myself thinking very often about George Orwell. His famous proclamation, according to which “War is peace, freedom is slavery, ignorance is force,” has never seemed to me to be more topical and pertinent than in the debate of recent months on Israel and Palestine.

#### For example, many people continue to speak of what is happening in Gaza as a “conflict.” Or, even worse, as a conflict that began on October 7, 2023. In this reading there is all the superficiality of those who start a book halfway through, ignoring the preceding pages that contain vivid traces of blood and pain, a story that actually has its roots much further back and that continues to remain ignored.

#### Similarly, the call to justice that the Palestinian people have been raising for almost a century, their protests against the regime of apartheid that has oppressed them for generations, remains muffled and unheard, just like the senseless tragedy of what has been happening since the end of 2023 and continues to happen even after the supposed ceasefire between January and September 2025: a full-blown genocide.

#### —

#### THE HORROR IN GAZA is unprecedented. When I say that Israel is writing one of the darkest pages of history, comparable to the genocides of the past, many people tell me that we do not yet know for sure, that we have to wait for the verdict of the International Court of Justice. But the court — the body established to settle disputes between states and issue advisory opinions on questions of international law — already affirmed the risk of genocide in January 2024, ordering states to take action to stop Israel’s genocidal acts. Many countries, however, seem not to have understood this, or have deliberately ignored it. The international treaty is called the Convention on the *Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide: How can states prevent it, if not by acting promptly when the* risk arises (as the Court of Justice states)?

#### And even leaving aside the legal aspect, how is it possible not to express oneself in the face of atrocities of this level of ruthlessness?

#### When I was in Berlin in May 2024, a few weeks after presenting a report called “Anatomy of a Genocide” to the UN, mine was still one of the few voices denouncing in these terms the crimes of Israel that were underway in Gaza. Excluding the pending proceedings initiated by the South African government at the International Court of Justice in December 2023, alleging that Israel was committing acts of genocide against the Palestinian population in Gaza, there was virtually no other literature on the subject.

#### Some illustrious scholars, such as the historian Raz Segal, had spoken of genocide immediately after October 7th, but theirs were isolated voices. Ilan Pappé, another well-known Israeli historian, also denounced Israeli *practices in the Gaza Strip as an incremental genocide in 2006: a genocide that gradually increases in violence and* intensity. Yet within the United Nations no one dared to utter that forbidden word about Israel. No one except myself and a few other UN speakers, especially those from countries of the Global Majority (or Global South), for many of whom the trauma of colonization and genocide that Europeans have perpetrated over the course of half a millennium from Latin America to Africa to Asia is still alive.

#### “Anatomy of a Genocide” was the first report to provide the United Nations with a detailed denunciation of the fact that Israeli military operations in the Gaza Strip revealed an intention to annihilate Gaza as such, to destroy everything. In Berlin, where a series of meetings and conferences awaited me, I was welcomed with great interest from civil society and the German think tank community.

#### Less than a year later, the reception in Germany for a new round of public events turned out to be very different. Today there are many voices that support my interpretation of the facts and their legal qualification as genocide: illegal occupation, settler colonialism, and apartheid, among other offenses imputable to the State of Israel. But the repression of the message I bring, of my functions, and of my person has grown in unprecedented ways, as has intolerance in the debate on the Israeli question. So, what has changed?

#### —

#### JUST BEFORE I ARRIVED in Germany in February 2025, the two university events I was supposed to attend were canceled under political pressure. The first — a lecture at the University of Munich — was canceled immediately. However, thanks to the students, I was still able to give the lecture in a refugee reception center that does not depend on the government but is supported by private funds and has a courageous director who did not give in to pressure.

#### At the University of Berlin I was supposed to give a lecture along with Eyal Weizman, an Israeli expert in forensic architecture. However, when we arrived, the university had already canceled the public event. They proposed holding it behind closed doors, but we refused; it wouldn’t have made sense to have gone all the way there to hold a meeting that could only be followed online. Some professors and students managed to move the event to a cultural center that could accommodate up to six hundred people (although at that point there were already twelve hundred registered). However, the Israeli ambassador, the police, several politicians, a government minister, and other institutional figures pumped up the pressure. After pushing the university to cancel the conference, they threatened to revoke the grants to the cultural center if it agreed to host the event. Faced with the risk of having to close due to lack of funds, the center gave in, only to find the next morning its walls daubed with the writings of the usual pro-Israel groups, insulting me and the United Nations: ALBANESE ANTI-SEMITE, ALBANESE TERRORIST.

#### *In the end, the event was held anyway, but at the headquarters of the newspaper Junge Welt, where there was* only room for a hundred people. Outside there were a lot of people crammed together. Meanwhile, the police had surrounded the building with officers in riot gear, with batons and machine guns in plain sight. It was in this setting that Eyal and I spoke of peace for a people who are suffering.

#### In Germany, as in other parts of Europe and increasingly, shamelessly in the United States, repression has taken on extremely violent tones. In recent months I have had the opportunity to read many times about police charges against students and those who demonstrate with them. And sometimes to witness these scenes with my own eyes. The forces of law and order beat, club, and imprison people of all ages and nationalities: first and foremost, Palestinians and anti-Zionist Jews.

#### The drama is twofold: Not only are these people fighting to stop atrocious crimes but they are doing so by exercising their sacrosanct right to criticism and dissent, a right which is a corollary to the even more fundamental freedom of expression and which should be one of the bulwarks of our so-called liberal democracies.

#### What does democracy consist of, if there can be no room for debate? Of the people from the think tanks I had met in Berlin the previous year, none showed up this time. Of the

#### eighteen NGO delegates, only three came. *Then, the evening before the event at the headquarters of Junge Welt, there was a threat of arrest. The German*

#### federal police contacted the sponsoring organizations to warn me not to appear, otherwise I could be arrested for violating German anti-Semitism laws. After an almost sleepless night, at six in the morning I called my husband and told him: “I don’t know what I have to do, Max…I know I’m doing the right thing, but I don’t want to be arrested, I haven’t seen the children for twenty days.”

#### He replied, seraphic: “You go ahead and do what you have to do. We are here.” So I went. But the UN had to intervene, reminding the German police that as the UN Special Rapporteur I enjoy diplomatic

#### immunity, and that my arrest would have been an unprecedented scandal. Only then did they back down, but in any case the event was practically under siege: In addition to the twenty or so police vans outside the newspaper’s headquarters, officers in riot gear packed the room. I arrived with a smile, pretending everything was fine. When I went onstage, my heart was full of indignation, but that did not prevent me from expressing myself clearly and precisely. At the end of the event, Michael Barenboim, a violinist and professor at the Barenboim-Said Akademie, played with Palestinian violinists. It was beautiful. And the next day, Melanie Schweizer, a German government

#### official who had attended the event, and who had already been suspended for her critical stance on Israeli policies, was fired.

#### This is the level of repression in Germany today.

#### —

#### AS MY COLLEAGUE IRENE KHAN, the UN Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of the right to freedom of opinion and expression, said a year ago, the crisis in Gaza is now a symptom of a global crisis.

#### I think more and more often that all of this, while it is bound to instill fear, must also give us courage. The system that represses the Palestinians — a well-established alliance between Israel and all the other states whose elites guarantee it the impunity it has always enjoyed — is the same one to which we belong. It is the system that decides for us on issues that are crucial to our lives, without listening to us and representing us; it is the system that transforms secure jobs into part-time and temporary work, rights into privileges, that alienates us from each other, making us all more fragile and insecure; that considers solidarity a subversive act and empathy a form of mental and social dysfunction. These are subtle mechanisms, that day after day contribute to unraveling ties and compromising our ability to act together for a just cause, from the environment to Palestine, from precarious jobs to gender issues. I *have often reflected on the fact that for me Palestine was the red pill in The Matrix, the one that opens your eyes to* the hidden reality of things. My work, all the study of the Palestinian question over the years, has helped me to see and understand better the system in which we live. And, in a counterintuitive way, to continue to love it.

#### Lately I have really understood the value of courage that is needed to clog the gears of the system. I have had many opportunities to observe and ask myself questions, during months of incessant travel in which I have met a multitude of people and heard their stories: representatives of the authorities, members of civil society, scholars and intellectuals, workers, trade unionists, and, above all, students and ordinary people. Special people who are searching for useful and important words, who want to find hope to exchange and share. It has happened to me in the United States, Australia, Spain, Norway, Denmark, Holland, Portugal, Egypt, Jordan, Canada, and, many times, in Italy. Even in Belgium, where the presence of the European institutions — sometimes more linked to bureaucracy than to the effectiveness of the result — often makes the air particularly heavy. It’s been a long journey that has allowed me to grasp the transversal impulse of many communities in search of justice, truth, dignity, and a better future, beyond our differences.

#### —

#### IN PUTTING TOGETHER the book that you have in your hands, physically and virtually surrounded by all of these travel companions, I have therefore chosen to dedicate to ten people dear to me the story of the themes that I consider fundamental to an understanding of the history, present, and future of Palestine. These ten people, with their teaching, their testimony, and sometimes even their presence, have accompanied my journey of learning through a land that has suffered for too long.

#### It will therefore be Hind, who died at the age of six for the crime of being Palestinian, who will open our eyes to what it means to be children in a country where for generations minors have not had the right to have a nest that protects them and respects their roots. It will be George, one of my closest friends from the years when Max and I lived in Jerusalem, who will introduce us to the streets on both sides of the city, among the wonderful houses of the past, the bookstores where today children’s books are seized by the Israeli military, and the clubs where, until a few years ago, it was possible to go dancing alongside those same Israeli boys, in this case not in uniform. It will be Ingrid, a European woman who chose Palestine and who gave so much to Palestine, who will explain to us the importance of a certain rigor in the thought and use of the legal framework of apartheid, as she made it clear to me in 2017. It will be Eyal, who left Israel long ago and feels he has no right to return until he can travel with a Palestinian passport, that is, the passport of a single and democratic state, who will shed light on the complexity of the physical and material conditions that generate genocide. It will be Gabor, marked early by the persecution of the Jews, who will enlighten us on the madness of what is happening to the Palestinian people and on the myth of normality. And then Abu Hassan, who guided us to see the places that reveal their fatigue and oppression; Alon, a great student of genocide and a precious friend, who helped me to understand more closely the contrasts that can dwell in the heart of an Israeli Jew who “sees” the Palestinians and feels their cause as his own, because the liberation of the Palestinian people from the oppression of apartheid holds the key to the liberation of the Israelis themselves; Ghassan, the surgeon who arrived from London to enter the heart of the most unimaginable horror of Gaza in the first months of the genocidal assault; Malak, the young painter who took the opposite path, leaving Gaza to go to London to tell the story of her people in art; and finally, Max, one of the people closest to me, in life as well as in the

#### search for an awareness that we can translate into action. Ten people, ten stories that are intertwined with the lives of many others — including me, my family, the clerk

#### of an Irish shop, or the children who came to eat mulberries in front of our house in Jerusalem — asking the questions that today seem too difficult to answer. For example: What are the living conditions of the Palestinian people? What are the consequences of the Israeli occupation? Where is “home” for a refugee? What does it mean to be anti-Semitic in battles for human rights? What are the limits of cruelty in a genocide?

#### Today we cannot avoid these questions. And, because of what is happening, new ones still arise. For example: Why continue to write about Palestine in a

#### country like Italy, where it is so necessary and so difficult to ensure a hearing for voices that expose the facts and fully explain their legal ramifications? Despite my institutional role, and although I have never done anything that could make me unpopular with the Italian media, I have been subjected to endless offenses and excluded, with a few rare exceptions, from the national media landscape. So the only answer I can give myself is this: Since the need to talk about it is not going away, on the contrary it is becoming more and more pressing, I choose to take every possible opportunity to do so, including in this book.

#### By cultivating in this terrible moment the germ of an idea that had been taking root in my mind for years, the idea of writing a book of “Polaroids from Jerusalem,” here I also want to tell the story of Palestine as I have experienced it: not as an activist but as a person who at first approached it with cultural curiosity and, later, from a legal perspective.

#### When I arrived in 2005 at the School of Oriental and African Studies I discovered two fundamental things. The *first was that Palestine could — and should — be discussed as a legal issue of protracted, institutional, and systemic* illegality, and not simply as a political issue with opposing claims. There was much more that remained to be said, and what was unsaid began to feel too tight for me, because it also authorized people who had never set foot in Palestine to express themselves, often in a superficial way and applying two standards in evaluating the parties involved.

#### The second discovery was the encounter with law firms influenced by critical race theory: a way of understanding law in a critical and decolonial key, framing it in the historical evolution not necessarily written by the victors but observed from the perspective of the peoples who, until recent times, have been subjected to international law — as it has been formulated above all by Western countries.

#### In 2010 I went to live in Palestine as an international official, and Max and I stayed there until the end of 2012. Then I continued to work as an academic. It is by virtue of this experience that I received the mandate of UN Special Rapporteur, which I try every day to honor by showing that the key points of law, after all, are and must be understandable to everyone, because they concern each of us. The international law that I deal with as Special Rapporteur consists simply of the set of rules that states give themselves to regulate their relations: rights, duties, reciprocal obligations. Then there are the rights of the people, human rights, which represent our protection, our shields, and, if necessary, our swords.

#### The desire that motivates me is to be able to articulate and explain the blatant injustice in the daily lives of the Palestinians.

#### This desire also runs deeply through the pages of this book, which was written in the era of a genocide that has shown the world its brutality and under great pressure. I was convinced that, because of all the absurd pressure brought to bear against me by influential actors, the Human Rights Council would not renew my appointment. And yet the council continues to place its trust in me, and the publication of this book coincides with the beginning of my second term as Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which will allow me to deal again with these issues that are now inextricably intertwined with my own life, now that the present, the future, and even the past of the Palestinian people is more than ever in danger.

#### In Palestine — after fifty-seven years of military occupation of Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and seventy-seven years after the ethnic cleansing that reached its historical peak with the Nakba, the forced exodus of the Palestinians that began with the establishment of the State of Israel in 1948, Israel is now committing genocide with the awareness and approval of the established system of power, the one that has so far kept everyone subjugated with the threat of retaliation.

#### The United States, under President Trump, has repeatedly tried to intimidate anyone who dares to touch Israel, saying that they will have to “deal with us,” a threatening language unbefitting of politics as we have known it until now, but which is entirely consistent with the substance of what Trump himself said when he declared, “Everyone *I’ve spoken to likes the idea that the United States owns that piece of land“ — referring to the Gaza Strip. In this* sentence there is all the violence of an unbridled power that can achieve everything through force, because, like a Caligula of the twenty-first century, he considers himself above the law. In fact, he doesn’t even know the law.

#### *Well, the time has come to deal with the United States and others: For us “Westerners,” especially for us*

#### Europeans, this is an opportunity to untie the knots of the colonial past and begin to pay off our debt. It is time to take a stand against the devastation of Gaza and what remains of Palestine, and to fight against an international system based on the use of force in the name of a so-called “peace” that is always evoked for the benefit of a few and always by using words that mystify the reality of what is actually being done, exactly as Orwell prophesied almost a century ago. Today the concept of “doublethink” advocated by the Ministry of Truth that Orwell imagined *in 1984 — a fundamental instrument of mind control wielded by the totalitarian regime described in the novel — no* longer seems so fanciful, and indeed invites us to open our eyes to see what we are facing.

#### Even for the most sophisticated doublespeak experts, it is no longer possible to deny the truth about Palestine. In July 2024, the International Court of Justice has found beyond a reasonable doubt that Israel’s occupation of Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem since 1967 is illegal and must be abandoned totally and unconditionally.

#### The occupation is illegal because, by its very existence, it prevents the Palestinians from enjoying the right to self-determination: the right of a people to exist and to determine itself, that is, to choose for itself, without foreign control over the territory and the lives of the people who inhabit it. Yet this simple right to exist as a people and to live in freedom is still disputed by some or dangerously confused with the two-state solution. But I do not think that it is necessary to be a jurist to understand that, without the right of self-determination, every other right loses its meaning and becomes a mere exercise in rhetoric.

#### What is happening in Gaza, and in the other areas of Palestine under illegal Israeli control, including the West Bank and East Jerusalem, is a colonialism of settlement through the execution of planned and methodical destruction. In Gaza this process is already a tangible accomplishment, and destruction affects physical and biological life in all its forms, annihilating everything that exists, including, of course, the human beings who live, or rather lived, there. In the West Bank, Jewish-only settlements are a continuously expanding pervasive presence and the Palestinians are increasingly isolated. There, the Palestinians may not be subject to carpet bombings like those that have devastated a large part of Gaza, but they are the targets of explosives and mechanical demolitions, which along with the violence of the settlers affects houses, schools, entire neighborhoods, including olive groves and beehives. There is no peace in Palestine if you are Palestinian. Security in that land — and not only there, unfortunately — is a one-way proposition; if you are Palestinian, it is invoked only to repress your freedom. To punish you.

#### —

#### WHILE WE WERE IN BERLIN, Eyal told me that friends in Gaza had confided to him that, faced with the shortage of bread, families in the Deir al-Balah area had organized themselves to protect the few resources available. “We have to put security guards to watch over the bread and flour,” they told him. The Israeli soldiers called the owner of the bakery and ordered him to put an end to the practice: “If you don’t remove these security guards, we will bomb you, the bakery, and the security guards as well.” What is the point of all this?

#### Today, it is not uncommon to come across arguments such as: “But Israel doesn’t want to destroy the Palestinians. Israel just wants to eradicate Hamas,” or: “Israel wants to free the hostages. If only Hamas would free them…”

#### I would like to point out that, first of all, if you go so far as to bomb a bakery, if you manage to kill tens of thousands of children, to mutilate or make orphans of ten times as many, it is evident that such actions are not in line with the stated objective of freeing hostages or eliminating Hamas, however dangerously vague such a purpose may be. After all, it is enough to think about it for a moment: Who is Hamas? Those who fought for Hamas in 2006? Those who worked in the hospitals under its authority? Who are resisting the occupation? Who are opposing genocide?

#### These kinds of motivations may very well exist in earnest, in the minds of Israeli leaders or of the hundreds of thousands of soldiers, often very young, who carry out their orders. But it is important to understand that they have nothing to do with what, in the identification of the crime of genocide, is called “intent,” or in legal jargon mens rea. *The intent to destroy must be understood as a determination to destroy. When the destructive idea is conceived and formulated against a group as such, whatever the reasons — even if it is an alleged legitimate defense — we are in* the category of genocide.

#### Genocide is a very serious crime, which should not be possible in the present era, given the guarantees and preventive mechanisms that exist in the various legal systems, both national and international. Instead, this is exactly what has been committed by Israel, conceived by its leaders and carried out by its soldiers, with the complicity of too many Western politicians and with the hateful connivance of the mainstream media, which has denied, watered down, and transfigured reality in order not to disturb the dictates of the Israeli embassies and the very powerful networks in support of Israel, “the last frontier of the West.”

#### The destruction of a group as such, when it is not accidental, not a mere “incident of war,” however brutal it may be, but an intentional act, constitutes genocide. This intentional destruction has been practiced on the body, on the collective life, on the spirit of the Palestinians — on their skin. Gaza has been the theater, certainly the most ferocious. The most horrible.

#### —

#### I AM AFRAID OF A SOCIETY in which the news coverage of killing, mutilation, torture, rape, hunger, and famine depends on who is the victim and who is the perpetrator. I have asked myself about this many times during my years as Special Rapporteur, in which I have often found myself at the center of discussions on the meaning of “impartiality.”

#### When human lives are at stake, impartiality becomes a duty that forces us to put ourselves on the side of the law, justice, and victims. Being impartial means having the courage to stand up for what is right, to give a voice to those who have been silenced or are simply ignored, and to fight against the abuses that torment our world.

#### Impartiality is not about pretending not to have an opinion in the face of atrocities, or about assuming you have to maintain an equidistant position between two opposing parties, even if their positions are structurally and historically unequal and when there is one party that is occupying, plundering, and oppressing while the other is being occupied, plundered, and oppressed, triggering disastrous mechanisms of violence.

#### How is it that truth has become a lie and a lie the truth? To this rampant evil, which would like us all to be entangled or simply defeated, we must respond with

#### conscious awareness and action. Knowledge is a fundamental weapon, because knowledge is the best defense against manipulation, exploitation, and deception; and action should flow from it naturally.

#### So wherein lies the possibility of salvation for all of us, for the Palestinians as well as the Israelis? I can see it, if only in my mind’s eye, but I see it, and I also see the shape of the path that leads us there. In addition, I know that this vision is truly shared: All of the people who since the beginning of the genocide have recognized in me a hope, a light, a point of reference, have given me a strength that I would never have imagined. Despite lawsuits and death threats, despite the fear that something could backfire on what you hold most dear in the world, fighting for a just cause is a command that some of us are not equipped to disobey.

#### I strongly believe in the possibility of coming together as a human family, rediscovering the true and profound *meaning of solidarity; the Latin term solidum expresses precisely the idea of a “one and the same”: something* whole, undivided, complete, often in opposition to what is fragmented or broken. And so, as one body, we should be able to come together and resist. Solidarity, in these terms, becomes a “political form of love,” as the American rabbi Alissa Wise sagely observed.

#### Alone we are as fragile as the wings of a butterfly, but united — solid and supportive — we can create a storm. This is not just fanciful hyperbole; it is a principle of physics that is called the butterfly effect. Every little gesture of ours is a flutter of wings that triggers a chain of consequences, like the gesture of Mary, one of the many cashiers in one of the many shops in an Irish city, who refused to pass through her register the South African grapefruit selected by a customer. How can we believe that her choice could have an impact on the overthrow of apartheid in a country so far away? Yet we must believe it, because history teaches us that this can happen.

#### It is in the interconnection of the struggles for emancipation and freedom — individual or collective — that we *must rediscover our solidum. Together, we can tackle any challenge.*

#### *So let’s flap our wings, let’s create a storm, or rather, as they say where I come from, let’s make ammuìna!*

# HIND

#### *What is childhood in Palestine?*

#### Not to be frightened any more. That’s the final aim of man. *— ITALO CALVINO, The Path to the Spiders’ Nests*

#### END OF JANUARY 2024. Hind Rajab is six years old. She is curled up in the backseat of her uncle’s car, hunched together with four cousins. As soon as the umpteenth evacuation order arrived in the western area of Gaza, her mother and brothers fled on foot, but since it is raining and cold, her uncles have put her in the car with them.

#### It is early afternoon; the exploding bombs can be heard even inside the car, which seems to be stuck in a traffic jam. Something is not right. The uncles sense that, they’re agitated, talking frenetically. Not far from a gas station near Tel al-Hawa, the car happens onto a barrage of fire from Israeli artillery. Then a surreal cold. Hind looks around: No one is talking, and they are all slumped over. With her hands surely shaking, she takes the phone from between the fingers of her fifteen-year-old cousin Layan, who was hit while she was talking to the relief workers from the Red Crescent. Hind explains that “the others are dead or maybe they’re sleeping” and begs for help. “The tank is right next to me. It’s moving. Will you come to get me? I’m so afraid.”

#### On the other end of the line, the aide — struggling to control her fear, because she knows the risk that Hind is *facing — answers with affection, “Habibti“ (Honey), and stays on the phone with her so she won’t be alone.*

#### After three hours on the phone — the time it took her colleagues from the Red Crescent to coordinate with the Israeli authorities to locate the car and get permission to rescue the little girl — the aide reassures Hind that two rescuers are on their way to help her. The recording of that heartrending conversation, with the little girl’s life hanging by a thread, has been conserved for history and hopefully, one day, for the judges who will punish those responsible for the massacre in which Hind was killed by the Israeli army.

#### Twelve days later, Hind’s lifeless body would be found in the car that was riddled with more than three hundred bullet holes, not far from the ambulance that contained the dead bodies of her rescuers, who had been killed by the Israeli army. The investigation by the British team from Forensic Architecture led by Eyal Weizman, after reconstructing the distances and the dynamics of the gunfire, demonstrated that it is “not plausible” that the Israeli soldiers who shot at the car from the tank could not have seen that the car was occupied by civilians, including the little girls.

#### —

#### HIND’S STORY has become a symbol of the brutality of the Israeli assault on the population of Gaza in the days following October 7, 2023. But Hind was killed more than three months after October 7th, when Israel had already killed ten thousand children. How is it possible to tolerate all this killing? And how is it possible that still today — as I am completing the revision of this book at the end of August 2025 — when the number of dead children has come to exceed twenty thousand, of whom more than one thousand were less than one year old, that impunity continues to reign and the death machine set in motion by Israel has not been stopped?

#### The answer lies in decades of narrative manipulation that has distorted the perception of the balance of power between Israelis and Palestinians.

#### In recent decades, this narrative has led many to believe that the Palestinians are to blame for their situation, that they are an existential threat to Israel. Even the children? Yes, even them, and maybe especially them, because in the logic of the Israeli assault begun on October 7th, every Palestine life is seen as a potential future danger to the survival of Israel.

#### Hind’s story, as atrocious as it is, is not an unusual one in Palestine. Mohammed Tamimi was two years old

#### when, a few months before October 7, 2023, the Israeli occupation forces — formally known as the Israel Defense Forces — shot him in the head while he was in a car with his father in the occupied West Bank. No one has been held responsible, as usual.

#### This is childhood in Palestine.

#### —

#### IN JERUSALEM, next to the garden of the house where my Max and I lived, there was a small hill with a huge, incredible, generous mulberry tree, which bore fruit for months on end. A purple carpet of fallen mulberries always formed under that tree, and children often came to gather them.

#### Just below the house there was a low stone wall with a piece of metal fencing, which must have been added to the wall years before, temporarily, but had been left in place. The children, by repeatedly slipping under the fence to come and get mulberries, had made their own passageway. One fine day, I saw them and said: “Hi guys, when you want mulberries, if you knock on my door I’ll open it, so you don’t have to go under the fence.” Most of them didn’t understand me, because almost none of them spoke English, except for a little boy with dark eyes, whom I had already noticed in the area with his friends and twin sister.

#### “Hi,” I repeated then, addressing him directly. “I know you are from this neighborhood, I have seen you playing a lot of times. When you want mulberries, don’t worry, just call us, so you don’t risk hurting yourselves by slipping under the fence.”

#### His answer, respectful but firm, left me stunned. “No, thank you,” he told me. “There’s no need to leave the gate open for us. We will continue to take them like

#### this, slipping under the fence, as we have always done.” At eleven, little Mohammed already seemed very assertive to me. His family had been one of the first in the

#### Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood to have their house expropriated by Israeli settlers — armed civilians who populate the colonies (“settlements” in common parlance)[\*] in the West Bank and East Jerusalem with the support of the army. Rifqa, the grandmother of Mohammed and his twin sister, Muna, had taken refuge there in 1948 after being driven out of Haifa (now in Israel). At the end of a long legal battle, in 2009 the main complex of their property was occupied by Israeli settlers, while the El-Kurd family had to build, in the garden, an extension of the house where all the family members were forced to live.

#### Mohammed’s reaction surprised me, because it is not obvious that a child of eleven — or seven, twelve, fourteen — has that kind of awareness of their rights, of their space, their identity. But for the Palestinians who have grown up under occupation, as well as for the millions of them born in the refugee camps scattered throughout Palestine, that’s how it is. Generations of people have grown up seeing their land, day after day, continuously pulled out from under their feet like a carpet, fueling an endless struggle for housing, for dignity, for everything that should be taken for granted in childhood. Palestinians have their childhood stripped away from them, they become adults with the bodies of children already burdened by worries, anxieties, fears, responsibilities that should not be part of their lives at that age.

#### That is why, as UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, I decided in 2023 to dedicate my third report to children, using a word from the English language that vividly describes the Palestinian *reality: unchilding, or “deprived of childhood.” The choice of this theme was rooted in the hope that showing what* life was really like for a child in Palestine, along with statistical and legal information, could help the public better understand the gravity of the situation.

#### When I conducted my research, everything was different from today: The report was presented two weeks after October 7, 2023, but it had been finished two weeks earlier. The situation was already terrible.

#### At that point in the autumn, the figures for Palestinian children killed by Israel in fifteen years (from 2008 to September 2023) were brutal: more than one thousand four hundred. Each of them, a small universe erased forever. From October 7, 2023 to March 2025, these already gruesome numbers have increased tenfold.

#### In Gaza, in August 2024, Mohammed Abu al-Qumsan was requesting birth certificates for his three-day-old twins, when he received a call: Your apartment has been bombed, your children and your wife are in the hospital. There was nothing that could be done for them. Dead before even opening their eyes to life.

#### This is childhood, in Palestine.

#### —

#### IN 2023, not having received the necessary authorizations from the Israeli government to conduct my research in the Occupied Palestinian Territory in preparation of the report for the UN General Assembly of that autumn, I decided

#### to take an alternative approach. With the support of Palestinian civil society and other collaborators, we created focus groups that allowed me to interview Palestinian children online.

#### At the time, I was on vacation with my family in Sicily, with my children’s grandparents (my in-laws). Every afternoon, after having lunch with my children and taking a quick dip in the sea, I got ready to go up to the beachclub terrace, where, with my computer plugged into one of the few available power sockets, I began the meetings that lasted for several hours.

#### The groups of children and adolescents interviewed soon proved to be well structured and disciplined. Divided by age and geographical location, both my young interlocutors and their parents and companions were enthusiastic to have the opportunity to share their experiences and accounts with me. Gathered around a table, or sitting on chairs sometimes taller than they were (as for the children in Jenin), they were all very attentive in front of the screen. Somebody translated, even though, especially in Gaza, most of the children spoke English well and so I could interact directly, without the need for mediation.

#### Those encounters put me in front of an authentic miracle of life, vitality, and tenderness, a setting in which energy and hope seemed to persist despite adversity. In the midst of all the difficulties of the permanent occupation, of the incessant wars in Gaza, where the de facto state of siege made everyone prisoners of a ghetto, along with the devastating proximity of Israeli colonies in the West Bank, and constant attacks by soldiers and settlers, the children I met that summer demonstrated an extraordinary ability to preserve fundamental values. Above all, their love for school. And then their manners and care for their appearance, especially in front of strangers. The boys wore elegant shirts for the occasion with their hair well combed and stiffened with gel, and the girls were in colorful dresses, their long hair gathered in a scarf or hanging free down to their shoulders; their voices spoke to me of a great thirst for knowledge and a burning desire for the future.

#### This, too, is childhood in Palestine.

#### —

#### ONE ASPECT THAT STRUCK ME DEEPLY, especially in the beginning, taught me something about myself and the prejudices that we sometimes involuntarily carry with us: The children were extremely prepared when it came to less personal and more general topics. Whether they were talking about problems related to water supply, education, or freedom of movement, they talked about the violations they suffered with a language so precise and assertive that it seemed almost artificial, constructed. “They sound like little lawyers,” I thought. But I soon realized that there was nothing strange about their ability to argue and interact. “They are not my children, who go to school, play, and lead a protected and cushioned life,” I told myself, realizing that those kids were used to hurtful and scary experiences, so it was understandable that for them talking about human rights could turn into a cry for life, an impassioned demand for answers.

#### How is it possible that this is happening to us, when on paper so many rights should be guaranteed for everyone? It is a question that resonates strongly among Palestinian children, a call to a justice that often seems to be unreachable. While my eight-year-old son has to worry only about memorizing the multiplication tables, the children of Palestine learn and speak the language of law to express their claim to their lives, their humanity. So, paradoxically, it was precisely because they had to defend their right to exist, to be children, that at times they became their own advocates, carrying an incredible burden on their shoulders.

#### An ancient burden, which has been borne by their society for generations: It is for this reason, I believe, that in their innocence they also demonstrated such a deep-seated awareness of injustice. It takes superhuman courage for a child to face the awareness of oppression: that state of permanent war, being separated from all the other Palestinians in the world, not being able to travel, or even dream about the simplest things in life.

#### For me, on those Sicilian summer days it was paradoxical to move a few meters from the world around me — a world in which my most important questions were “Have the children eaten?,” “What have they been doing?,” “Who is fighting with whom?,” “Who has eaten two ice creams behind my back?”—to spend every afternoon with the children of Gaza City, Khan Yunis, Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Nablus, Ramallah, or Masafer Yatta, and let myself be absorbed in another, completely different dimension.

#### On some rare occasions it also happened that my son, Giordano, who was six years old at the time, with the spontaneity typical of his age, would come over to see who I was talking to, unmindful of being in a bathing suit. I remember that one day a child asked me: “Why isn’t he dressed?”

#### “Because we are at the seaside,” I replied. But that day I was talking with children who had never been to the sea, who had been trapped in the West Bank since they were born. We had many more meetings with children living in the West Bank than with those in the Gaza Strip, because the logistics were more difficult in Gaza: It was difficult, for example, to organize buses to pick them up or have them accompanied by their parents, often because

#### of the hundreds of checkpoints, fixed and mobile, created by the Israeli army to “monitor” the movements of Gazans. We had to organize many different dates, each with groups of only four or five children whose members often changed from time to time. They would be waiting for me, sitting composed, excited, and prepared with what they wanted to tell me. I let them speak. I had already collected data on wars, attacks, the destruction of houses, hospitals, schools, evictions, killings, arrests, and so I wanted them above all to talk about their lives: their homes, their games, their travels, their families, so that the report I was drawing up would be “theirs,” and speak, as much as possible, in their voices.

#### The focus groups never lasted less than a couple of hours; toward the end, after we had gotten to know each other for a while, I felt ready to ask, “Is there anything that scares you?” Inevitably, everyone talked about death. The greatest fear of these children was of dying or losing their parents. Second on the list, being arrested; third, “that they’ll knock down my house.” These are the most frequent fears of Palestinian children. This is how they grow up. That alone seems to me to be an unfathomable brutality.

#### “We have to fight for the right to breathe, to stay here, to stay in our land without having to suffer every day,” said Rawan, eleven years old. And Aladdin, fourteen: “We always have to run away from some danger, if it’s not the soldiers, it’s the settlers.”

#### In the descriptions of the children and young people I spoke to, I heard an infinite number of stories where violence and fear were expressed in myriad ways: the violence of checkpoints, the loss of Dad’s job, being slapped, beaten, stripped naked in public, the threats of someone taking your land or forcing your parents to humiliate themselves, the suffering for the lack of parents at home, because, if they are arrested or killed, then you have to grow up with some relative, near or far, who certainly loves you, but is neither Mom nor Dad.

#### That’s what Palestinian children’s daily lives were like, even before October 7, 2023. “They were bombing us from all sides, they were everywhere, we were very afraid that our parents could die,” Yasmine, sixteen, told me, who at that point had already experienced five wars in Gaza. And this is the story of Samer, eleven years old: “My father was killed near a settlement by soldiers. They said he was violent…Not only did I lose the most important person in my life but they also came to take our house. First I became an orphan, then they left me homeless.” Fares, age twelve, said: “Last year the soldiers attacked my school three or four times. They launched tear gas canisters and fired live ammunition. Many of the teachers and my classmates couldn’t breathe.”

#### This is childhood in Palestine.

#### —

#### UNFORTUNATELY, this is not the only thing that steals the childhood of Palestinian children. The violence of which *they are witnesses as well as victims is not only brutally sudden but also — just as brutally — systemic: something* that makes its way into the daily life of every person and outlines its contours. When I wrote the report on children, we also counted the children who were injured and maimed for life; the children of parents who died, were injured, or maimed; and all the people, including adults and children, who were traumatized. These numbers take your breath away, but at the same time they mean nothing, so much so that the Palestinians have been rebelling for years against the risk of trivializing statistics: An organization of young writers founded in Gaza by the academic and poet Refaat Alareer is called We Are Not Numbers. This organization was constituted in opposition to the destruction of the culture, image, and hopes of the Palestinians of Gaza, threatened by the permanent occupation. By the permanent conflict.

#### It is the entire way of life of the Palestinians — especially the youngest — that seems to be on the precipice, ready to be destroyed. Take, for example, their existential spaces.

#### For all children, the home should be the center of their childhood, a safe haven where they can grow, explore, and dream; but in Palestine the certainty of protection is not found even within the walls of their homes. The expropriation and destruction of houses have become a tool of Israeli occupation, so those who grow up in this reality are forced to live with an “unbelonging” imposed from outside. Every apartment building razed to the ground is not just a demolished structure but a piece of life, history, and past erased, and a mortgaged future, which irreparably marks the soul of the youngest. This violence inflicts a deep wound, a loss that transcends materiality, severing bonds, fragmenting communities, and casting the shadow of a precarious existence on the innocence of youth.

#### Israeli settler colonialism, designed to progressively (and illegally) annex what remains of Palestinian territory, is not limited to this but creates a coercive environment that undermines the possibilities of growth and development. Children and their families are pushed into poverty, as they are denied basic resources such as water and electricity. Spatial segregation and the restrictions imposed by the occupation prevent them from accessing adequate education and medical care, both in Gaza (even before the current attacks) and in the West Bank.

#### The occupation, therefore, affects every aspect of Palestinian life. In the occupied territory, punitive demolitions and forced evictions leave many families homeless, condemning children to live a childhood marked by anxiety and uncertainty. The isolated Gaza Strip — a veritable open-air prison for sixteen years, before its recent total destruction — and the repeated military attacks have for years destroyed essential infrastructure, forcing millions of people to depend on humanitarian aid. Generations of children have not only witnessed the loss of their homes and land, their family and friends, but have internalized the trauma of seeing their own people constantly humiliated and deprived of a livelihood and dignity.

#### Today’s Palestinian children, who make up almost half of Gaza’s population, have lived their entire lives under occupation, like their parents before them. A system that for generations has deprived them of fundamental rights such as self-determination, life, security, dignity, and development, transforming every day of their childhood into a struggle not to succumb. These children grow up surrounded by violence, seeing their homes demolished, their schools destroyed, and their land confiscated. The images of children moving through the rubble of their homes, picking up toys and pieces of books that escaped the bulldozers, or consoling their despairing parents, are etched in my memory.

#### In that summer of more than two years ago, which now seems so far away, in addition to the focus groups with children, I interviewed adults who were minors at the time of the first and second intifadas and who in the meantime had become parents or even grandparents. One thing that was clear is how much more aggressive the occupation has become. Ahmed, now an actor and educator, told me: “At least, when we were little, at the time of the first intifada, we could go running in the hills. Now there is the wall. There are too many checkpoints. Now we don’t even have the room to run.”

#### Over the years, the expansion of the Israeli settlements has been constant: from the Oslo Accords in the 1990s to the construction of the wall in the early 2000s, to the continual violent attacks in the West Bank, the space in which the Gazans can live has progressively shrunk and fragmented.

#### The children have been deprived even of the space to imagine. They are trapped. This made me aware of another crucial element of the occupation: the aesthetics of imprisonment. Growing up under Israeli occupation is like growing up in an open-air prison, made up of checkpoints, control towers, settlements that observe from on high what is left of the territory, armed guards that enforce their version of order at every presumed threat. The violence that is suffered in this space is not only physical but also psychological. I think of the children I have known, and I imagine that many of them will end up leaving their homeland, where there seem to be no horizons anymore, and where their dreams are smothered by the brutality of the occupation.

#### In this open-air prison the numbers of arrests of Palestinian minors is also chilling: Between 2000 and 2023, more than thirteen thousand minors were detained, arrested, and imprisoned; and since October 2023 there have already been more than three hundred. Arrests are carried out under any pretext, like the case recounted by fourteen-year-old Abir: “A [Palestinian] boy was walking down the street. The soldiers stopped and searched him, beat him, and finally arrested him because he refused to take off his trousers during the search.” Having witnessed myself innumerable similar abuses and harassment of Palestinians by the Israeli army or police, none of that horror was new to me. But it hurts to hear it recounted by someone so young.

#### When I was organizing the focus groups with Palestinian boys and girls, violence at checkpoints and armed raids night and day by the Israeli army in Palestinian villages were regular events. Israeli soldiers themselves, for example, members of Breaking the Silence — an organization of former Israeli soldiers who publicly denounce the abuses of the Israeli army in the occupied territory — candidly acknowledged that they had orders to invade the villages, sometimes every night for weeks on end, if not months. Their objective was to exhaust the population and to convince them to leave, in the name of “Israeli security.”

#### —

#### TO THIS STRUCTURAL VIOLENCE that invades people’s homes and threatens their safety and dignity every day, we must add the eruptive violence of wars, pogroms by armed settlers (more and more numerous in the West Bank), and military attacks.

#### On closer inspection, for all Palestinians, including the younger segments of the population, protection is a chimera: It is not available from institutions or elsewhere. Children grow up with the constant, terrible exposure to violence and the whole of society is afflicted by it. There is a very heavy intergenerational trauma, which I witnessed when I met the young people who had been detained. They were traumatized. Even those who are later given rehabilitative care and are able to improve bear deep emotional wounds forever. Some go back to school, but it’s very difficult, because if you get out of prison too early it means that you have squealed, and you are ostracized from your community. If, on the other hand, you resist for six months, a year, two years, at that point you are a hero.

#### But if you get out, your parents probably had to pay for your release. It is not normal to grow up in a system like this. When people ask themselves, “Where does the violence come

#### from?,” all they have to do to understand is broaden their vision and put aside their prejudices. The year 2023 had been very violent: There had been at least seventeen assaults on Palestinian villages by

#### settlers, ending with cars and houses burned, and Palestinians killed. I remember a twelve-year-old boy who lost his sister during a military attack in Jenin in the summer of 2023. The city had been under siege for days, and his sister had been killed in the backyard by the Israeli army. Everyone in the Jenin focus groups had told me about this girl, about the void she had left in the refugee camp where she grew up, in the Freedom Theatre of which she was a part. That theater, which has given itself the name of Freedom, is an institution that allows children in a high-tension area to explore their creativity, to express what they carry inside. “How much pain can such small bodies hold inside?” I thought while that child told me, lucid and composed, the story of his sister killed almost before his eyes.

#### —

#### LAILA MOHAMMED AYMAN KHATIB was two years old and was having dinner at home with her family when an Israeli soldier shot her in the back of the head. It happened in January 2025. How many newspapers wrote about it? Almost none, because the life (and death) of Palestinians seems to have no place or voice in our (Western) societies.

#### Furthermore, this is how Israel plants the seeds of hatred among the Palestinians, and it seems incredible to me that this is not understood.

#### Yet another of the things that deeply struck me on those summer afternoons of 2023 is the strong sense of discipline, resilience, and mutual respect that was felt in the focus groups in Gaza. There were councils for the rights of minors, nongovernmental organizations that had created meeting spaces where children could discuss the situations they were experiencing, the deprivations they suffered. I remember an exchange between two little girls who were arguing gently. One said: “It’s true that the closure and state of siege are terrible for everyone, but at least you, with leukemia, were able to go to the West Bank and see the mountains! I have never seen the mountains.”

#### Illness is another of the themes that often emerged in my dialogue with children. In Gaza, for example, even before the genocide, the land was polluted, overpopulated, full of the remains of unexploded ordnance, the water undrinkable. Contamination was everywhere and the number of people suffering from leukemia and cancer, even among minors, was very high. Several reports by the United Nations and other humanitarian organizations have documented tragic situations where children in Gaza, as young as four or five years old, have been forced to travel alone to receive medical care in the West Bank. Their parents did not have permission to accompany them. These restrictions are part of Israel’s broader security measures for the population of Gaza since 2007 and have had a devastating impact on all types of Palestinian mobility. Gaza lacked adequate health care facilities, forcing many families to seek medical care elsewhere. Not only did this practice put children’s safety at risk but it also caused enormous emotional stress to both the young patients and their families, who were forced to separate at times of great vulnerability. But usually the Palestinians are extremely supportive: There was always someone to welcome them, a friend, a relative, a member of a humanitarian organization.

#### This is childhood in Palestine. *Or rather, it was, when the children I spoke to were all still alive and Gaza was teeming with life. Now there is*

#### no longer anything that has not been dismembered by the war: from homes to neighborhoods and landscapes, from families to individual lives. The Gaza that those kids were telling me about in 2023 no longer exists and a large part of the West Bank that I knew is being destroyed as I write these pages. Although those who have so far survived the slaughter want to rebuild, what remains is rubble, and the dust has not yet settled in Gaza. After more than five hundred days of almost uninterrupted bombing, in fact, the bombs continue to rain down.

#### Right in the middle of the genocide of the Palestinians that began in October 2023, during a conference we held together in London, I heard Dr. Ghassan Abu Sitta recount: “Children are arriving, dead, torn to pieces, seriously injured. I would ask about their medical history and no one knew anything. They were not the children of their rescuers. The parents had been killed.”

#### This, too, is childhood in Palestine.

#### —

#### GROWING UP IN PALESTINE means being a child in a climate of constant fear and insecurity, surrounded by the violence of settlers and soldiers.

#### So I understood that it was not so surprising that the children in my focus groups behaved like adults and claimed their rights even when they spoke to me. I told them: “I’m here to listen to you and I really want my report

#### to the UN to be yours and that everything I report speaks with your voice. I don’t know if it will change anything.” In the end it turned out to be even worse. Much worse than we could have ever feared or imagined.

#### “But that’s all I can promise.” Along with everything else, I also remember that summer as the first moment when I felt questioned by my own

#### children: “Why do you spend so much time with the children on the computer and not with us?” I realized how strange it was for them, and I tried to answer, almost certain that I would not be understood, but at least for future memory: “Because, if I were the mother of a child living in a situation like that of those children on the computer, I would really like there to be someone else capable of helping me. And if I were her, I would think that my children, too, those who live in Palestine, have the right to the same things as the children of this other mother: those who are now at the seaside, they walk around all day half naked and, at most, they can be afraid of getting a sea urchin’s spine in their foot or arguing with a friend about who came in first in the race to the buoy.”
