#### It was as if on either side of that computer screen — where on one side there were those sharp and prepared children and on the other those who were enjoying their carefree holidays — I could hear the voices from inside and voices from outside: only some days it became difficult to tell them apart.

#### A little over a year later I was at home, in Tunis. It was afternoon and outside the window, a few meters from me, I could see Giordano jumping rope and laughing; meanwhile, on my laptop, were images of a mother from Gaza running desperately toward her house, where her son was burning alive.

#### This is childhood in Palestine.

#### —

#### THE PROTECTION OF CHILDREN should be at the center of any debate on the so-called “Palestinian question,” in an effort to guarantee every child the right to grow up protected, in a framework of safety, dignity, and freedom.

#### Instead, in that situation, it is not only Palestinian children who grow up in a totally unjust system, which constantly exposes them to violence, but Israeli children, too. In the end, they are victims too, because, as the Israeli philologist Nurit Peled-Elhanan argues, being educated from an early age to fear and suspect the Other, to normalize violence, to perpetuate a worldview based on racial domination and oppression, shared by the ideology of their political leaders and often even their own parents, was not a choice.

#### But children grow up, and the children of today are the adults of tomorrow. If there is one thing that generations of Palestinians can teach us, it is that their people do not bow to the occupation and they resist, as best they can and as best they know how. They did it against the British who were selling off their land in 1936–1939. They did so in the late 1980s, at the outbreak of the first uprising against the occupation (the first intifada), when the killing of four Palestinians in an incident with an Israeli military truck in the Jabalia refugee camp in the Gaza Strip triggered demonstrations throughout the occupied territory. They did so during the second intifada that broke out in 2000, and which, unlike the first, was marked by lethal violence on the part of the Palestinians. The resistance has continued in a generally peaceful way, but not always. And unfortunately, the more violent and hateful the oppression, the more the force that aims to remove it risks being violent. Like October 7th, an unprecedented horror for Israelis, marked by the sheer ferocity of the attack and the shocking scale of crimes committed against civilians. I have strongly condemned these acts, because while international law recognizes the right to resist oppressive occupation, apartheid, and annexation, it cannot justify targeting civilians.

#### My choice not to dwell on October 7th here is deliberate, and for two reasons. First, the pain and suffering of Israeli victims, survivors, and their families has been widely documented and continues to be so in the West. By contrast, the suffering of Palestinians — and the structural injustice that underpins it — is often obscured, minimized, or ignored.

#### Second, the violence of October 7th, even stripped of the grotesque distortions and fabricated atrocities that Western corporate media have added, has been wielded to depict Palestinians as an existential threat to Israel and to justify the widespread and ongoing violence against them wherever they live.

#### Palestinians have always wanted to lead their own emancipation from occupation and apartheid. This collective determination has taken an increasingly concrete and decisive form over time: for example, during the great protest movement of 2021, after yet another wave of harassment and abuse that had massively targeted Palestinian residents of Jerusalem. At the head of this protest were many young people from Sheikh Jarrah — the neighborhood where I had lived — including twins Mohammed and Muna. When, years later, I had the opportunity to read about them, their faces seemed familiar to me, but in that moment I couldn’t connect them to anything precise; only later, seeing the photos of Mohammed El-Kurd as a child, did I realize that I knew him: He was that little boy who came to play and pick mulberries in front of our house, and who even as a child, with his rejoinders in perfect English, stood eye to eye with a thirty-year-old foreigner.

#### Today Mohammed El-Kurd is a journalist, a writer, one of the strongest Palestinian voices in defense of his people. This is one of his verses: “I wasn’t a victim / until the world told me I was.”

#### —

#### IN PALESTINE, childhood is a story of victims, of fear, of minors stripped of their right to grow up safe and protected, although many parents do their utmost to let their children live a life that is somehow serene and to give them a *sense of normality, a bit like Roberto Benigni’s film Life Is Beautiful, even within a reality that is not beautiful. A* reality where, today, many of the children and young people I met in the course of my personal and professional experience in Palestine are dead. A reality where it can happen that a person’s life is extinguished at the age of six inside a car riddled by hundreds of bullets, as happened to Hind.

#### Today the Hind Rajab Foundation, an organization that is committed to taking legal action against those responsible for or complicit in war crimes and crimes against humanity in Palestine, is named after her.

#### This is very important, yet it does not erase death and suffering, and it does not erase fear. Just as fourteen-year-old Ouadia told me: “Being afraid of death doesn’t stop you from dying; it prevents you

#### from living.” This is childhood in Palestine.

SKIP NOTES

* While the term “settlement” is commonly used to refer to the cities and towns only for Jewish Israelis, erected in occupied Palestine since 1967, I prefer to call them “colonies,” as in Italian or French. That term defines them more precisely as part of a colonization project, centered around the transfer of the colonizer’s population to the colonized territory, a war crime according to international law.

# ABU HASSAN

#### *What are the consequences of the occupation?*

#### Our houses to others The women widowed Stones scattered at the entrance of the road. — CCCP – FEDELI ALLA LINEA, “Palestina”

#### IN JERUSALEM he is an institution, and he was the first Palestinian that Max and I met upon our arrival in the Holy City. It was at the time of my second interview with the legal department of UNRWA, for a job that would change my life forever. After we moved there, we got together with him regularly. He was a pillar of many of our experiences and choices, yet I do not remember his real name. Everyone has always called him Abu Hassan.

#### In the Arab world of the Levant, putting Abu or Umm before someone’s proper name is a way of recognizing the passage from adolescence to maturity, generally marked by the arrival of children (and the acquisition of the name of the first son or daughter), since Abu means “father of” and Umm “mother of.” For example, our Arab friends, jokingly, call Max “Abu Leila” and me “Umm Leila.”

#### —

#### IT WAS IN 2010 that we first set foot in Jerusalem, and Max and I, both curious travelers, took the opportunity to explore the city. Of course, we knew some things about it, but we had no idea what was waiting for us. So much so that the first thing we did was take a classic tour of old Jerusalem accompanied by Israeli guides, who took us to see the Western Wall, underground Jerusalem, the Silwan district…

#### I remember that right there, in Silwan, we visited a part of the underground city and at one point one of the guides said to us: “See? On these rocks there are still the signs of the Exodus of the Jewish people!” We were quite *doubtful; before leaving home Max had read Israeli historian Shlomo Sand’s The Invention of the Jewish People,* and that day at lunch we had discussed the possibility that the Israelis would use this kind of narrative about archaeology as part of “their own colonial work,” in an attempt to prove that they were already there two thousand years ago (what was meant at that time by “colonial work” was rather nebulous). The biblical presence of Jewish populations in the land of Israel, that is, more than two thousand years ago, is one of the key arguments used to defend Israel’s right as a Jews-only state, for those who had returned to the land from which they had been driven out some nineteen hundred years earlier. For many people, this somehow justifies the endless occupation and all the other atrocities that have been committed against the Palestinian people every day for decades: “We have come back and now you must all go away, usurpers.”

#### We were having lunch at the Jerusalem Hotel (another institution that is located on the edge of the Old City), where we were chatting with a person who worked there. We were telling him how surprised we were by the tour we had just taken and that it had seemed like some sort of archaeological propaganda. He appeared unruffled by our frustration and left. A few minutes later, he came back and handed us the business card of Abu Hassan, the owner of Alternative Tours. He told us to contact him, as he would show us Jerusalem under a very different light than what standard Israeli guides do.

#### Abu Hassan was right around the corner. When he wasn’t working as a guide, he spent most of his time at Mihbash, a café located on the first floor of a historic building, a stone’s throw from the hotel. As soon as we entered, we were greeted by a whiff of fried food and smoke. The place was really kitsch, yet we immediately felt at home: Shortly thereafter, in fact, it would become our hangout in Jerusalem. We asked for Abu Hassan, introduced ourselves to him, and asked if he had time to take us on a tour in the following days. We arranged to go with him the

#### next day. To begin with, he took us to places in Jerusalem where families were divided by the wall and children had to

#### crawl through sewage pipes to go to school because of the obstacles put in place by Israel. He gave us the lowdown on the archaeological tours like the one we had taken the day before. Thanks to him we met a priest who had been trained as an archaeologist and who explained to us in detail how much political-ideological manipulation there was behind that kind of historical narrative. Then Abu Hassan took us to see the houses that the settlers had just taken from the Palestinians in the Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood, throwing out those who lived there (including the family of Mohammed El-Kurd), along with most of the furniture and personal property: refrigerators, blankets, clothes, children’s notebooks…When we arrived, the Israeli religious settlers who were then living in one of the expropriated houses came out of the house and started throwing things at us, shouting: “Go away! Go away! This is a Jewish home.”

#### At the end of the tour, Abu Hassan took us all to lunch. Obviously at Mihbash. While we were eating, noticing how upset I was by what we had just seen, he asked me: “But why are you here?

#### Are you tourists?” “I came for a job interview,” I replied. “I’m hoping to move to Jerusalem to work with UNRWA.” He immediately thundered: “Those vultures from the UN! It was better here without you, because you don’t do

#### anything, your presence makes no difference, the only thing that’s happened since you’ve been here is that life has become more expensive for everyone.”

#### Feeling stung to the core, I reacted badly: “It’s not true! Because if they decide to take me for this job, someone who deals with human rights, it means that the organization wants to give them much more attention!”

#### I will never forget that my words provoked almost no reaction; all he did was look me straight in the eye and *ask: “But you, what do you want to do?”*

#### A question which, after so many years, I am perhaps still trying to answer. Within a few weeks, in fact, I was offered the position I had interviewed for, and so Max and I returned to

#### Jerusalem, this time on a permanent basis. Immediately we went to Mihbash to look for Abu Hassan, who was there as always. Whether it’s summer or winter, unless it’s raining or snowing, the first thing you see when you arrive at *Mihbash is his silhouette from behind, smoking shisha while looking at the Old City.*

#### Since that day we have done many other tours with him, and sent our visiting friends too. We have come to know him and through him we have understood so much about Palestinian culture. Abu Hassan had a privilege: As a Jerusalemite, he could move freely in both Palestine and Israel. The Palestinians, in fact, are divided according to four different legal identities: those with Israeli citizenship living in Israel (also known as Israeli Arabs, a nomenclature hated by the Palestinians, who prefer “Palestinians of ‘48”); residents of East Jerusalem, who are permanent residents but without Israeli citizenship; Palestinians in the West Bank; and Palestinians in the Gaza Strip — the last two groups generally hold identity cards, formally issued by the Palestinian National Authority (PNA) but de facto controlled by Israel, which regulates their issuance, renewal, and revocation, thus determining the holders’ rights to move, which is largely confined to the respective Gaza or West Bank enclaves for these groups, as well as the right to work and to access services. Each group has different rights, especially in terms of travel, access to services, and legal status and the status of Jerusalemites differs from that of residents in Gaza, the West Bank, or Israel. According to Amnesty International, “Under Israeli law, Palestinian residents of East Jerusalem are not Israeli citizens or residents of the West Bank. Instead, they receive precarious permanent residency status, which allows them to reside and work in the city, to benefit from social services provided by Israel’s National Insurance Institute and National Health Insurance, and to vote in municipal elections, but not in national elections.”

#### It was with Abu Hassan that — having passed yet another Israeli checkpoint — we made our first visit to Hebron. That day he explained to us how the city was divided into two with one part, called H1, formally governed by the PNA, while the other, H2, is under Israeli military control, with some areas of the Old City made inaccessible to the Palestinians. More than thirty thousand Palestinians live in H2, compared to the seven hundred Jewish settlers who have exclusive access to an area of the center. The trip to Hebron was part of a “consciousness-raising” tour whose first stop was the Ibrahimi Mosque/Tomb of the Patriarchs, a religious building, originally a mosque, that Israel had divided in two following a terrorist attack decades earlier.

#### In 1994 an Israeli American settler, Baruch Goldstein, entered that holy site in military uniform, armed with a machine gun, and exterminated twenty-nine Palestinians who were praying, wounding a hundred. At last, someone managed to stop him and he was overpowered and killed, but in addition to the carnage caused by his intrusion, this event sparked an uprising in the city: More than twenty Palestinians and four Israelis died in clashes with the Israeli army. Yet, the Israelis do not consider that a massacre, or more simply they don’t remember it. Following the events, Israel closed off Al-Shuhada Street (which means “the street of the martyrs”), the main commercial road leading to the mosque, and carved out part of the mosque to establish a synagogue. As a result, Muslims (who can

#### access the mosque only through a checkpoint for pedestrians) and Jews pray separately to the god of the same figure: Ibrahim for Muslims, Abraham for Jews.

#### Goldstein was given a solemn funeral and his tomb in the occupied West Bank is still a destination for pilgrims. In the decades since the beginning of the Israeli occupation, there have been many horrors like this for the Palestinians, but many people do not want to acknowledge them, as though they refuse to understand.

#### In Hebron there is also one of the last factories of keffiyehs still in operation: There are many beautiful ones, handwoven. Historically it was a city of merchants, also famous for ceramics and blown glass; today it has fallen in on itself, beaten down and exhausted.

#### Shuhada Street, once crowded and full of life, remains sealed off to this day. Palestinians can live there but not walk there. The doors of houses and shops have been walled up by the army, so many residents have built bridges to be able to pass from one house to another. You see scenes resembling the theater of the absurd: children, late for school, climbing over gates, being chased and reprimanded or beaten by soldiers.

#### —

#### ANOTHER TRIP WE TOOK with Abu Hassan was to Nablus in the northern West Bank. All Palestinian cities have a medina, the historic center enclosed by walls, but Nablus is unique because it is surrounded by mountains. It is very green and is famous for olive oil, which is also used to produce soap, and for knafeh, a traditional Palestinian dessert as well-known as it is delicious. “The one they make in Nablus is a magical thing,” several friends in Jerusalem had told me. And they were right. Knafeh is made with soft, sweet goat cheese, covered with kataifi pastry, a sort of phyllo in very long filaments, and drizzled with hot honey or syrup, rose or orange blossom water, cooked in huge round pans, then cut into diamonds or triangles and eaten within an hour of being baked, accompanied by tea. Even just seeing it prepared is an experience. In Nablus, we also had the opportunity to meet various people and talk with them to understand better, and more intimately, the reality of the place. For example, we met some former political prisoners who had been arrested only for protesting against soldiers, demanding freedom for their people, or participating in so-called “political activities.”

#### They were the ones who told us that the mayor of Nablus at the time, Adly Yaish, belonged to Hamas: an Islamic nationalist movement born in the 1980s from the political tradition of the Muslim Brotherhood during the first intifada. Over the years, Hamas has been both a form of armed resistance against the Israeli occupation and the apartheid system — through the al-Qassam Brigades, which are responsible for numerous tragic attacks against Israeli civilians and soldiers, culminating on October 7, 2023 — and a political party. In 2006, Hamas won the Palestinian legislative elections, overcoming Fatah, the rival party founded in the late 1950s by Yasser Arafat and other Palestinian exiles. After the election result was disavowed by the international community, violent clashes broke out between Hamas and Fatah, at the height of which, in 2007, Hamas took control of the Gaza Strip, which it still maintains today despite the rampant destruction, while Fatah governs the West Bank.

#### Abu Hassan also accompanied us on our first visit to the refugee camps of Balata and Jenin, in the northern West Bank, even before I went there for my work with the UNRWA. After the Palestinians were driven from their homes in 1948 by Jewish militias who later merged into the army of the newly formed State of Israel, Balata and Jenin became the largest refugee camps in the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Some of the displaced people from Galilee or the coast of Haifa moved to Lebanon, but many people settled in Balata and Jenin, waiting for the day when they could return home. The first generation lived mostly in tents, waiting for the fateful return. The second generation, on the other hand, was that of the resistance, of the fighters — the first to understand that no one would help them. Neither the neighboring Arab states nor the United Nations would ever pull them out of the camps, much less out of the grip of the occupation. The camps then became the cradle of armed resistance in the West Bank.

#### Palestinian resistance goes back to the time of the British Mandate. The resistance against Israel began in the late 1950s, when various movements were born, such as Fatah, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, and the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine, which then associated or federated into the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), becoming the core of the armed resistance. All these groups were strongly rooted in the refugee camps, which is why Balata and Jenin are among the areas ritually attacked by the Israeli army. We were able to see all this from the inside because the Jenin refugee camp still existed, although much of it had been destroyed by the Israeli army during the second intifada, and then, with great sacrifices, rebuilt. Since January 2025, the camp has been heavily struck by Israeli bombing, and in only a few weeks about twenty thousand people were left homeless.

#### —

#### WE TALKED AT LENGTH with Abu Hassan about Palestine pre- and post-1948, bonding more closely with him over

#### time. Our friendship was a process of symbiosis: He entered our lives, and we entered his, respecting each other, but also accepting that there were things that we instinctively did not understand at first. Abu Hassan, in fact, did not only take me to see the colonies in the West Bank; he accompanied me around the city of Jerusalem and helped me to distinguish which products came from the Israeli colonies and which didn’t, what was better to buy in supermarkets to support the Palestinians and what not to buy at all. After a year, I had a fairly precise idea of who were the ordinary traders and who were the “collaborators,” that is, those who did business with the Israeli occupation, which imposed the sale of products from the colonies by prohibiting the entry into Jerusalem of Palestinian goods produced in the West Bank. (As for products from Gaza, forget about it!)

#### When we moved to Jerusalem, Abu Hassan was one of the friends we consulted to find out which of the houses that were offered to us for rent had been taken from the Palestinians in 1948, so that we could avoid them.

#### In addition to the tours he took us on in the early days of our stay in Palestine, we always ran into him at Mihbash and wondered if the place was his. We would later discover, over the years, that it was not his, but it was practically a second home for him.

#### We were always happy to go there, and bring all our friends too, even though the food was nothing to write home about and the young people who waited tables did not seem particularly cut out for that work. It took me a while to understand that, if they sometimes behaved inhospitably, there was a reason — indeed, more than one. Not only did some of those young people come from traditional cultural backgrounds only to find themselves serving alcohol to or having to smile at people who were there, in their land, without truly understanding it or respecting it, but, on top of that, many of them came from terrible situations and had experienced great traumas that they still carried on their shoulders. In fact, the people who worked as cooks or waiters at Mihbash were generally not professionals but young people who came from difficult lives for whom that place offered their only opportunity.

#### Many Palestinians, often in the fragile age of childhood and adolescence, experience detention in Israeli prisons. Between 1967 and 2006, more than eight hundred thousand Palestinians, including children, were arrested and detained by Israel, and, obviously, job opportunities for those released from an Israeli prison are hard to come by. So Abu Hassan helped some of these young people find work in what was now his headquarters. This is one of the reasons for the dark clouds that accompanied some of the waiters at Mihbash.

#### For me, Max, and our closest friends and colleagues, the place was a refuge, and we were happy to adopt it as our hangout, because we also considered it a very practical way to make our small contribution to the difficult life of the Palestinians in East Jerusalem. It didn’t matter that the service was not up to Michelin Guide standards or that *the place smelled of fried food mixed with shisha, which was the argument sometimes used by our friends to get us* to go elsewhere: “Why do we always have to go to that place where when we come out our clothes stink?” But, in the end, one way or another, Max always managed to win them over.

#### —

#### AMONG THE VARIOUS TOPICS of our endless conversations, one of the most frequent was undoubtedly detention. Later on, when I was preparing to write my second report to the United Nations—”Arbitrary Deprivation of Liberty in the Occupied Palestinian Territory: The Palestinian Experience Behind and Beyond Bars” — I had the opportunity to do much more in-depth research on the subject, from which gruesome information emerged. In that report, presented to the Human Rights Council in July 2023, I defined the arbitrary and systematic deprivation of liberty as carcerality: a system of large-scale confinement that stifles every aspect of Palestinian life. As Israel had refused to grant me access to Palestine, for more than six months I conducted my investigation remotely to prepare the report, which revealed that this control is effected on three levels: physical (through checkpoints, walls, and the blockade of Gaza, transforming the whole area into an open prison), bureaucratic (with a system of restrictions that regulates and limits every movement), and digital (thanks to surveillance technologies that monitor the population constantly).

#### People are often jailed without charges or due process, and the Israeli judicial system, which applies the civil law to settlers in the colonies in the West Bank, applies military law to the Palestinians in the same area. Not to mention the absurd and degrading conditions to which children and young people are subjected, the special forms of violence and blackmail suffered by women and the LGBTQ+ community, or the widespread use of torture in prisons. This is the state of things: practices that are manifestly contrary to respect for human rights, and which should therefore be prosecuted as war crimes and crimes against humanity. A legal system that treats an entire population as a collective threat can have no legitimacy.

#### —

#### IN ADDITION TO the numbers of Palestinians arrested — frightening figures because, under any conditions, arrest and

#### imprisonment mark you forever — my investigation focused on the terrible reality of Israel’s detention of minors. The arrest of children is instrumental to repression and is one of the weapons that Israel uses to persecute the

#### Palestinians and deprive them of their fundamental rights. Persecution, that is, the “intentional and serious” deprivation of fundamental rights by virtue of one’s group identity, constitutes an international crime, recognized by the Rome Statute that established the International Criminal Court, which is responsible for crimes against humanity, war crimes, crimes of aggression, and genocide.

#### For a child, being arrested on charges such as throwing stones at Israeli soldiers, army vehicles, or settlers, and then being harassed and forced to provide information about the people of his city or neighborhood, is an experience that will mark him or her forever, triggering a series of life-changing consequences. First, exposure to such violence, moreover without the assistance of a parent or lawyer, leaves children alone and vulnerable: abused, threatened, slapped, beaten, deprived of the opportunity to defend themselves. They are often chained by their hands and feet to chairs for long periods of time, they feel pain, they cannot go to the bathroom, they defecate or urinate on themselves and are ridiculed for it.

#### It has happened several times that children have been put in isolation for more than two weeks. But UN standards on the treatment of prisoners indicate that solitary confinement for more than fifteen days is to be considered a form of torture and is expressly prohibited for adults, let alone minors. Children should not be imprisoned; prisons are not a place for them, especially military prisons, which is where Palestinian prisoners generally end up. Over the years, various international organizations have recommended that the Israeli military detention system must respect the rights of childhood. But in hindsight that was a mistake. They should simply have insisted that children not be arrested by soldiers, not be accused of vague crimes established by military orders of a vexatious nature, and not be tried by military courts. Instead an attempt was made to make the occupation more “acceptable.” But how could an occupation organized as a permanent instrument of oppression ever be considered acceptable?

#### Over the years I have attended several trials against minors, and I have seen with my own eyes their absurd brutality. The children were brought into the courtroom in chains, and I felt like I was watching scenes of slaves in labor camps. Small, emaciated, exhausted, anxious at the thought that, for the first time since their arrest, they would be seeing their parents again, in these hearings that lasted no more than a few minutes. The judge often did not even look at them; he heard the charge — “He was throwing stones” — and handed down the sentence. Two years in prison. Three years in prison. And so on. Lighter than usual sentences in these cases, given that the punishment for Palestinians who throw stones is up to ten years (twenty if done with the intention of harming someone).

#### After such a nightmare, how can anyone be surprised that when jailed Palestinian children return home they are traumatized, do not want to go out, are afraid, wet the bed, and exhibit disturbances or violent behavior? We are talking about twelve-, thirteen-, fourteen-year-old kids, but even younger kids are arrested. There were children as young as five or six being taken away by Israeli trucks; perhaps not detained but interrogated and then sent home (all you have to do is search the Internet to learn about this). The consequences are dramatic, and the message is very clear: “You are under our control. You are not free.”

#### *How can one speak of conflict, as a synonym for war, to describe such a situation?* Conflict requires two vaguely comparable sides. Israel and Palestine are not comparable antagonists: one is the

#### occupier and the other the occupied, one is the colonizer and the other the colonized, placed in a condition of structural subordination and the victim of a system of control and segregation. No, this is not a conflict, at most it can be seen as an inhuman relationship with one side oppressing the other.

#### Furthermore, the oppression of the Palestinian people by the Israeli occupation is aggravated paradoxically by the role of the PNA, a political institution created in 1993 following the Oslo Accords.

#### These agreements, cosigned by Israel and the PLO, were supposed to mark the first mutual recognition between the two parties and establish a path toward the creation of a Palestinian state. For the Palestinians, however, they have not produced any concrete results, except for the strengthening of the matrix of control that has made the occupation even more rapacious in the acquisition of land and the repression of Palestinian life. The promised state has been formally established and exists (it has even been recognized by a hundred and thirty-five countries of the United Nations), but in practice it has never materialized: The Israeli occupation has continued, expanding geographically, and the colonies in the occupied territory have multiplied, aggravating the oppression.

#### But even if the Oslo Accords had been respected, they were still based on a marked asymmetry of power between the parties, which would allow Israel to maintain effective control of the territory, leaving the Palestinians only fragmented autonomy devoid of real sovereignty. This has been stated by many scholars, both Palestinian and Israeli, such as Edward Said, Tanya Reinhart, and Ilan Pappé, as well as American scholars such as John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt, or even by reports by organizations such as the Israeli B’Tselem. Although the Oslo negotiations marked an important symbolic turning point, they did not question the architecture of Israeli control.

#### That is why many believe that it was precisely these agreements that legitimized the occupation, transforming the PNA into an administrative body that governs the Palestinian population in some areas but remains under Israeli military surveillance and domination. In fact, apart from exercising full civilian and security control in the major Palestinian cities (the so-called Area A) and civilian control in the peri-urban areas of the occupied territory (Area B), the main role of the PNA, according to the Oslo Accords, is to maintain security coordination with Israel, which is free to raid Area A cities too. But whose security? The answer is obvious.

#### Many Palestinians see the PNA as an obstacle to achieving self-determination. Unfortunately, this aggravates the social and political fragmentation of the Palestinians.

#### —

#### TODAY MORE THAN EVER, a Palestinian does not have many alternatives for the future. In the exercise of the basic functions of life, clashing with Israelis is inevitable, and it is not uncommon for Palestinians to be imprisoned or killed. Involvement in politics also leads to the same outcome.

#### There are figures such as Khalida Jarrar, a member of parliament duly elected in 2006 as a member of the Palestinian National Council, who finds herself continually under arrest for security reasons. In 2021, while she was in prison without charges and without a trial, Israel did not release her even for the funeral of her daughter, Suha, who died very young of a heart attack.

#### Detention by the Israeli army makes many Palestinians political prisoners: They are not arrested for common crimes, but the charge, when issued, is very often related to the political situation. There has always been a natural solidarity between society and political prisoners who are seen in some way as fighters. Helping each other and supporting the families of those in prison was a priority initially for the PLO, as it has been since for the PNA. At least until February 2025, when, under pressure from the United States, the PNA suspended support for Palestinian prisoners and their families. This has deprived many people of essential help, as often it is the heads of families who are arrested, leaving the entire family without resources. That’s why Abu Hassan was so keen to get those guys a job at Mihbash.

#### It is true that resistance can be violent, and civilians must always be protected from violence. I am not here to justify any crimes that the Palestinians may have committed against Israeli civilians in the long course of their oppression. But I am reminded of a reflection by Bertolt Brecht that I find extremely fitting in this case, as well as in other situations of systemic and protracted oppression:

#### *The rushing river they call violent But the riverbed pressing it in Nobody calls violent.*

#### The time has come to solve violence by going to its roots, removing the causes that trigger it, which in the Occupied Palestinian Territory are essentially the oppression and apartheid of the colonial project.

# GEORGE

#### *What does it mean to live in Jerusalem?*

#### All in all, it’s just another brick in the wall. All in all, you’re just another brick in the wall. — PINK FLOYD, “Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2”

#### JERUSALEM FOR ME is an utterly religious but not very spiritual city. Indeed, I have often had the impression that it is precisely there that one breathes the religion that stifles the spirit, despite the fact that so many people — including Jews, Muslims, and Christians — feel it is the fulcrum of their faith.

#### Geographically it is a city like many others. Politically, however, it is divided in two and, if you know it well, is a shattered city, starting from Road Number One, which crosses it from north to south, marking the dividing line between the predominantly Arab areas to the east and the Jewish areas to the west. Today, the road is urbanized and incorporated into the city fabric (to the east, it passes near the Damascus Gate, Sheikh Jarrah, Musrara), but it was once an important physical, political, and cultural boundary line drawn by the 1948 war, and retains a strong symbolic and historical value.

#### —

#### IN 1947, the United Nations General Assembly approved the so-called Partition Plan for Palestine, which provided for the division of Palestine into two states, assigning about 55 percent of the territories to the future Jewish state (although Jews were less than 35 percent of the population and owners of only 6 percent of the land) and the remaining 45 percent to the Palestinians, who individually or collectively owned 94 percent of the land at that time.

#### The plan was rejected by Palestinian leaders and Arab countries, who considered it unjust, and this led to a civil war, which then resulted in the 1948 conflict with the neighboring Arab countries after the proclamation of the State of Israel.

#### The battles between the Zionist militias and the Palestinian and Arab forces focused on strategic points, including the road that connected Tel Aviv (at the time a settlement of Eastern European Jews who had come to escape persecution) and Jerusalem: the future Road Number One. During the conflict that broke out in May 1948, in what the United Nations had indicated as the territory of the Jewish state, one of the crucial nodes was the area around the city of Latrun, the scene of violent clashes between Israeli troops and the Arab Legion, which intervened at that point from Jordan.

#### After the armistice of 1949, the Green Line of ceasefire was drawn in that area, and in some places Road Number One still follows it today, continuing to mark the separation between the Palestinian neighborhood Sheikh Jarrah and the Orthodox Jewish neighborhood, on the opposite side of Road Number One, in the Israeli area of West Jerusalem.

#### *In the UN partition plan, Jerusalem was envisioned as a corpus separatum, a city under international* administration, but this has never actually come to pass. Israel had been allocated 55 percent of historic Palestine, but instead grabbed 78 percent by 1949, leaving the “Arab state” imagined by the UN, and opposed by the Arabs themselves, only 22 percent and thus grossly violating the terms of the partition. During this period, clashes between Zionist militias and Palestinian armed resistance and attacks on villages, especially Palestinian ones, led to the expulsion or forced flight of about seven hundred and fifty thousand Palestinians (out of the one million originally inhabiting today’s Israel). This is the so-called Nakba, the Arabic term for catastrophe, which is still commemorated as such by Palestinians across the globe.

#### Jerusalem was then divided into two parts: the west, under Israeli control, and the east, under Jordanian control,

#### with the Old City rising just beyond the former Green Line (the other name of Road Number One, from the color with which the armistice line with Jordan was drawn). The historic center is spectacular. Surrounded by ancient walls, it is made up of four quarters: Armenian, Jewish, Christian, and Muslim (or Arab).

#### Just outside the Old City walls, in the Muslim Quarter, is Salah al-Din Street, where the Educational Bookshop is located, the best-known bookstore in East Jerusalem and a meeting point for foreigners like myself and my husband, and for Palestinians with access to Jerusalem.

#### *On the ground floor of the Educational Bookshop there is the main bookshop itself, which has (or rather had, as* long as it was permitted to) a large selection of modern and historical books on Israel-Palestine, along with a small café where homemade cakes were served; on the lower floor there is a conference room and a small kitchen; on the mezzanine floor there is a space for sitting and, for some, working. Max — who at that time was working remotely for a British think tank — went there often; it had become his de facto office when we moved to Jerusalem from Geneva. One day, during one of Max’s loud online conversations, a character who used to sit on the mezzanine of the bookshop came down the stairs and tapped him on the shoulder: “How on earth am I supposed to work if I can’t even hear my own thoughts over your loud voice?” This is how he met George, and this is how their (and our) friendship was born, to the detriment of the other patrons of the café. Thanks to their boisterous voices, they soon came to be known as the quintessential “noise polluters.”

#### George is a Palestinian engineer from Jerusalem, a very intelligent, extremely warm person. He studied in the United States, worked for years in Silicon Valley, and at the beginning of the 2000s, after living there for twenty years, decided to leave everything and return home to help build what he hoped would become the Free State of Palestine, especially its IT sector.

#### In Palestine, George found it hard to keep a job worthy of his education, especially because of his independence of thought. He had a hard time working with international organizations, where a Palestinian was expected not to speak about occupation and apartheid. The idea was more or less: “If you want to work with us [that is, Westerners with dough], you have to adapt to our style.” But George was a nonconformist, and above all a person of principle, *reluctant to concede to the depoliticization of Western donors. Moreover, working with the Israelis was even more* complicated, because even the most progressive of them always maintained a certain sense of superiority and paternalism over Palestinians, and he could not bear the idea of feeling beholden to the “generosity of others.”

#### For a Palestinian, living in Jerusalem means dealing daily with the implications of the structural subordination imposed by Israel, starting with the terminology, which we tend to think is clear, even though it is not.

#### Even the opposition between “Arabs” and “Jews,” for example, can be seen as a reverberation of socialist thought, which tends to simplify this terrible situation of apartheid in ethno-religious terms, obscuring the political, colonial, and national dimensions. Calling the people of Palestine generically “Arabs” — as is often done in Israeli textbooks or in mainstream media around the world — contributes to denying their national identity. Referring to Palestinians simply as “Arabs” risks subscribing to the idea that there is no such thing as a Palestine and that the Palestinians are temporary guests or, indeed, an invention.

#### It takes a conscious effort for others to appreciate what it means for a Palestinian in Jerusalem to live all day, every day immersed in this tension that touches everything, including the words that appear to be the most banal but which, on closer inspection, are very problematic.

#### —

#### IN ADDITION TO Abu Hassan, our closest Jerusalemite friends, who left their mark on our lives and helped us navigate the complex space of the city in those early years, were George and Ibrahim: two complementary souls. One Christian and one Muslim; George always full of energy, a bottle of champagne just uncorked, Ibrahim serious, studious, and often silent. Ibrahim came from the Husseini family, one of the most important in Palestine, descendants of the Prophet and above all of the Grand Mufti of Jerusalem, a figure strongly discredited by a narrative aimed at delegitimizing his political role in the years of the creation of the State of Israel in Palestine and reducing his figure to the controversial proximity to Nazi Germany, while obscuring his central role in the Palestinian resistance to the British Mandate and to Zionism. At that time Ibrahim lived in a beautiful, airy, spacious house in the center of East Jerusalem. He was a journalist for a Western broadcaster and had to struggle constantly with the need to measure his every word: Telling the truth about the events on the ground involving the Israeli occupation meant risking not being published or, worse, losing or being forced to leave his job, as happens to many.

#### I don’t know how I could have lived without them and our other friends during those intense years in Jerusalem, when I often felt discouraged. After six months, I was almost ready to leave, because I could not tolerate the heaviness, the oppressive tension, that forced and persistent separation imposed by the always fluid but nonetheless impassable boundaries of apartheid, even if at the time I did not yet use that word.

#### Every day just crossing the city turned out to be a journey that left me speechless. I remember that a few days after meeting Ibrahim we went with him to the Western Wall, one of the main holy

#### places of Judaism, venerated as the only surviving part of the wall that once surrounded the Second Temple of Jerusalem, which some say was destroyed by the Romans in the first century AD, while others claim it never existed or did not exist there. Close to the Western Wall is the area of the Esplanade of the Mosques, otherwise known as the Temple Mount, one of the holy places of Islam.

#### Like many sites in Jerusalem, this place carries with it a history of violence and dispossession. In June 1967, with the military occupation of East Jerusalem by Israeli forces, the Moroccan Quarter, which was right in front of the Western Wall, was placed under the control of the occupation. Overnight, the entire area of ninety thousand square feet was razed to the ground and about six hundred and fifty inhabitants were evacuated, deprived of their homes to make room for Jewish pilgrims — a part of history that is not told to the thousands of tourists and faithful who visit this sacred place every year. Max, Ibrahim, and I were taking a couple of friends and Max’s brother, who were visiting from Italy, for a walk in the Old City that evening, trying to imagine what that place must have been like before the occupation, when we noticed a man who was talking in a rather excited way, like a street vendor trying to attract the attention of the crowd, in front of a small group of people who looked like tourists. The scene intrigued me, because usually no one is so exuberant in Jerusalem, at least none of those I saw daily: not the Palestinians, always with their heads bowed to be noticed as little as possible, nor the ultra-Orthodox Jews who always run through the Arab Quarter to go to pray at the Western Wall, nor the soldiers, posted everywhere to control the lives of the Palestinians. When he realized that I was staring at him, the guy looked at me with a toothy *smile and his arms open wide, like Kate Winslet on the bow of the Titanic, and then he said to me in a thick Australian accent: “Welcome to Israel!”*

#### “Occupied Palestine. It’s occupied Palestine, this part here,” I told him with a trace of a smile. He retorted sharply: “Palestine does not exist, this is Israel.” At that point Ibrahim, who was walking next to me, asked him animatedly: “And if Palestine does not exist,

#### what am I?” “You don’t exist,” the man replied without batting an eyelash. Years later we would discover that this man was

#### the head of one of the most aggressive settlers’ organizations, trying to take over as many Palestinians’ homes in Jerusalem as possible. We had just come across, without knowing it, a man who, if we lived in a just world, would have been sent to prison long ago.

#### —

#### GEORGE AND IBRAHIM were not guides, but hanging out with them meant exploring the Old City with fresh eyes. We often spent hours chatting in the beautiful garden of the Austrian Hospice, a structure dedicated to pilgrims, where many young Austrians worked. Or we went together to Mihbash, where we always ran into Abu Hassan.

#### In East Jerusalem there were not many places open in the evening, but during the day there were plenty of places to have breakfast. On Saturday mornings Max loved to sleep in, so I, who was more of an early riser, often went with George to Salah al-Din Street, to a small place that was accessed through a narrow staircase. In the basement there was a very simple room, with tiled walls, white plastic tables, black-and-white chairs, an old refrigerator for drinks, and a counter with a fryer where hot food was served. There we had the classic Palestinian breakfast: hummus, hummus basar (served hot, with meat) for George, tomatoes, olives, cucumbers, various types of cheese with olive oil, the inevitable kilo or two of bread to dip in oil and za’atar. I remember that in the last few days I spent in Jerusalem I was in the middle of my first pregnancy and had a craving for spicy foods, so I used to binge on hot chickpea cream that I ate with filfil akhdar, spicy green peppers, instead of bread (which earned me the nickname Ghazaouia among my friends, “woman from Gaza,” since these peppers are all the rage there). The owners were terrified that I might feel sick in there and feared a raid by the Israelis because of a pregnant Italian who risked poisoning herself in their restaurant.

#### Sometimes — often with George, Ibrahim, and Abu Hassan — we went to West Jerusalem in the evening. We went to a place called Toy Bar, one of the rare meeting places for young Israelis and Palestinians in the city, where dance nights sometimes evolved into wild parties with dancing on the tables until dawn. It all happened within a radius of a few streets; not far from the Toy Bar was the Diwan, Arabic for “sofa,” a disco bar with DJs and plenty of space to go wild. After all the accumulated tension, dancing was liberating, but I would never have gone to a place where my Palestinian friends may have been harassed and that was a kind of free zone. Moreover, Amir, the Israeli boy posted at the entrance, knew Abu Hassan, and this was enough to make us as welcome as if we were the pasha with his court in tow.

#### Of course, there were often Israeli soldiers, but it must be borne in mind that almost all Jewish Israeli citizens

#### have been soldiers at some point. For Jews, but not for the Palestinians living in Israel, conscription is compulsory: three years for boys and two for girls. After those initial years, it is possible to be recalled up to the age of forty, with a few exceptions, which is what has been happening en masse since October 7th. Israelis who refuse to take part in the army, as conscientious objectors, can be imprisoned, even for months.

#### Then there was Uganda, a place opened by Palestinians in 1948, also in West Jerusalem — and which closed its doors shortly after our departure from Jerusalem. Its name was a provocation: Before the British Mandate (1920– 1948), when the possibility of establishing the State of Israel in Palestine materialized, Uganda was one of the places that was proposed — and eventually refused — for the settlement of Zionist Jews and the creation of a Jewish state.

#### Among the many places we went for walks with George, I will never forget Talbiya and Baka, two contiguous areas in the heart of West Jerusalem where today, among tree-lined avenues and cafés that would seem to belong to any Western city, there are some wonderful houses. Very elegant, unique houses, mixing Arab taste with Ottoman and European influences and built in the 1920s and ‘30s by wealthy Palestinian families. That was the wealthy part of the city pre-1948, where Jews, Muslims, and Christians lived together, before the war separated them and before the arrival of European Zionism.

#### Most of the houses are made of light stone — the cream-colored stone of Jerusalem that lights up with golden reflections at sunset, hence the nickname “golden city” — with high ceilings and large arched windows often framed by wooden shutters. Many overlook small internal gardens with stone benches and colored-tile floors, now enclosed by modern gates through which a few tufts or rebellious branches of bougainvillea, figs, lemon trees emerge. Some retain their original doors, sturdy, carved by hand, with brass knockers, and inside there are still ceramic floors of geometric shapes or floral motifs, wall niches, and the vaults and fireplaces chosen by those who had them built. But after 1948 most of these houses were attacked by Zionist militias, the Palestinian inhabitants forced to flee, with the hope of being able to return soon. But no, seventy-seven years later, with the houses still there, returning is not something even to be talked about.

#### When we were out for a walk one day, George showed us the outside of the house that had been expropriated from his grandmother, so I asked him: “Do you want us to ring the bell and get them to open up, so at least you can see it from the inside?”

#### But he replied with a curt no: “Let’s forget it. I’ve already tried, and I won’t tell you how they treated us. Now they live there, or someone who pays them rent, because often these ‘new owners’ no longer even live in our houses.”

#### I have heard this same story many times. Palestinians who manage to return to the places of their childhood, recounted to them by way of the memories of their displaced parents or grandparents — the survivors of the Nakba — and, when they arrive, they often find nothing. Sometimes the building has been razed to the ground, other times new structures have taken its place, but what happened to George may hurt even more: coming back and seeing his family’s house still standing, trying to enter even just to be able to look at it once and being gruffly turned away by the people who live there, who may not even be the new owners but are tenants. Many of these houses, in fact, are often left empty for long periods, because many Israeli Jews have dual citizenship and live abroad. I knew people who worked for international organizations and had rented from Israelis houses that had belonged to Palestinians who had become refugees in 1948 — something aberrant for me, but which unfortunately does not surprise me too much because the expatriates, a group that also included Max and myself, rather than being ineffable bearers of peace, are often so detached from reality that they do not feel the breath of the land they live on. I noticed that the *idea of being there in the guise of the white savior prevented many of my colleagues and friends, especially those* who worked for the United Nations, from questioning themselves, and I began to see in their work and in the very fact of living on that earth a part of the problem that we had ideally come to solve.

#### —

#### ALTHOUGH TALBIYA AND BAKA are objectively beautiful areas, full of nice clubs and restaurants, for me they have always been a place of internal conflict. Because you feel the cultural appropriation very strongly there, starting with the strange fusion between Palestinian cuisine and Eastern European influences. Restaurant menus always feature hummus, baba ghanoush, falafel, olive oil, and za’atar, next to turnip soup, cabbage…Of course, the idea of a fusion, even gastronomic, between Palestinians and Israelis would be interesting, if it did not inevitably bring with it the aftertaste of apartheid, if Israel were not the country that more than any other tries to annihilate the identity of the Palestinians and in the meantime demonizes it. For me, therefore, the cuisine of Talbiya is not cultural fusion but a symbol of the normalization of the ethnic cleansing of the Palestinians, which is also effected through the misappropriation of what was and continues to be Palestinian culture. Barring a miracle, I fear that it will take decades before we eliminate the sense of privilege and abuse that today permeates everything, including restaurant

#### menus. That is why I believe that, on the other side of the city, East Jerusalem — an integral part of the West Bank

#### under Israeli military occupation — represents a sort of colonial frontier: a place marked by the constant encounter with and clash between the local Palestinian population (Muslim, Christian Armenian) and the work of Judaization, that is, the progressive imposition of the Jewish Israeli presence, control, and culture that touches all areas of daily life. This is not to deny Jerusalem’s strong Jewish heritage; there were many Arab Jews living in pre-Israel Jerusalem. But, as many historians, including Israelis like Menachem Klein, have written, the common life of Jewish Arabs on the one hand and Muslims and Christians on the other was compromised by the spread of Zionism from the first half of the twentieth century onward. Those wounds have never healed, or at least not yet.

#### This is where one of the most complex and delicate questions emerges for most people who do not have a thorough knowledge of the history of Palestine. An issue that we have often addressed, in our conversations and *walks with our Palestinian friends and, later in life, with Israeli friends: Who are the real indigenous people of those* places? To say that Palestinians (identified as non-Jews who live, or whose history originates, in that part of the land we call Holy) are genuinely indigenous does not mean that Jews are not.

#### At the end of the nineteenth century, while the Ottoman Empire was beginning its decline and part of European Zionism was emerging with projects for the creation of a Jewish state, centered on Jewish immigration that would achieve political and cultural control over the local population, historical Palestine was home to a population with a large Muslim majority, and Christian and Jewish minorities: They were all “Arabs of Palestine.” Following the persecutions in Eastern Europe and the anti-Semitic discrimination throughout the Continent that led to the horror of the Holocaust, thousands of Jews progressively emigrated to what was first Ottoman territory and then the British Mandate. This represented an important step forward for the Zionist colonial project, whose founding fathers included the Austrian Theodor Herzl, the Russians Chaim Weizmann and Vladimir Zeev Jabotinsky, and the Pole David Ben-Gurion, who in 1948 became the first prime minister of the State of Israel.

#### The aliyah, meaning “return” and used to describe Jewish immigration to the land of Israel, became central to the Zionist movement as early as the late nineteenth century.

#### So it is correct to say that there was a pre-Zionist Jewish community in Palestine (equal to less than 10 percent of the population at the time); it is correct to say that most of the Jews who went to Palestine before and immediately after the creation of the State of Israel, especially the survivors of the Holocaust, had few or no alternatives because so many Western countries were reluctant to accept them, and thousands found themselves without shelter, with communities destroyed and families decimated. It is equally correct to mention that today many of the Israelis living in the colonies in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, occupying the homes and land of the Palestinians, have American, Belgian, French, Australian, Canadian, Argentinean names and accents. Often neither they nor their parents were born in Israel, but they come from cities where they often remain for most of the year: Although they reside abroad, they retain ownership or control of real estate in the occupied territory, contributing to the systematic dispossession of the Palestinians.

#### —

#### LIVING IN JERUSALEM also means walking down the street and seeing a family’s personal belongings piled up on the sidewalk, while someone else is moving into their house as if it were perfectly normal.

#### There are various ways for Israelis to acquire Palestinian homes. There is nothing wrong with wanting to buy property per se, but the point is that in Jerusalem, it is not simply a matter, as in other places, of an individual who falls in love with a house and decides to buy it but of organizations that pursue a precise political project of Judaization of what remains of Palestine. One of the central figures of this system, as well as one of the most aggressive, is Daniel Lauria, the same person with whom my friend Ibrahim and I had that spat at the Western Wall. Years later, I recognized him in a documentary on the settlers, in which he proudly explains his commitment to “facilitating” the buying and selling of Palestinian homes and land to help the return of the Jews. In the documentary describing the work of Ateret Cohanim, the organization led by Lauria, there is a scene in which Muna El-Kurd, Mohammed’s twin sister, tells a settler “You are stealing my house!” and he replies without any shame: “If I don’t steal it, someone else is going to steal it.” And with people like Lauria on the rise, how can you blame him.

#### Ateret Cohanim essentially manages to evict Palestinians — often with highly questionable property titles — or to convince them to sell their homes. Some agree to do so out of desperation and, after being ostracized by the community, they sell in secret before fleeing abroad. Others are simply kicked out.

#### Even when acquisitions are legal, they are still part of an occupation because they make use of vexatious tools. Right above our house in Jerusalem there were settlers, and their presence was always exhibited with security guards, Israeli flags, reproductions of gigantic menorahs poised on the rooftops. Even Ariel Sharon had bought a

#### house in East Jerusalem, and it was not in a side street but in a clearly visible spot in the Old City, a clearing near the Damascus Gate that I used to pass by regularly on my way to the Austrian Hospice and where more than once I saw brutal searches and beatings of young Palestinians by Israeli soldiers. It was essential that that house be located in a place of passage, precisely because it was meant to be a symbolic building. This also contributes to the tense atmosphere in Jerusalem. When you cross the Arab Quarter of the Old City to go to the Western Wall or the Esplanade of the Mosques and you look up to the sky, you see many Israeli flags and Jewish symbols in houses that until recently had been inhabited by Palestinians. For a Palestinian, the possibility of returning home and finding settlers inside, as has happened to so many, is a source of permanent anguish.

#### —

#### BEYOND JERUSALEM’S MANY CHARMS — the busy life of its alleyways crowded with shops and the faithful on their way to pray, the magic that embraces you when you look at it from atop its massive walls, a roof, or a terrace during the Islamic hour of prayer when captivating chants flow out from all the minarets — it has always conveyed a sense of melancholy to me. Both when I lived there and all the times I’ve gone back, I was happy to be there, yet at the same time I felt an emptiness, an inner cold. Every time I set foot there it felt like a deeper plunge. Despite being a vibrant city, it is as if something has been snatched from it and will never come back. The Palestinian population of the city is especially distressed.

#### Jerusalem has always been an important center for the life of the Palestinian people; not only for religious reasons but also because, at least until the construction of the separation wall that Israel erected in the West Bank, it was a commercial crossroads that functioned as a bridge between north and south. The other nodal points are Nablus and Hebron, but before the year 2000 Jerusalem was the central hub toward which everyone converged. Today it has been cut off, shut in by the wall, which Israel built officially to prevent Palestinian attacks from the West Bank, but which has effectively served to seize around 12 percent of the West Bank territory and to further undermine Palestinian territorial integrity (an opinion issued in 2004 by the International Court of Justice described the Western Wall as illegitimate and directed that it be dismantled, a directive that was never implemented). So today, Palestinians in Jerusalem and in Israel can go to the West Bank, but those who live in the West Bank can only enter the city with Israeli-issued permits, which are often difficult if not impossible to obtain.

#### This closure has catastrophically affected the local Palestinian economy, because shepherds, Bedouins, and many Palestinians engaged in rural and artisanal activities traded goods in the city and Jerusalem was a nerve center for the sale, for example, of dairy products, which were distributed from there throughout the region. Now it’s all over. As Amnesty International also highlighted in its 2022 report “Israel’s Apartheid Against Palestinians,” Palestinians live under separate jurisdictions and are subject to strict permits that separate them from each other and isolate them from their lands and families.

#### Getting Palestinian products into the city has become so complicated that traders end up selling products from the Israeli settlements. I remember that in the early days this surprised me a lot, but it is only another aspect of that schizophrenic space, so difficult to navigate.

#### Since the tragic events of October 2023, as restrictions, attacks, and abuses increased and the number of visitors decreased, almost all of the Palestinian shops I knew have closed. A few orange and pomegranate juice stands have remained open for the small number of pilgrims who still visit the city, but what about the rest? In Jerusalem, many Palestinian families, working in hospitality and catering, depend almost exclusively on international tourism. I remember that already ten or fifteen years ago it was very rare to see Israelis venturing into the Arab areas of the city. It is even true that taxi drivers from West Jerusalem often refuse customers who want to go to East Jerusalem because they fear being attacked. Whether these fears are well-founded or not, they make Jerusalem a “naturally” divided city: like certain lakes where currents of water flow past each other without ever mixing. But here the division is man-made. The substance is that of a regime of racial or, more precisely, ethno-religious separation: apartheid.

#### —

#### I LEFT JERUSALEM at the end of 2012, with my daughter, Leila, about to be born. Max had left shortly after the end of the summer, to move to Washington, DC. While waiting to join him, I stayed as long as my pregnancy allowed. I waited for the house to be emptied of all our furniture and said goodbye to it on a late-October morning, while the sunlight cast the shadow of the pomegranate tree on the terrace across the floor of my bedroom, in which only the mattress was left.

#### That’s how George found me: sitting on the floor looking at my bare feet, as that play of shadows skimmed over

#### them. He reached out to help me get up and we went to have a last breakfast on Salah al-Din: the last near apoplectic stroke for the restaurateur who was fed up with me and my obsession with green peppers for breakfast. Then we moved on to say goodbye to the Muna brothers, the owners of the Educational Bookshop, where I bought yet another stack of books before saying goodbye. George accompanied me in this string of farewells with his kind and *mischievous smile. “Habibti,” he would say to me affectionately every time I said something stupid. When he was* serious, he called me “Frenci” (which has eventually become the name my closest friends call me) or “Kbire.” From Jerusalem onward, I have been Frenci Kbire (“big”) to differentiate me from our other dear friend, Francesca Bombi. She, for all of us, was and remains Frenci Sghire (“little one”).

#### —

#### AFTER LEAVING JERUSALEM, Max, George, and I met again relatively early: In March he was the first dear person, after Max and my mother, to hold Leila, on her second day of life, in a clinic in DC. And over time we have never lost sight of “Uncle George,” who continued to come and visit us in the United States and Italy, just as I have found a way to see him every time I returned to Palestine, during the years of research and writing a book on Palestinian refugees.

#### Then genocide came down on all of us like a cleaver. We lost contact with each other. After a year, George and I started writing to each other again. He told me that he was not doing too well, maybe he also suffered from a bit of depression; after all, what Palestinian doesn’t feel depressed these days?

#### For me too there were moments of despair. I remember the first weeks of the genocide, between October and November 2023, when I often cried because I couldn’t get over my grief at all those deaths: two hundred, two hundred and fifty people a day, the children, the horrible stories I heard…I tried to resist, but at that time I was not there for anyone, sometimes not even for my children or my mother, whose mind in the meantime was continuing to evaporate. Every morning I had to get up, count the dead, try to understand what had happened, verify the information, talk to the other experts, respond to those who called me from Gaza or the West Bank, respond as much as possible to interview requests from journalists, remind myself to breathe. I have a vivid memory of an October morning when I was in Italy and did an interview with the BBC with my eyes looking like frog’s eyes, so much had I cried since the early hours of the day, looking at the images of the destruction of Gaza, unable to quell the anguish aroused by the constant inhuman cry of revenge shouted by the hordes of young soldiers in assault gear.

#### Months of pure asphyxia followed. Then, very slowly, it was as though I had to learn to construct a wall between me as a person and everything

#### else, to be able to return to my life, but always a little half-heartedly, always faltering, struggling to accept the idea of having changed definitively, of having lost something that can never come back.

#### Meanwhile, in the early months of 2025, the Educational Bookshop jumped into the news. The Israeli army raided the store twice, arresting the owners and looting the shelves, removing all the books that had a Palestinian flag on the cover or something that was not to the liking of the military, including a copy of an Israeli magazine, a children’s coloring book that was confiscated as evidence of incitement to terrorism, and an international law *textbook, Palestinian Refugees in International Law, which I cowrote with Lex Takkenberg and which Oxford* University Press published in 2020. Israeli settler colonialism, in fact, represses even the creation of a collective, Palestinian, international consciousness, which highlights the reality of the occupation. Why else would they destroy the places of culture, which on closer inspection are nothing more than spaces of peaceful resistance to the occupation?

#### This is also what it means to live in Jerusalem.

# ALON

#### *How do you recognize anti-Semitism?*

#### *Apartheid was a new term but an old idea. It literally means “apartness”…What had been more or* less de facto was to become relentlessly de jure. The often haphazard segregation…was to be consolidated into a monolithic system that was diabolical in its detail, inescapable in its reach, and overwhelming in its power. *— NELSON MANDELA, Long Walk to Freedom*

#### TODAY MORE THAN EVER, when Palestinians and those who defend them are accused of anti-Semitism, we must understand what is meant by anti-Semitism and what dangers can derive from the misuse of this term.

#### In May 2022, when I became the UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, I had already been on the receiving end of an indecorous number of insults and the target of several reports issued by an organization called UN Watch. In theory, UN Watch is an organism established to monitor compliance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, which promotes human rights on the part of governments within the system of the United Nations. In practice, however, it is purely and simply an instrument of Israeli propaganda inside the UN, an agency as charlatan in spirit and understanding of human rights as it is zealous in defaming anyone who dares to criticize the State of Israel. In the first summer of my tenure as Special Rapporteur, I was invited to appear at a hearing before the Foreign Affairs Committee of the Italian Chamber of Deputies. Responding to my presentation, and forgetting his role as a mere moderator, the chairman of the committee — one of the oldest parliamentarians of the center-left party and, as I would discover, a notorious pro-Israel advocate in Italy — judged my interpretation of the Palestinian-Israeli question to be “unilateral” and recommended greater “impartiality.” In other words, he accused me of being biased.

#### In my naivety as a novice in my UN role, I was dumbfounded. In what sense would I be biased? Why would a politician call for impartiality from an international official who had diligently done her job, documented and legally analyzed facts, and agreed to accept the committee’s invitation to report on an extremely serious situation? The clash sowed chaos within the commission and eventually went public.

#### It was in the middle of this controversy that I met Alon Confino, an Italian Israeli university professor who taught history and Judaic and Near Eastern studies at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he was also the director of the American Institute for Holocaust, Genocide, and Memory Studies.

#### Alon wrote a lovely open letter in my defense and proposed it to several Italian newspapers. In the end, it was never published, but a very strong collaboration and a beautiful friendship was born between us that lasted until the last days of his life, in June 2024.

#### In the early days of our acquaintance, Alon brought my attention to a very important issue, introducing me to the heated debate among Jewish scholars around the world concerning the definition of anti-Semitism proposed by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA).

#### In truth, the definition of anti-Semitism should be self-evident: It consists of hatred, discrimination, prejudice, violence against Jews as Jews, just as Islamophobia is hatred, discrimination, prejudice, violence against Muslims as Muslims…and so on.

#### Instead, in 2016 the IHRA proposed a special definition of anti-Semitism that was verbose, complex, and mellifluous: “Anti-Semitism is a certain perception of Jews that can be expressed as hatred for Jews. Manifestations of real and physical anti-Semitism are directed at Jews or non-Jews and/or their property, Jewish community institutions, and buildings used for worship.” The definition, which is apparently innocuous, is accompanied by eleven practical examples largely conflating anti-Semitism with criticism of the State of Israel and its policies.

#### The risk of this definition is that it allows consideration of any criticism of the State of Israel as anti-Semitic. In

#### summary, since Israel defines itself as a “Jewish state,” to criticize it would be anti-Semitic, whether or not there are documented violations attributable to Israel. As Alon often told me, confusing criticism of the State of Israel with anti-Semitism is very risky both for the people of Palestine and for Jews themselves because, by reasoning in these terms, one makes an immediate association between all Jews and the State of Israel. But this is not the case. Alon was Israeli, he loved Israel deeply, and like him there are many American and European Jews who want nothing to do with the crimes of the State of Israel. Many of these Jews are anti-Zionist, some are not openly so, some not at all.

#### Moreover, by making improper equations between anti-Semitism and criticism of the State of Israel, one fails to *focus on the real anti-Semitism that is repugnant and still exists: It is the anti-Semitism of those who see Jews — as* well as Arabs or homosexual people — as something impure to be eliminated from the (Western) system in order to preserve its purity. In the words of Raz Segal, an Israeli professor of Holocaust and genocide studies at Stockton University in New Jersey, it seems that the idea of the superior race, transformed into a political ideology of extermination by Nazi Germany a century ago, did not disappear with Hitler. This ideology has been hidden and transformed, but it still pulsates in the veins of our societies, even in Western societies that preach respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms.

#### Segal has highlighted how concepts of racial supremacy have reemerged in contemporary contexts, emphasizing the use of rhetoric that dehumanizes Palestinians and recalls ideologies of racial supremacy.

#### —

#### THE MYTH OF RACE, on closer inspection, was not even invented by Hitler. It hovers through five hundred years of colonization, starting in 1492 and the European “discovery of America.”

#### A striking example of the instrumental use of the myth of race is the popular notion that the history of the United States began on July 4, 1776, when the thirteen colonies officially broke from the British crown by issuing the Declaration of Independence. This event is seen as the birth of the United States as a sovereign nation, leaving aside the first two hundred and fifty years of European colonization of the Americas, during which it is estimated that tens of millions of Native peoples, entire civilizations, were exterminated by military conquests, slavery, deportations, and the spread of diseases brought by Europeans, against which the Indigenous peoples had no immunity.

#### These genocides, which in many regions caused a demographic collapse of from 70 to 90 percent of the original *population, are rarely spoken of, or they are recounted in a reassuring way, normalizing the abomination. The Rediscovery of America, by Ned Blackhawk, is one of the most enlightening books I have read in this long two years* of genocide in Palestine, and it is nothing more than a history of the genocides that preceded and then led to the creation of the United States from the perspective of its Indigenous peoples.

#### —

#### TODAY NO ONE (or almost no one) denies the reading of European colonialism with regard to the Native peoples of the United States. Many centuries have passed and certain aspects of that colonialism continue to be illuminated with ever greater clarity. It seems that the discussion gets into hot water, however, when you touch on situations that concern the present.

#### I used to talk a lot with Alon about these topics. After our first emails and chats over the phone, we started an intense exchange. I had him and his close friend Amos Goldberg — a professor of Jewish history and contemporary Jewry at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and one of the few Israelis who promptly denounced the post–October 7th genocide perpetrated against the Palestinians — read the report on self-determination that I was preparing in 2022 for the United Nations, my first as a Special Rapporteur, and they both said something like: “Good luck!
