The problem is not how you construct the idea of the right to self-determination but that you accuse Israel of being a colonial state.”

#### “But it is…” “Yes, we know it is, but be prepared, because they will unload on you with everything they can.” They were right. My visit to the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which had been scheduled for December 2022,

#### was blocked (as had happened to my predecessors since 2008) and the accusations against me of anti-Semitism have never subsided, despite the outcry in my defense from many parts of the world, from academics, journalists, and activists, with progressive Jews always in the front line.

#### At the same time, thanks to Alon and Amos, I immersed myself in a world of Jewish — mainly Israeli, British, and American — scholars with whom I have collaborated to counter what has been happening at the United Nations, where pro-Israel pressure groups, using every means at their disposal, were pressuring the secretary-general and

#### others so that the United Nations would adopt the IHRA definition of anti-Semitism. Those pressures have had real effects (such as the recent US sanctions against the International Criminal Court

#### and myself). Twenty-five of the twenty-seven European states to date have adopted this definition in some form, which

#### though not legally binding has become a standard used by governments, universities, and even companies. In Italy, the Council of Ministers adopted the definition of the IHRA in 2020. Lufthansa and many other airlines have made it their own as well.

#### This means that if you wear a keffiyeh or a pin with the flag of Palestine, you may one day be considered subject to sanctions, since according to those parameters the flag or other symbols of Palestinian identity could be seen as an affront to the State of Israel or a denial of its existence. This means an unprecedented level of oppression and rejection of reason.

#### Of course, we are also witnessing an unprecedented level of awareness. Never before has there been such a sustained questioning of the State of Israel. Never before has there been such a mobilization. I am not only talking about demonstrations and marches but also about important legal actions that are underway, such as those supported by various international organizations against the governments of the countries where they operate — for now the United Kingdom, Denmark, and the Netherlands — for having given support and transferred weapons to Israel at a time when it was committing very serious international crimes against the Palestinians; or like those initiated by the Hind Rajab Foundation, the association that calls for justice to be meted out to all Israeli soldiers about whom evidence of involvement in war crimes and acts of genocide has been collected.

#### Yet, in many countries, attempts are made to block these legal proceedings, precisely because they are accused of being “anti-Semitic.” Therefore, on the one hand there is certainly more knowledge and awareness but on the other hand there is also a growing repression: a symptom of the global oppression of which the Palestinians are victims. And this is happening not only at the hands of Israel but also in the United States, Canada, Australia, and Europe, where Palestinians are often discriminated against precisely because their very existence is thought to be a detriment or an embarrassment to the State of Israel.

#### The logical distortion, the lack of rationality, is evident. At times it almost seems like an obstinate desire to not understand, to show oneself unable to see what is right before your eyes. Perhaps because understanding demands action.

#### I am left speechless when I read certain articles that speak of “hateful Palestinians.” How can anyone, today, not feel anger or pain in the face of Israel’s actions, at the way it conducts them, and its ability to silence debate everywhere?

#### In any case, whatever one’s feelings, it is not feelings that should guide political choices. The criterion must be legality: that is the yardstick that marks the limit of what politics can — and cannot — do.

#### In 2022, when I was becoming friends with Alon and Amos, hundreds of Jewish scholars worldwide had signed the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism (as an alternative to the IHRA and true to the premise that anti-Semitism is hatred of Jews as Jews). At the time, faced with the risk of the IHRA definition being adopted by the United Nations, I decided to consult other Special Rapporteurs, those who from a thematic point of view could help understand and deal with the issue: defenders of freedom of expression, freedom of association, human rights. Jewish scholars sought our support against the dissemination of the IHRA definition, which in the meantime had also been rejected by its original drafters, given the shameless use that Israel and the pro-Israel pressure groups were making of it. Along with other Special Rapporteurs, I wrote to the UN secretary-general and the High Representative for the United Nations Alliance of Civilizations, who had been given the mandate to deal with this definition of anti-Semitism.

#### In one year, we tried to make the consultative process initiated by the UN slightly more democratic, open to progressive and critical voices. How could the United Nations adopt a definition that not only did not define anti-Semitism but that was also extremely controversial and dangerous?

#### To date, that definition has not been officially adopted; moreover, although the United Nations has continued to hold discussions and seminars with these pressure groups, in the meantime the opposition has also grown and the doors have been opened to a group of scholars, including Alon, Amos, and others, who have repeatedly gone to confer with the United Nations.

#### In October 2022, a report by the UN Special Rapporteur on contemporary forms of racism, E. Tendayi Achiume, studied the matter and declared in black-and-white that the IHRA definition, in addition to being contested by leading experts on the subject, was extremely dangerous: “Its de facto influence on the policies and practices of governments and private actors has contributed to violations of human rights, including freedom of expression, the right to assembly, and political participation, among others.”

#### In the meantime, I was preparing for my visit to the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which was scheduled for

#### December. For the first time, after fourteen years (from 2008 to 2022) in which the Israeli government had never responded to the requests of the Special Rapporteurs, I had decided to change my technique. Instead of asking for permission, I simply informed them: “I will be in Palestine from this date to this date and I will hold these *meetings.” I wanted them to read between the lines: “You cannot stop me, because you are just the (illegal)* occupying power; so I am going. I have been invited by the Palestinian National Authority, and I am informing you so that you can facilitate (and not obstruct) my mission as best you can.”

#### One day later, the Israeli authorities had already protested to the United Nations, complaining that I had not followed the rules, that I would still need their authorization to enter the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and indicating the procedures that I was to follow.

#### No problem. I complied with all the required procedures and went ahead with the organization of the mission. *However, seven days before my departure, an Israeli newspaper — The Times of Israel — gave great prominence to* a piece of news artfully prepared as a media bomb.

#### At the heart of the article was the accusation that I was indisputably an anti-Semite, as evidenced by a post I had published on Facebook at the time of the Israeli offensive in the Gaza Strip in July 2014, in which more than two thousand people were killed, including about five hundred children, and eleven thousand were injured. My post contained an appeal to a priest in my hometown to help finance the United Nations Relief and Works Agency, which at that time was giving assistance to the affected population, and a criticism of the West which, in the face of the umpteenth scourge of Palestinians, remained inert, unlike the African, Asian, and Latin American countries. My post argued that neither Europe nor the United States were stopping the carnage, as the former was dominated by its sense of guilt for the Holocaust and the latter by the influence of “the Jewish lobby.” The unfortunate choice of words in that post is extremely obvious: While it is true that there is a very strong pro-Israel lobby, and that it is indeed possible that many Jews are part of it, it is wrong to speak of a “Jewish lobby.” Beyond being offensive to the Jewish people, such a formulation also overlooks the role of other groups in supporting Israel — for instance, Christian Zionists for whom the return of the Jews to the Holy Land is seen as the fulfillment of a biblical prophecy, and whose religious fervor has exerted dangerous influence in the United States and beyond. What was even more problematic in my wording was the failure to distinguish between Zionist Jews — especially those who claim exclusive Jewish sovereignty “from the river to the sea” (a project that is discriminatory in nature and, as such, prohibited by international treaties, such as the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination) — and Jews who oppose this vision, or who simply do not wish to be identified with this political project. In other words, Israel does not represent all Jews, just as Italy, Spain, or the United States do not represent all Catholics.

#### It was December 15, 2022, and I remember every twist and turn of that day when this news spread rapidly, generating a broad echo, and I suddenly saw my head as Special Rapporteur rolling down the hill and ending up in the mud. But once again my Israeli friends and comrades came to my aid. That very evening, I connected via video conference with Alon and five others, who had read the news and were willing to help me deal with the situation. I *still have the image of Alon, in his studio in Massachusetts, telling me: “Don’t panic, Francesca. You can’t apologize. They will mop the floor with your face if you apologize. You will have to distance yourself from the* words you used, which were clearly infelicitous.” I had to understand what I had done wrong and own it, take responsibility for it as any mature person in good faith would do with a mistake made out of ignorance rather than ill or “anti-Semitic” intentions, which I clearly did not have. All the more, they encouraged me, do not take it *personally; that attack had nothing to do with me but rather aimed to distract me and the general attention from the* real issue. The focus of the discussion — Alon insisted — had to remain absolutely on the systemic and structural violence to which the Palestinians were subjected.

#### *Alon was very good with words, sophisticated in thought as well as expression, so the concept of the infelicitous* words proved to be fundamental to my public response, in which I asserted that the terms used at the time were not the same as those I would use now, that I was more educated on the matter, even more so in view of my mandate. That also turned into an opportunity to use the space created around the controversy to address the topic of anti-Semitism and articulate the distinction between heinous discrimination against Jews and mere criticism of the government of Israel.

#### The words of Alon, but also of Amos and of Daniel Levy, a former Israeli peace negotiator of whom I later became a huge admirer, had strengthened my position, helping me to build an armor around my commitment that still accompanies me today. Holding my head high in the face of such fury on that occasion earned me the respect of many sectors of civil society, including various progressive Jewish groups and many intellectuals who have since often mobilized in my support against the incessant accusations that have rained down on me.

#### For example, Avi Shlaim, a well-known Israeli historian and professor at Oxford University, published a letter a few days after that media assault in which he wrote: “The three main pillars of Judaism are truth, justice, and peace.

#### Albanese embodies these values to a remarkably high degree. And there will be many Jews worldwide, disturbed by Israel’s betrayal of these core Jewish values.” In those difficult days, his words had a political and personal meaning that I will never forget. The whole affair only strengthened the collaboration and mutual esteem between Alon and me.

#### —

#### *AT THE START OF 2023, at the initiative of the Italian journal Altreconomia, Tino Magni, an Italian senator from a left* party, invited me to present my report on self-determination to the Italian Senate, and I suggested that Alon be involved as well. Despite pressure from the Israeli embassy in Italy not to hold that event, I arrived in Rome enthusiastic to face this institutional moment in my country having a figure of Alon’s intellectual and human caliber next to me. Also, I was delighted to finally be able to meet him in person.

#### We arranged to meet in the afternoon the day before the presentation at a bookshop in the center of Rome. There I found this distinguished gentleman with an umbrella under his arm and a head of voluminous white hair moving in the breeze, which gave him the air of a person who does not take himself too seriously. We greeted each other and started walking. The destination was to walk, to keep talking, wherever our feet might lead us.

#### We walked for a long time through the streets of the Jewish Ghetto, we went to a bookstore, and we spent a lovely evening eating artichokes, drinking, discussing music and books along with a couple of friends of mine. I remember that at the end of the dinner, when we said goodbye after sending a selfie to Amos in Jerusalem, Alon laughed and said to me: “I wonder if anyone noticed that I was with you at dinner…Will I be safe crossing the Ghetto alone, at night?”

#### The next morning, we met near the Senate to make our presentation. They hosted us in a magnificent room, and we had the opportunity to touch on themes that were deeply felt by both of us. It was a beautiful event, and I appreciated immensely not only that Alon went out of his way to defend my reputation with his unquestionable authority but also the words he used, which in Italy are so rarely heard in relation to Palestine and Israel. Alon began his speech by talking about anti-Semitism, explaining its origin and evolution. He recalled that the term had been coined in 1879, marking a turning point in the nature of hatred of the Jews, which changed from religious to racial and political. He then spoke about the subject that first allowed us to get to know each other, namely the ideological use of the accusation of anti-Semitism, pointing out that too often it is used to silence well-founded and legitimate criticism of Israel and Zionism, thus diverting attention from the human rights of the Palestinians. According to Alon, “The accusation of anti-Semitism is often an ideological weapon against individuals, academics, journalists who dare to support equal civil, cultural, economic, political, and social rights for Palestinians or denounce violations of international law in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.”

#### Alon also addressed the complex position of Israeli Jews, saying that they can be both victims and aggressors to the extent that Israel, although born out of the ashes of the Holocaust, today exercises oppressive rule over the Palestinians. He criticized the politicization of the memory of the Holocaust, reiterating that it cannot be used to justify human rights violations, and precisely for this reason he insisted on the need to distinguish between anti-Semitism and anti-Zionism, arguing that “talking about political aspects of Zionism and Israel is not anti-Semitism, *it is part of the conversation and the debate we must have.”*

#### He felt it was his duty to denounce the apartheid to which the Palestinians were subjected, precisely in the name of his Judaism and his love for Israel. In the same way, I feel that it is also a duty for me, as an observer in this disturbing period in which Palestinians are being massacred and at the same time blamed and vilified in many influential quarters, as are those who defend and support them. I feel a sense of responsibility as a European who is aware of what Europeans have done for centuries, and as an Italian who is aware that Italians participated in the Holocaust, in the name of a racist ideology, less than a century ago. I fear that these ideologies may reemerge, and therefore I strive every day, with all the means at my disposal, to create a social fabric that will nip them in the bud.

#### In my speech that day, alongside Alon, I spoke of self-determination as the right to exist as a people, a right that cannot be negotiated — as I wrote in my report, “violations of international law should not be subject to negotiation, since this would legitimize what is illegal” — stressing that for too long the Palestinian issue has been reduced to a humanitarian crisis, instead of being dealt with as a political issue to be resolved in accordance with international law. To confine ourselves to giving aid without addressing the structural causes of the crisis is to perpetuate injustice by normalizing it, rather than doing everything possible to eradicate it. Furthermore, I challenged the narrative that presents the situation in Palestine as a “conflict,” when in fact it is a structural condition of domination and oppression, which falls within the paradigm of settler colonialism.

#### I explained that the Israeli occupation is not temporary but is part of a broader project that combines settler colonialism, apartheid, and military occupation. It is not possible to talk about development or “economic peace”

#### without first ending domination, and that continuing to inject money and humanitarian aid is comparable to trying to mop the floor without fixing the leak, and on this the international community has failed, by adopting inadequate paradigms that do not address the roots of the problem. The basis of everything is the Palestinian people’s fundamental right to self-determination, a collective right that has been violated continuously for decades.

#### It seems obvious to me that this analysis has nothing to do with anti-Semitism, but only with the urge to apply the international laws that states have ratified. Laws are such — and therefore have the power to delimit the perimeter of politics, distinguishing what is granted from what is forbidden — only if they can be considered objective and universal, and therefore they must be guaranteed to every person on Earth.

#### I was happy that day to be able to speak in a formal and public setting of the hope that I see above all in the younger generations: certainly among the Palestinians, but also in international civil society, and among many Jews in the diaspora, especially in the United States. I explained that, in my opinion, most of the debates on various social demands are articulated, or should be articulated, through the language of human rights, which shows us how politics often arrives late or sometimes even opposes change. I gave the example of apartheid in South Africa, recalling that it had not been dismantled because, suddenly, other states had witnessed those atrocities and decided to act on their own initiative and impose sanctions. On the contrary. At first, many Western governments resisted both the condemnation and the idea of demanding accountability, until they found themselves practically forced to recognize that they could not oppose a global campaign of support for the anti-apartheid movement.

#### In the end, they had to give in to a reality they could no longer ignore. Yet that change had not come from above; it had also been the result of an internal struggle within South African society itself and years of mobilization of civil society throughout the world.

#### These words, spoken from that podium, with the support of many interviews published in various newspapers, had resonance in Italy. And since Alon was who he was, no one dared to attack him nearly as fiercely as they did me. His reputation, his temperament, that day, were a wonderful demonstration of how unity can really be strength.

#### —

#### AFTER THE MEETING, we went for a walk around Rome again. Alon was a great intellectual, he had a powerful way of speaking and made you feel the strength of his ideas; yet at the same time he showed himself to be a simple, gracious, lighthearted man. After lunch with the journalists, the first thing he said to me was: “Come on, let’s go to the Colosseum, so we can take a picture to send to Amos and make him die of envy!”

#### There was no break between the friendly chat, the conversations regarding his beloved companion, Tal, and his children, who lived in Israel, and the continuation of the discussion we had started a few hours earlier at the Senate. I even remember that at a certain point, just as we arrived near the Colosseum, I was saying something to him like: “Don’t you believe that European Jews went to Palestine because they had nowhere else to go, and not because they really felt they had a connection with that land?” The narrative about why the Jewish state had settled in Palestine seemed a bit flat to me. Certainly, compared to other countries such as Argentina or Uganda, Palestine had a biblical appeal, but it also had much less available land. “So for all intents and purposes we can call it settler colonialism, right?” I continued. “Because the European Zionists would not have gone to Palestine if they had not in some way exploited or emphasized the religious element.”

#### At that point Alon stopped in the middle of the street, burst out laughing, and said to me: “Well, Francesca, if you were one of my students, now you would risk failing the exam!” And then, in a more serious tone: “It’s not really like that. What you say is not accurate. But maybe I can try to explain it better.”

#### And there, against the backdrop of the Colosseum, he spoke to me at length about the complex matrix of the claims for self-determination of European Jews. We didn’t even try to enter the Colosseum to see it from the inside, since the line was too long and we were both immersed in that conversation, so we stayed there on a bench chatting. “There is much more for us. The Jewish people have a very strong bond with that land and with Jerusalem in particular. It is our history. Obviously, the fact that there is this link between us and the land does not mean that we are the masters of it. But we must always be able to present the complexity of the historical process, including the fact that there was indeed nowhere else where many of us could feel safer. That is an important point. After the Holocaust, it’s not that we were suddenly protected, it’s not that at some point everybody opened their eyes and said, ‘Oh, poor Jews, let’s help them.’ No, they still didn’t want us. No one wanted us in Europe. We were the plague victims; we had to somehow disappear from their gaze. Because the Europeans could not even tolerate the idea that there were Jews who were victims of everything that had happened.”

#### Alon was not opposed to the idea of using the paradigm of settler colonialism in reference to Israel. “However,” he told me that afternoon, “we need to understand well what the specificities of Israel’s settler colonialism are. Because at the base there has always been a very strong bond with those places, and it would be wrong to say that

#### the interest of the Jews in Jerusalem and Palestine is false and only an excuse. The love for that land is deeply rooted in our history and our culture.”

#### His words were poignant. Since that conversation, I have always carried with me the thought that the State of Israel gave protection, legitimacy, visibility to the Jewish people and to European Jews during a historical phase in which a very strong and widespread anti-Semitism was still alive, making them, as a collective, feel they had a safe place for the first time in history. This understanding for me will always remain linked to Alon and that afternoon on the streets of Rome.

#### Even more important and unforgettable was the smile with which Alon ended the conversation, taking out his telephone and approaching me: “Come on, let’s send the photo to Amos and then, even if it’s cold, I would like to get some ice cream, what do you think?” I don’t remember if we really went to get an ice-cream cone. Certainly, however, we went from there to Trastevere, across the river, always walking and chatting, and then again to eat artichokes with my friend Rania Hammad, the daughter of the historic representative of the PLO in Italy, Nimer Hammad, and other friends. Parting in that jovial atmosphere was a nice way to say goodbye; and anyway, Alon and I already had a plan to see each other shortly thereafter.

#### In March 2023 we were organizing Alon’s participation in the presentation of my report in Geneva, when, on a video call of which I vividly remember his green pullover and imperceptibly troubled face, he said to me: “Do you know that I don’t know if I can come? I’m not so well, I have to do some tests.”

#### A couple of weeks later, in April, Alon was diagnosed with leukemia and his torment began. In the meantime, I was drafting my second report on the deprivation of personal liberty in Palestine, and Alon, along with Amos, proved again to be very supportive, reading various versions and giving me their comments, even while Alon was undergoing chemotherapy. After that, our correspondence thinned out and I tried to involve him less, because I realized that he was getting very tired.

#### —

#### THEN, SUDDENLY, history went crazy again. October 7th exploded in our face with incredible violence. Just a couple of weeks later I went to the United States to present my report on childhood under occupation, which went completely unnoticed despite the fact that it was, as Amos said, “heavy in everything”: the numbers of children killed, injured, maimed as a result of the various wars and attacks, the catastrophic situation of the lack of care which subsequently degenerated disastrously, but which even before October 7th was unbearable for many. Since 2006, it had been impossible for Palestinians to leave Gaza and almost nothing had entered without Israel’s consent, and this meant that no treatment was available for otherwise treatable diseases like diabetes. There have been children requiring special treatment that is unavailable in Gaza, who died within the walls of their homes because they did not have the necessary permission to go outside Gaza to be examined by a specialist or to receive the necessary medicines.

#### Yet, all this did not seem to be important to anyone. On the contrary, in Europe and other Western countries the focus of many people in power, for a long time, continued to be the attacks of October 7th, which were defined as “the worst anti-Semitic attack since the Holocaust.” Even the French president Emmanuel Macron, to whom one fine day I replied publicly, on social media: “The ‘greatest anti-Semitic massacre of our century’? No, Mr. Macron. The victims of October 7th were not killed because of their Judaism but in reaction to Israeli oppression. France and the international community have done nothing to prevent this. My respects to the victims.” This cost me the interruption of relations with French diplomacy, to put it mildly, but even in that case I could rely on the important words that Alon was writing in those months, which I drew on as a gift. He and Amos, along with other scholars of *the Holocaust and anti-Semitism, had signed an article in The New York Review of Books in November 2023 in* which they criticized the instrumental use of historical memory to justify the aggression in Gaza. They denounced efforts to equate Hamas to the “new Nazis,” to attribute to the Palestinians a collective responsibility, and discredit those who defended their rights. They stressed the importance of distinguishing between Hamas and the Palestinian population as a whole, and warned that “the confusion between anti-Semitism and criticism of Israel” not only undermines the fight against real anti-Semitism but also legitimizes the repression of dissent and the erasure of the Palestinian cause from public debate.

#### In October 2023, the very day I set foot in the United States, I called Alon and said: “I’m coming to see you.” He was not well, and replied: “Excuse me, but I am not in a condition to see anyone, my immune defenses are

#### very low, I can’t have you come to my home, I’m sorry.” But at the suggestion of Amos, I took the liberty of insisting and in the end, we decided that I would visit him in

#### Boston and, instead of seeing each other at his home, we would go out somewhere. We met in a restaurant, where I finally met his partner, the wonderful Tal. We had found a completely empty

#### place where we could see each other while keeping a distance, and he never took off his mask. We stayed a long time, chatting away and, effectively thwarting our efforts to take all those precautions, we ended the evening by embracing each other.

#### Alon was very dejected, and not only because of his health. He said: “Israel is finished. Now I really see the end of it, but I no longer have the strength to do anything.”

#### That was the last time I saw him. Alon Confino died on June 27, 2024.

# INGRID

#### *How do you overthrow apartheid?*

#### The naked man lifted his arms from his head. He had fallen and he stared about him. He stared at the one who had struck him, blood was

#### coursing down his face, and the bitch Gudrun caught the smell of his blood. *“Fange ihn!,” said the captain. Gudrun bit into the man, tearing open his shoulder. “An die Gurgel,” said the captain.*

#### *— ELIO VITTORINI, Men and Not Men*

#### THE FIRST TIME I HEARD an articulate speech on the need to define the situation in Palestine as apartheid was in May 2017, at a conference organized in Jordan by academics and Arab civil society. Now it seems an obvious notion, but until a few years ago it was not obvious at all.

#### Let’s start with the assumption that there are various instruments of international law to protect people, such as human rights treaties and, in situations of armed conflict, international humanitarian law (IHL). These were adopted after the two world wars basically to make conflicts less atrocious and to protect the civilian population as much as possible from the horror of war, but they also elevate individuals — and so not only, or not anymore only, states — to be subjects of law in the international sphere.

#### Human rights have not been gifted to us. Each of them is the result of the struggles and achievements of individuals like us. The slave trade was eliminated thanks in part to the abolitionist movement; apartheid and racial segregation were banned thanks to real civil battles; and in the same way we have made important steps forward in the rights of workers, women, minors, people who are differently abled. The path to human rights is not linear, and the mission is never properly accomplished.

#### —

#### BUT LET’S GET BACK to Palestine. Until a few years ago, the main — if not the only — legal framework of reference for many, in relation to the

#### Occupied Palestinian Territory, was that of IHL, that is, the laws of war and military occupation, according to which military occupation is accepted only if temporary, if it is linked to specific military needs, and if it takes place in full respect of the rights of the civilian population.

#### Israel, instead, has occupied Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem since 1967 without time limits or valid justification. The United Nations itself had called for its withdrawal, with a resolution approved a few months after the beginning of the occupation (Security Council Resolution 242), recalling that it is never legitimate to acquire territories by force.

#### Yet Israel not only has ignored that resolution but has extended its presence in the occupied territory, including the Syrian Golan Heights and recently swaths of southern Syria and Lebanon, none of which my UN mandate covers, replacing the local authorities with Israeli military personnel, imposing military law, expropriating land, demolishing homes, and building more than three hundred colonies, where about eight hundred thousand Israeli settlers live today. All this, even though such actions are recognized as illegal by international law. Two of the *fundamental principles of the Charter of the United Nations are respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples [Article 1(2)] and the prohibition of the threat or use of force against the territorial* integrity or political independence of any state [Article 2(4)]. Accordingly, the International Court of Justice has repeatedly reiterated that an occupying power must guarantee the fundamental rights of the occupied population and cannot impede the realization of the right to self-determination.

#### In Palestine, however, fundamental rights are not guaranteed, and the Palestinians are denied their right to self-determination.

#### To cover up its violations of international law, Israel has used terms such as “disputed” instead of “occupied” territory, of a “hostile” instead of an “occupied” population. The international community has also often preferred to cling to such terms rather than decisively address the unacceptable reality of permanent occupation and its consequences.

#### Meanwhile, in the shadow of this debate about terminology rather than actions, Israel has continued systematically to bulldoze not only the territories but also international law, distorting the very essence of law and justice. The illegality of this conduct is irremediable, because it touches one of the cornerstones of the international order, that it is the rule of law that must govern relations between states, not the arbitrary will of the strongest.

#### —

#### THE YEAR 2017 was another powerful intellectual turning point for me, like the eye-opening experience of attending the School of Oriental and African Studies in 2005.

#### At a conference I attended in Jordan, Michael Lynk — my predecessor in the role of UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territory — explained why, based on the case law relating to South Africa’s occupation of Rhodesia and Namibia (then called South-West Africa), the Israeli occupation of Palestine and the West Bank should be considered illegal.

#### In a nutshell, the jurisprudence of the International Court of Justice had established that the South African presence in South-West Africa was illegal precisely because a) it did not respond to military purposes and b) it violated the fundamental obligations of the occupying power. These obligations provide that occupation must safeguard the well-being of the occupied population and not subjugate it, alter its identity, or change the status of the territory or the occupied population’s legal system. Furthermore, South Africa’s occupation had not been temporary: It had turned into a permanent condition.

#### —

#### AS MICHAEL STATED THAT DAY in relation to the Namibia case, military occupation can never be considered a vehicle for the unlawful acquisition of territory, or annexation, and because this is what Israel’s occupation in the West *Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza was doing, it was unlawful. Bingo! With those words, he had broken a barrier. If the* occupation is unlawful, then it must not be normalized at all: Every aspect of an occupation must be monitored constantly and its end must be imposed, it cannot and must not become permanent.

#### My tenure at the United Nations had ended five years before that conference, but as I listened to Michael, he took me back to the time I had worked in Palestine, and suddenly everything became clearer. In my years in Palestine, I had often asked myself these kinds of questions: Why do we continue to refer to and rely on international humanitarian law, when the military occupation that this body of law regulates is serving to take away the land and destroy the lives of the occupied people?

#### The fact that the legal instrument of IHL had become inadequate to protect people was a notion that was somehow already present in me, but the words of my predecessor were important and, looking back, I said to myself: “Michael Lynk is right.”

#### After Michael, Ingrid Jaradat Gassner, a longtime expert on Palestine, addressed the conference. Continuing the analysis of the most appropriate legal framework to apply to the Palestinian situation, Ingrid insisted on the use of the concept of apartheid. At the time, talking about apartheid in relation to Israel’s conduct was not at all usual, especially outside of certain activist circles. The scope of what Ingrid said was so revolutionary that many of us did not fully understand it. Proof of this is that, in the scientific volume on Palestinian refugees on which I was working at that time with Lex Takkenberg, we considered the apartheid regime only marginally. Although Ingrid was not a jurist, her contribution proved essential to the development of an integrated interpretation of all the rules protecting individuals and groups.

#### Ingrid was Dutch but had been living in Palestine for a long time, in Beit Jala, near Bethlehem, in the occupied West Bank. In 1998, she and her husband, Mohammed Jaradat, were among the founders of BADIL Resource Center for Palestinian Residency and Refugee Rights. In 2005, she cofounded Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS), inspired by the global resistance against apartheid in South Africa and based on international law. The movement was born shortly after a major advisory opinion in 2004 by the International Court of Justice, which ruled that the construction of the wall started two years earlier and Israel’s practices in the West Bank and occupied Jerusalem were in serious violation of international law and the fundamental rights of Palestinians, such as freedom

#### of movement, access to essential resources and services, and, above all, the right to self-determination of the Palestinian people.

#### —

#### THAT WALL, which cuts off the Palestinians from Jerusalem and which even today, more than twenty years later, no one has managed to demolish, greatly reduces their possibilities. A group of people within a city like Jerusalem, surrounded on one side by Israel and on the other three sides by colonies in the occupied territory, cannot sustain an economy when their contacts with those outside the city have been severed. The wall also prevents families from staying together and in contact, as well as Christians and Muslims from going to Jerusalem to pray.

#### The landmark decision of the International Court of Justice was based on the right to self-determination, a right so central that, according to the law on the international responsibility of states, it must be upheld by all the member states of the United Nations and implies an obligation for all of them not to recognize the illegitimate situation created by the occupation and to take action to ensure compliance with international standards, including human rights. Therefore, UN member countries would be obliged not to assist or support the occupation in any way, and also to ask for the demolition of the wall.

#### From a legal point of view, the decision of the International Court of Justice was epochal, because it was the first time that a court had ruled on the Israeli-Palestinian issue.

#### Yet, from a practical point of view, the decision changed nothing. This is how in 2005, in response to the inaction of states after that pronouncement, BDS was created: a

#### grassroots movement with the intention of promoting boycott, divestment, and sanctions against Israel to push it to return to the rule of international law and to comply with the principles of human rights. A perfect example, in my eyes, of what civil society should be: the immune system of a healthy society that respects universal rules, both nationally and internationally.

#### The movement Ingrid cofounded was inspired by the movement against apartheid in South Africa, which had conducted a major boycott, disinvestment, and sanctions campaign before states decided to act. Even today we cannot think of South Africa without the word “apartheid” coming to mind, but in that case the bulk of the work was done from below, and it all started from civil society, or rather from a single person: a young worker, who had decided to take the practical actions that were within her capacity.

#### It began in Ireland in 1984, when Mary Manning, a twenty-one-year-old supermarket cashier, in accordance with the directives of her union, refused to handle grapefruit from South Africa. When Manning and her union representative, Karen Gearon, continued to refuse to handle any South African products, calling on the other workers to do the same, they were suspended and started a strike that was joined by eight other colleagues.

#### The strike lasted almost three years, until April 1987, and set off a chain reaction that led Ireland to become the first Western country to impose a total ban on the import of South African goods, thanks to public pressure aroused by the courageous refusal of Mary and her colleagues.

#### The ban remained in place until the end of the apartheid regime in 1994. Nelson Mandela himself recognized the value of their gesture in 1990 when he was awarded honorary citizenship of Dublin. On that occasion, Mandela declared that the strikers had shown South Africans that ordinary people far from the scene had played a pioneering role in the struggle against apartheid. This thought, he said, had also helped him to resist in prison. But that’s not all. When Archbishop Desmond Tutu was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984 and invited the Irish protesters to attend the ceremony, the anti-apartheid movement that was born in Ireland was hit by a wave of support that fueled growing opposition to apartheid, taking a decisive step toward bringing down this system.

#### —

#### TO MAKE THEM COLLAPSE, oppressive regimes must be struck at their heart, that is, in their pockets, which is where they receive the proceeds of exploitation. This is the philosophy underpinning BDS, which in fact undertakes to publicly expose international complicity — not only political but also economic — with the apartheid regime imposed by the State of Israel on the Palestinians. The apartheid analysis of the Palestinian situation, which Ingrid helped to develop, has also been taken up and strengthened by various human rights associations.

#### It is only recently that the apartheid framework has started to become common in describing the situation in occupied Palestine, after Palestinians and certain daring academics and politicians — e.g., Jimmy Carter in *Palestine: Peace Not Apartheid — had used the concept for decades. In particular, two Israeli nongovernmental* organizations that deal with documenting Israel’s human rights violations in the occupied territory have helped mainstream the apartheid framework linked to the Israeli occupation. In 2020, Yesh Din spoke of apartheid limited

#### to the West Bank, where Israel applies two distinct legal systems: one for Israeli settlers, the other for Palestinians. In 2021, B’Tselem published a high-impact report, accompanied by an iconic presentation to the UN Security Council by then-director Hagai El-Ad, in which he said that Israel imposed an apartheid regime on all Palestinians from the shore to the sea, that is, “from the River Jordan to the Mediterranean.” According to B’Tselem, Israel effectively controls the entire space between the Jordan River and the sea, ensuring the supremacy of Israeli Jews at the expense of Palestinians. The apartheid policies they identified included the political and territorial fragmentation of Palestinians, unequal access to land and resources, restriction of movement, and a discriminatory legal system, based on emergency laws, military orders, and regulations, such as the 2018 law recognizing the right to self-determination “only to the Jewish people.”

#### In 2021, Human Rights Watch reinforced these analyses in a detailed report, calling Israeli apartheid an institutionalized system of domination and oppression. The report concluded that Israel was not only committing the crime of apartheid but also persecution, that is, the systematic and intentional deprivation of a group’s fundamental rights. “The Israeli authorities methodically privilege Israeli Jews and repress Palestinians,” with the stated aim of maintaining demographic, political, and territorial control.

#### In 2022, Amnesty International confirmed that Israel practices apartheid both in the occupied territory and within its borders, adding that the system also involves Palestinian refugees, who are excluded from the right of return to the property that they or their ancestors were forced by the Israelis to leave in 1948 and 1967. In its report, Amnesty International explicitly indicates that “the Israeli authorities and others involved must dismantle the system of apartheid against the Palestinians and put an end to the related human rights violations.”

#### So then, is Israel an apartheid state or not? According to international law, it certainly is. The Israeli occupation of Palestine is a system created to maintain the supremacy of one racial group over another through discriminatory and oppressive practices. Although historically one immediately thinks of the South African regime, the International Convention on the Suppression and Punishment of the Crime of Apartheid classifies it as a crime against humanity that any state can commit by means of inhuman gestures — such as forced deportations, illegal arrests, torture, and restrictions on freedom of movement — carried out to systematically oppress one racial group, keeping it under control in favor of another. The Rome Statute also classifies apartheid as a crime against humanity, in that it consists of acts committed “in the context of a widespread or systematic attack against civilian populations.”

#### It is not just a question of discrimination but of the denial of fundamental rights, of the separation of people on racial and territorial grounds, and of the use of coercive measures to keep the oppressed group isolated and subordinate.

#### Thus, broadening the perspective beyond the case of South Africa, the characteristic of apartheid is institutionalized segregation that has as its objective the domination of one group over another, something which, on closer inspection, is also the pillar of, especially, settler colonialism. Who would say that France in Algeria or King Leopold’s Belgium in the Congo did not practice an apartheid regime? Apartheid can exist — and certainly does exist — even in contexts of colonialism that are different and much broader than those with which we customarily associate the term.

#### —

#### ONLY A FEW YEARS AGO, even in 2022, when I became Special Rapporteur of the United Nations, talking about apartheid in relation to Israel — as my predecessor, Professor Michael Lynk, had done in March of that year — seemed very difficult, so much so that some people in international diplomatic circles limited themselves to whispering “the A word,” as if “apartheid” were an expletive. Today, awareness of the nature of the occupation is already much more widespread and I am sure that in a few years the word “apartheid” will automatically be associated with the State of Israel, as it was in the past with South Africa.

#### —

#### IN THE CASE OF ISRAEL, its many violations must include millions of lives broken, killed, maimed in body and soul, and a destroyed Gaza. The genocide that has been going on since October 2023 cannot be erased from the history of the State of Israel, and I suspect that the whole world will feel a chill on seeing the Israeli flag, for what has been done in its name and under its aegis.

#### Today we are experiencing this reality without being fully aware of it, because humans need time and distance to observe and reflect. But we must not forget that the longer this time lasts, the more innocent people will die. That is why it is essential to continue to explain what we are facing and to support the movement of reaction necessary to

#### counter it. Even simply informing oneself and others is an important contribution to defeating apartheid. Of course, in the case of South Africa the apartheid policy had much less support than that enjoyed by the State

#### of Israel today, which comes from multiple and varied sources. Here, we are not dealing merely with a substantial part of the Israeli administration but also with the vast network that has been built up throughout the Western world and beyond, through hyperactive embassies and refined communication techniques that market Israel as “the only democracy in the Middle East” and “the start-up nation.” This new narrative has replaced the slogans in vogue at the time of Golda Meir: “A state that made the desert flourish” and “A people without land for a land without people.”

#### Israel is now supported by the political, cultural, and financial elites of various countries, first and foremost the United States, thanks in part to a very effective political lobbying structure and to the connivance of Israel’s military *apparatus with the powerful American war industry (a very interesting book by Antony Loewenstein, The Palestinian Laboratory, analyzes these relationships in depth).*

#### Another important component is represented by the now ubiquitous Christian Zionist groups, which are very active, especially in the United States. Based on conservative interpretations of the Bible, they see the “return of the Jews to Palestine” as a fulfillment of prophecy and support for Israel as an integral part of their faith, thus significantly influencing US foreign policy. Moreover, Christian Zionism is booming even in the Global Majority, or Global South, where Christian proselytism carries with it, in an increasingly ubiquitous way, the Israeli flag. To cope with such massive obstacles, BDS has had to organize itself in a much more structured way than the antiapartheid movement in South Africa. Within BDS, therefore, the Palestinians have created the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel, which promotes the boycott of Israeli academic and cultural institutions that are complicit with or loyal to the occupation, apartheid, and the denial of Palestinian rights — and a widespread transnational network of organizations and experts who support calls for specific boycotts, divestments, and sanctions, weaving the web of peaceful, strategic, and active resistance to Israeli apartheid.

#### This is where the economic factor comes into play, which leads me to say: If Palestine were the scene of a crime, all of our fingerprints would be found there. There are many companies, pension funds, banks, foundations, organizations from various countries that continue to invest in the Israeli economy, and this is of course an inextricable element of the occupation. While the strong sectors of the Israeli economy, such as armaments and surveillance, are the most obvious, it is important to remember that any investment in the Israeli economy may have an implication or connection with the occupation and exploitation of Palestinians and their resources, and thus become a de facto act connected to criminal conduct. Just like the grapefruits that Mary Manning refused to pass through her supermarket register forty years ago. My June 2025 report “From the Economy of Occupation to the Economy of Genocide” focuses on this type of economic linkages and must have hit a nerve so sensitive that the US administration sanctioned me a few days after its publication.

#### Faced with a situation like this, the call of the BDS movement — which is fully in line with international law — must be supported in every possible way: from what we buy to how we invest, from where we go on vacation to whom you elect to office. Each of us is called upon to make “apartheid-free” choices. Justice for Palestine begins with the steps each of us takes.

#### This justice is becoming more necessary every day, given the crimes that Israel continues to commit today. South African whites never reached a degree of violence intended to annihilate the entire Black population; their goal was to segregate and dominate rather than to exterminate. Today, in Israel-Palestine, the reality is completely different. Denouncing and overcoming apartheid, which could have been a great opportunity for change, has instead become a missed opportunity, especially after the catastrophic events following October 2023.

#### —

#### AT THE END OF MARCH 2025, my friend and former colleague Lex Takkenberg, with whom I worked on the book on the history and legislation concerning Palestinian refugees, wrote to me: “These days we really need Ingrid. I miss talking to her, discussing, understanding.”

#### Ingrid was a constant source of inspiration and positivity. On my visits to Bethlehem, during the period in which I was teaching at the local university, I happened to meet her several times, and also to visit her in the beautiful stone house covered with climbing flowers where she lives with her husband, in a quiet area, far from the buzz of Bethlehem and the Church of the Nativity, which was built around the cave where Jesus is said to have been born.

#### The last time I saw her, in 2019, we had arranged to meet right there, basically because getting to Ingrid’s house, with my painful Arabic, would have been a nightmare for me and for the unfortunate taxi driver. The stone walls of the Grotto of the Nativity, covered with flickering candles, create an intimate and mystical atmosphere; and although I did not feel any particularly religious call, in front of the silver star that marks the supposed birthplace of Jesus I could not help feeling a deep respect for the sacredness of that place and for the history and hopes of so many who

#### venerate him. It was a very short meeting: Ingrid was called away by commitments elsewhere. A pity, because I was going through a delicate period and felt the need to be reassured by someone whom I trusted and respected. Lex and I had just finished our book and launched a consultation involving Palestinian civil society, some Israeli scholars *and activists, and international experts on the durable solutions for Palestinian refugees that we proposed in the final* chapter. Under international law, we affirmed that Palestinians have the right to return, compensation, and self-determination, but we also affirmed that anyone — from refugee camps in Lebanon, Syria, or Jordan, or from Egypt and other parts of the world where the people of Palestine live as stateless people — who wishes to move elsewhere *and apply for citizenship should be able to access opportunities for resettlement, or legal transfer.*

#### This last proposal, however, aroused suspicion among many Palestinians, some even accusing me of promoting a “pro-Israeli” agenda and of wanting to threaten the right of return.

#### I knew that Ingrid had understood my intentions when I spoke of a policy of rights against the “policy of pain” promoted by those who want to keep the refugees in the camps at all costs, waiting for their right of return to be honored even though, in the seventy-seven years that have passed since the Nakba, that return has not moved one millimeter closer.

#### But on that day, I kept those thoughts to myself and, having said goodbye to Ingrid, I went to seek out a little silence in the church that was built in memory of a Palestinian born two thousand years ago, who must necessarily have been dark-skinned, because with very rare exceptions, populations of blond people with fair complexions had not arrived in those parts; a church where, during the second intifada, the young people of the Palestine resistance had gone to take refuge to avoid being besieged and beaten — of course, without success.

#### Every time I see the Basilica of the Nativity I cannot help but think of the birth of that boy and his crucifixion, which today I seem to see again in the destruction of his people, who have tried to resist but are succumbing. If we make the effort to view this people organically, as a body that has resisted with all its strength, that has sacrificed itself to defend itself, perhaps our perspective of Palestinian resistance to the Israeli occupation will also change.

#### Understanding resistance does not, of course, mean justifying violence against Israeli civilians, but it allows us to see that it arises first and foremost in response to the destruction of a people that is now reaching its final phase.

#### In Palestine today there is essentially no room for resistance; some fight here and there but they can’t make it: They have no weapons to face the most impressive army in the Middle East, supported by the strongest military power in the world. Many no longer have the strength to react; they can’t get back on their feet. It is not an equal fight, and in unequal struggles those who have no means defend themselves as best they can.

#### We are no longer in the era of Italian partisans or decolonization after the Second World War, when resistance was seen as something heroic; today we have forgotten that Mandela entered prison to serve almost thirty years on terrorism charges, and that it was only in 2008 that the United States removed his name from the terrorist blacklist. We have forgotten that in the eyes of the Nazis the Italian partisans were terrorists, and that within a mechanism between oppressor and oppressed each person can be seen as a terrorist by some and as a hero by others.

#### Unfortunately, resistance is sometimes also violence, and it is usually all the more violent the more violent the oppression. Right now the Palestinians are desperate. If every people is like a body, the Palestinian body has been belted many times, for a very long time, and today even more so.

#### I was a child at the time of the first intifada in 1987, but I will never forget the images I saw on TV, squeezed on the sofa between my brother and my mother, with police vans taking the boys who threw stones and blindfolding them. There was this boy in a green shirt, his curly head and eyes covered, I remember the soldiers who held his arm and broke his bones with stones. I remember the Palestinians who were on the ground, attacked by dogs…How many years have the Palestinians suffered like this, and how much are they suffering now that cruelty is overflowing any conceivable barrier?

#### In this strange spring of 2025, it is difficult for me to imagine the future. It is almost impossible for me to imagine a rebuilt Gaza except as a great monument commemorating the genocide, but that does not mean that I see the end of the Palestinian people: The Palestinians will rise again, but now the Israelis are tearing apart the body of this oppressed people, just as the Roman politicians did two thousand years ago with the body of that boy. And we are called to ask ourselves if we want to be part of the ranks of those who wash their hands of it, of those who, paraphrasing Fernando Pessoa, will be condemned to suffer from the wounds of the battles they have not fought.

#### Beyond my inveterate anticlericalism, I think that Jesus was a revolutionary of love, one who was not afraid to *go to the Temple to make a credible ammuìna, as we say in my area. He was aware that he was bringing with him a* higher, more human, and salvific truth than that proclaimed by the sages of his time, the men of the Temple. He did *not limit himself to making the revolution, he was the revolution, with all of himself and in every act of his life,* without normalizing anything: That is what we must do too.

#### *Either we commit ourselves to being the revolution or we will fail, because no change can happen in the world if* it does not first happen within us. We must strip ourselves, one preconception at a time, of all the baggage that each

#### of us carries in order to go more and more toward the truth every day.

#### —

#### INGRID JARADAT GASSNER was a tireless and silent revolutionary. Her revolution was expressed in the way she used the international regulatory system like a Lego box, seeing all the pieces of the legal system at her disposal, dismantling them and putting them back together to strengthen rights and ensure protection. By explaining how the apartheid framework applies to Palestine, Ingrid revealed what our eyes could not yet see. Here too it is important to do the exercise of always considering the Palestinian people organically, as a single body. That is why we must not forget that even the refugees who are outside their land are still victims of apartheid, which controls them by other means — for example by preventing them from returning.

#### Refugees are an integral part of the Palestinian issue, and by helping to set up the BADIL research center, Ingrid helped to do an immense job of mapping refugees, analyzing data, and making recommendations.

#### Finally, her latest project of “defending defenders” has been to offer pro bono legal assistance to anyone who finds themselves the victim of attacks on the basis of the instrumental use of accusations of anti-Semitism — used by Israel as a shield against criticism — including a large number of BDS people who were criminalized simply for telling the truth and calling for the application of international law. A strategy, therefore, to protect and defend those who in turn defend the cause of the people of Palestine.

#### Ingrid passed away on November 16, 2023. I didn’t even know she was sick. I was very sad that a woman like her — a true revolutionary, activist, intellectual, altruistic fighter, capable of

#### working behind the scenes, contributing her vision without any interest in taking center stage — had gone without my having had any way to see her again. I would have liked to bid her farewell and thank her for the teachings she gave to me and to all of us.

#### Some maintain that knowledge is not a process of acquisition but of progressive unveiling, of liberation from preconceptions. In my understanding of the Palestinian question, Ingrid has certainly been one of the figures to whom I am truly grateful for helping me to open my eyes and see more clearly. I once talked about her with Omar Barghouti, one of the cofounders of BDS. After expressing his esteem for me, Omar told me clearly and firmly: *“Don’t think that even you are exempt from racial bias!”*

#### “I know,” I replied. “And yes, I’ve removed it. In fact, I’m still removing it bit by bit, as if I were peeling off the layers of an onion.”

#### It is precisely for this reason that the cultural legacy that Ingrid leaves us never ceases to be precious — indeed, crucial — to peeling away the layers of ignorance and preconceptions that we inevitably, unconsciously, carry and that weigh down our understanding of reality.

#### Among Ingrid’s most important lessons is a fundamental concept: When people are oppressed, they deserve total, unconditional, and principled support. We need to know how to listen, we really need to look at who we have in front of us, to have a “horizontal” vision of co-resistance and avoid any form of paternalism toward others.

#### *A striking example is the 2024 documentary film No Other Land, directed by Basel Adra, Hamdan Ballal, Yuval* Abraham, and Rachel Szor, an Israeli-Palestinian collective of activists, which deals with the Israeli occupation of the West Bank, the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and the destruction of Palestinian property by Israel. Many people, myself included, found it admirable. The film has won numerous awards, including the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature in 2025.

#### And yet some in the BDS movement saw it as a form of normalization and criticized it. I didn’t understand. I *said: “Seriously? Are you going to try and poke holes in a project like No Other Land?”*

#### “Be careful, this is the most insidious form of normalization,” they replied. Today, I understand. I also see the danger. It is true, at the Oscars ceremony, Basel Adra spoke first: “About two months ago I became a father, and my

#### hope to my daughter [is] that she will not have to live the same life I’m living now, always fearing settlers’ violence, home demolitions, and forced displacements that my community, Masafer Yatta, is living and facing every day *under Israeli occupation. No Other Land reflects the harsh reality that we have been enduring for decades and still* resist as we call on the world to take serious actions to stop the injustice and to stop the ethnic cleansing of the Palestinian people.”

#### And it is also true that Yuval Abraham, whom I hold in high esteem, clearly articulated the relationship of inequality between him and Basel in his speech: “We see each other. The atrocious destruction of Gaza and its people, which must end. The Israeli hostages brutally taken in the crime of October 7th, which must be freed. When I look at Basel, I see my brother. But we are unequal. We live under a regime where I am free, under civilian law. And Basel is under military laws that destroy his life and he cannot control.”

#### Everything Yuval said is true. Yes, the destruction of Gaza must stop. And yes, the hostages must go home. But all hostages should be included: the Israelis and also the thousands of Palestinians, including hundreds of

#### children, who are languishing in Israeli prisons, mistreated, often tortured unbearably. For Palestinians, the reality of occupation, ethnic cleansing, apartheid, and now genocide is often neither

#### admissible nor understood unless it is immediately relativized, tempered by Israeli experience and narrative. As if the Palestinians could only tell their story, their resistance, express their suffering, denounce the injustice they suffer in the presence and with the approval of a more legitimate voice, that of the Israelis. Can a Palestinian voice exist for itself? One has to wonder how many Palestinian-directed films have been funded, produced, distributed, seen, and recognized in an industry like Hollywood. One has to wonder if Basel would have had the chance to speak, or even to come to the Oscars, if he had been alone, without Yuval.

#### This is not to question Yuval’s commitment nor the impact of the film, but the biases and mechanisms of normalization are powerful and arrayed against any Palestinian narrative to such an extent that it is Yuval’s word that ultimately serves as a scale of legitimacy and captures attention and sympathy.

#### Yuval’s life in Israel has become hell. But Awdah Hathaleen, a Palestinian activist who collaborated on the film, paid with his life. He was shot dead on July 28, 2025, in the West Bank by Yinon Lev, an Israeli settler already sanctioned by the European Union and the United States for previous violence.

#### —

#### THE RIGHT WORDS are very important as a prelude to and preparation for the right actions. So, in 2017 for me it was absolutely not an exercise in pure theoretical jurisprudence to understand how much the definition of apartheid was appropriate to the ongoing situation in Palestine, and it is not such an exercise today to recognize the need to adopt the word “genocide” to define everything that was already in preparation for some time and that has been unleashed in a more striking way since the end of 2023.

#### Seeing, understanding, placing the situations we witness in the correct framework are essential preparation for action.

#### In my fourth report to the United Nations, which I called “Anatomy of a Genocide,” I denounced the fact that *Israel was carrying out a veritable pseudo-humanitarian camouflage of its systematic and predominate violations of* the law. In this way, Israel has overturned the foundations of international humanitarian law, giving the world the perception that it is legitimate to target civilians, considering them human shields or collateral damage.

#### When Israel uses Palestinians as human shields to enter homes or takes inmates from prisons to use as shields *during assaults, that is literally human shielding: a well-defined concept that is explicitly forbidden under* international law. And this behavior turns that prohibition on its head.

#### Israel tends to speak of “evacuation orders,” of “protected zones,” but it has inverted the language of international humanitarian law to justify its military conduct and its war crimes, erasing the fundamental principles of discipline and protection in times of armed conflict: the distinction between civilian and military, military necessity, proportionality.

#### *On closer inspection, is it not humanitarian camouflage that Israel has always practiced in the Occupied* Palestinian Territory, blowing smoke in the eyes of the international community, which has allowed it to do so? Why have all of us involved in Palestine in various capacities — human workers, diplomats, international officials, experts in the field — been too cautious about denouncing the total and progressive oppression of the Palestinians? Instead, we have been obsessed with the idea of not disturbing Israeli sensibilities.

#### This attitude has allowed Israel, which aimed, well before 1967, to expand its hold over what remained of historic Palestine, to advance its interests hidden behind the facade of the law of war, while sowing the seeds of conduct that today appears in every respect as the precursors of genocide.

#### The will, especially in the West, to maintain a “neutral” narrative free of de facto conflicts has permitted injustice and suffering, ignoring what the Palestinians have always said and demanded.

#### When I lived in Palestine, I felt this profound incongruity within me, and one of the things that made me suffer the most was having the perception that even the United Nations, the development sector, and the humanitarian sector were an integral part of the glass ceiling that prevented the Palestinians from advancing the fulfillment of their rights.

#### The facts are what make the difference, because the correct knowledge of a situation and the correct choice of words to describe it are certainly an indispensable element in being able to defeat apartheid and stop the genocide of the Palestinian people. However, as always, the words in themselves are not enough and must be translated into actions, otherwise all discourse will be in vain and unable to change by as much as a comma the atrocity of what is happening.

#### Another thing that has happened in these very days, while I’ve been writing, is that I participated in a meeting with a high-ranking official of a European government closest to Palestine, a meeting that I came out of with so much anger I felt like crying the minute I signed off. I found myself arguing again with this high state official, trying to understand what concrete actions the government he represents had taken to oppose the injustice of the settlements and facilitate their dismantlement. When I asked, “What are you doing about this?,” he gave this tightlipped response: “Come on, you can’t be so critical of us, we’re certainly not the worst in Europe.”

#### I pointed out to him that their country invests more than any other in the occupied territories, but he just shrugged his shoulders. “What do you want us to do, boycott Israel?”

#### When I insisted on the fact they could at least avoid using their profits to make the situation worse, he told me loudly and clearly that I was neither diplomatic nor constructive, and that I didn’t understand how much they had been committed to supporting the Palestinian National Authority, with the objective of helping them kick Hamas out of the Gaza Strip.

#### “But that is none of our business,” I told him, in a calm tone and pronouncing every syllable. “It is not up to you to choose who governs in Palestine. You just have to give a useful contribution to ending the occupation, so that there will be something left of Palestine.” That is what international law requires.

#### Yet I will admit that those who have criticized me over the years have been right, at least on one point: It is true that in some ways I am not constructive. No, I am not constructive when I talk to certain politicians who keep repeating their lies. I am not good at bearing the wounds of unfought battles, to use Pessoa’s words again. But at least I am not destroying the lives of a people and cheering about it, and I hope that when I come to the end of my life, I will know that I did everything I could to help them. I am doing and will continue to do what is in my power, going on to learn and peeling away the layers of “my onion” with the help of the people who can teach me. As Ingrid did. She will always remain a teacher for me.

#### These are the words engraved on her tomb, near Bethlehem: “We promise to smile every time we can, as you did; to go on at all costs, fighting, reflecting, defending hope in the face of pain, falling, getting up, changing paths, resuming the struggle and finally winning our liberation!”

# GHASSAN

#### *How far can the cruelty of genocide go?*

#### The propaganda machine had already been activated in favor of the “fight against terrorism,” supporting with great ease the need to do justice and defend human rights without paying much attention to the fact that war is itself legitimized terrorism, absolute injustice, irremediable violation of every right. — GINO STRADA, on Emergency’s intervention in Afghanistan in 2001

#### SOME THINK THAT in Israel-Palestine there are two parties to this so-called conflict. Others believe that this is not the case and, if this story could be staged as a Greek tragedy, the main characters

#### would be the Palestinians, the Israelis, and Western imperialism, the latter supported by a chorus representing the vassalage and oligarchic selfishness of various Arab governments.

#### “This ‘war,’ ” says Ghassan Abu Sitta, a surgeon who is a naturalized British citizen, “has shown that the link between Western imperialism and Israel is a continuum without interruption. Israel is an integral part of the Western imperialist project in that area: a colony linked to the West, like all the colonies of past centuries.”

#### Ghassan spent several weeks in Gaza after the onset of the Israeli military campaign to take revenge against the people of Palestine who were assumed to be collectively guilty of the bloody assault on October 7th. He made his personal contribution to the hospitals of Gaza for as long as it was possible for him to operate. Then he made the enormously difficult decision to return to Britain in November 2023. “When I left Gaza and arrived in the United Kingdom, I realized that the genocidal project was like an iceberg. Israel is only the visible tip, but the rest of the iceberg — which is not so clearly visible from Gaza — is the entire apparatus that makes genocide possible: the *BBC, CNN, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, the organizations that support it.”*

#### Ghassan was elected rector of the University of Glasgow in March 2024, and since then all kinds of things have happened to him. Far from giving him the hero treatment he deserved, the Western establishment was preparing to retaliate against him.

#### To begin with, the pro-Israel group UK Lawyers for Israel filed a complaint against him, accusing him of being “unfit” to practice medicine because of his presumably incendiary social media posts; hence the request for suspension of his medical license submitted by the General Medical Council, rejected by the court of interim orders for lack of evidence and for the presentation of unreliable translations of the posts. The court accepted the arguments of the defense, which had shown that the accusations set out in the complaint were politically motivated and aimed at undermining his public credibility and limiting his freedom of expression.

#### Some BBC journalists then told him that the broadcaster had placed him on a list of Palestinians who could no longer be interviewed and, in the spring of 2024, he was prevented from entering France, the Netherlands, and Germany, where he was supposed to give lectures, because he was banned by the German authorities from the entire Schengen Area, a maneuver subsequently declared unlawful by the Potsdam Administrative Court.

#### “Meanwhile,” Ghassan points out, “Germany has been increasing its arms supplies to Israel tenfold, while the British air force is taking charge of electronic espionage by flying its planes over Gaza. Furthermore, the Italian air force refuels the Israeli F-35s that are preparing to bomb Sanaa in Yemen. All this shows that the Palestinian problem is not a matter of misunderstandings. The problem is that the Western powers are using Israel as an instrument to protect their interests in the region. But these Western political elites will have to come to terms with the fact that public opinion is changing. To observe this change, all you need to do is measure the level of oppression in the West itself: Thousands of university students have been arrested in the United States. In the United Kingdom, even Holocaust survivors and organizers of anti-war demonstrations have been arrested. In Germany, police brutality against demonstrators has become systematic.”

#### As soon as he returned to the United Kingdom, Ghassan decided to cooperate with Scotland Yard, providing his testimony on the war crimes he accuses Israel of committing. Calling the current situation an unprecedented wave of destruction compared to the previous wars on Gaza, he declared that the attacks of the last year and a half constitute “a real tsunami of violence.” For example, he reported seeing wounds that were certainly caused by white phosphorus, wounds that were familiar to him. “The use of white phosphorus is prohibited by international law. I immediately recognized those burns: I had already treated them in 2009.”

#### —

#### ONE EVENING, in London, I sat at Ghassan’s side during a conference at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and I was able to listen to his terrifying stories, which have been ruining my sleep for months.

#### During the course of his work at Al-Shifa and Al-Ahli hospitals, where he treated the victims of Israeli bombings, Ghassan performed up to twelve operations a day, many of them on children, including a sad night in which he had to carry out six amputations on minors.
