According to his estimates, in the first months since the beginning of the conflict in Gaza, some nine hundred children underwent amputations. “When you start operating on a minor, you know that that child will have to undergo at least ten or fifteen more operations between now and adulthood,” he told us that evening. Who is going to do those operations? Where are these operations going to be carried out if there is nothing left of the health system in Gaza? What will happen to the future of those children, assuming they manage to survive?

#### Israel’s justification for bombing Al-Shifa Hospital (and any other hospital for that matter) is based on the claim that it was a Hamas operations center, which Ghassan categorically denied that evening. “In the hospitals I have only seen wounded and dead. Not even a shadow of Hamas.” This knowledge is also shared by assistance workers and the media, and the Israeli army itself has been unable to provide a shred of evidence that did not appear to be fabricated. For example, an image circulated at the beginning of the genocide by the Israel Defense Forces showed an Israeli officer pointing to a sheet of paper with writings in Arabic on the hospital wall, which had been presented as a Hamas operational plan but later was discovered to be simply a planning chart of the shifts of hospital staff.

#### That the hospitals were only hospitals is also demonstrated by the photographic images that Ghassan has collected — and which the media have judged too crude to be broadcast to the public — which show nothing but corridors overcrowded with people screaming in despair, mutilated limbs, charred bodies.

#### “When the Israelis besieged Al-Shifa Hospital,” he told us, “I was stuck in Al-Ahli, which had become the only functioning hospital in Gaza, even though it had already suffered great damage. In other hospitals in south Gaza, I saw my colleagues sitting around and not being able to do anything because there was no power to run the operating rooms. At least in Al-Ahli there were still two operating rooms and an X-ray machine, even if we could no longer use the CT scan. In addition to myself, there was an orthopedic surgeon and a couple of other general surgeons, but the air raids were so monstrous, and the number of patients arriving was such that we were forced to operate continuously for twenty-two hours. At that point, however, we had finished everything. At five o’clock in the morning, the anesthetist came out of the operating room and announced: ‘That’s it, there’s nothing, there’s no propofol, there’s no oxygen, there’s nothing with which I can sedate the patients.’ The Al-Ahli Hospital also had to stop. We had no drugs to administer, and that was when I realized that the biggest problem was not the shortage of doctors; it was that the health care system was progressively being emptied of its ability to function, to the point that doctors were actually in excess, compared to the available supplies and facilities. On that last night I was in the south, the wounded were taken to Al-Ahli in donkey carts, because there was no petrol for the ambulances. I also believe that over two hundred and fifty health workers were arrested by Israeli forces during that period. Some of them were tortured and many people, probably hundreds, are still prisoners in Israeli jails. I myself probably avoided arrest only because at some point I moved from Al-Shifa to the south, where I could still try to do something.”

#### What has continued to happen in Gaza since the autumn of 2023 confirms Ghassan’s words and fears. How could anyone refuse to accept the definition of genocide in the face of the horror that has struck Gaza? Who could possibly believe the propaganda that attempts to frame such an atrocious extermination as a “conflict”? Would they use the term “conflict” to define what the European colonists who created the United States did in sweeping away with blasts of gun powder and continuous famine hundreds of tribes of Native North Americans, massacring an entire people and impaling the heads of the most-loved tribal chiefs for everyone to see to sow terror among the people and discourage resistance?

#### *Some time ago, in The Guardian, I read the testimony of Dr. Issam Abu Ajwa, who said that, after he was* arrested by the Israelis, his torturers were explicitly asked to break his hands so that he could no longer operate. Then there was the story of Dr. Adnan al-Bursh, head of the orthopedic surgery department of Al-Shifa Hospital and a close friend of Ghassan, who died at the age of fifty in April 2024, shortly after his arrest and transfer to Ofer

#### Prison, in the occupied West Bank. Some colleagues and fellow prisoners have stated that he died as a result of sexual violence, which led to the perforation of his intestines.

#### “The torture and killing of nearly a thousand health workers is a key component of the destruction of the health system,” Ghassan told us that evening in London. “The Al-Shifa Hospital can be rebuilt in a couple of years, but it took twelve years to train a doctor like Adnan al-Bursh. Considering the main medical specialists that Gaza urgently needs, it can be said that of the five pathologists present before October 7th, only two are still alive. In Gaza, there are no longer qualified doctors to perform emergency surgery. All nephrologists have been killed. A biostatistics researcher analyzed both intentional and systematic killings and found that a health worker in Gaza is two and a half times more likely than anyone else to be targeted and killed by the Israelis. Even if there is a ceasefire and the Palestinians have a respite from the bombs,” Ghassan declared to a packed room of people listening in religious silence, “you can rest assured that the genocide will continue. Because thanks to this strategy, people will continue to die anyway, even from conditions that could very well be treated.” Unfortunately, time has proved him right. And more than a thousand health workers have been killed between October 7, 2023, and January 2025, while over two hundred and fifty have been imprisoned.

#### “Genocide,” Ghassan concluded, “is clearly recognized when destruction falls on everything: present, past, and future. Everything that the people of Gaza have ever been is razed to the ground, erased.”

#### Sitting next to Ghassan that evening I felt full and empty, noble and insignificant. The strength of our words would not have saved any human lives, at least not in the immediate future. But the debate changes, day after day. *Suffice it to say that, right after October 7th, our host that evening, the director of the journal Lancet, had described* Gaza as follows: “I walked on the streets where images of ‘martyrs,’ in combat dress and with machine guns held across their chests, looked down from the walls over children walking to school. Or where you could see men in balaclavas, assault rifles in hand, parading unstopped. This is the environment Hamas has created and into which every new generation of Gazan children is born. It is an environment that nurtures and propagates terror.”

#### But reducing Gaza to an “environment that feeds and spreads terror” is unjust and superficial, and generalizations such as these are misleading and dangerous. That Hamas has ruled Gaza with an iron fist is beyond doubt, and the Palestinians have been their first victims. But Hamas controlled Gaza for some seventeen years with the approval of Israel. As for the images on the walls, many people do not know that for the Palestinians the celebration of martyrs, or rather of those fallen in combat dress, is not an exaltation of violence in itself but the desire to honor those who have lost their lives in the occupation and to remind the community that they must support its innumerable victims.

#### But it is true that children are affected by the environment in which they grow up. That is why, for years and years, Palestinian and Israeli human rights organizations have been imploring the world to stop the occupation, the annexation, the apartheid.

#### There is so much arrogance in the posture of us Westerners with respect to cultures and words of which we ignore the meaning, roots, and essence. An arrogance that is widespread in all environments — from journalism to academia, and clearly in a large part of the world of politics — which has helped to render invisible the humanity of the Palestinians, pushing their salvation farther into the distance. This is also why it is essential that the debate change, that it break down ignorance by spreading knowledge, and that we insist on asking ourselves the most important questions: What can we do to stop all of this? How long will it go on while the world seems to be sleeping a stone-cold sleep and cannot keep its eyes open in the face of this wound that is as large as an entire people, this wound that no one seems to want to soothe or heal?

# EYAL

#### *How to calculate conditions that lead to the destruction of a people?*

#### The genocide of one people, however, soon leads to the genocide of another, a truism borne out through the centuries by successive generations of invaders and those invaded. For the totalitarian empire being constructed in front of our eyes, punitive expeditions give life meaning. Today one group is sent to the guillotine, tomorrow a different one. The day after tomorrow it will be the turn of little Liana, and later still, we need have no doubt, it will be our turn. — ANNA POLITKOVSKAYA

#### ANY RIGOROUS DISCUSSION OF WHAT CONSTITUTES GENOCIDE should be based on what international law establishes in this regard. Here, then, are the first five articles of the convention held in New York by the United Nations on December 9, 1948, in the aftermath of the Holocaust that had led to the death of about six million European Jews, more than two hundred and fifty thousand Roma and Sinti, and three hundred thousand people with disabilities.

#### *Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide*

#### The Contracting Parties,

#### Having considered the declaration made by the General Assembly of the United Nations in its resolution 96 (I) dated 11 December 1946 that genocide is a crime under international law, contrary to the spirit and aims of the United Nations and condemned by the civilized world,

#### Recognizing that at all periods of history genocide has inflicted great losses on humanity, and

#### Being convinced that, in order to liberate mankind from such an odious scourge, international cooperation is required,

#### Hereby agree as hereinafter provided:

#### *Article I* The Contracting Parties confirm that genocide, whether committed in time of peace or in time of war, is a crime under international law which they undertake to prevent and to punish.

#### *Article II* In the present Convention, genocide means any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such:

#### (a)  Killing members of the group; (b) Causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group; (c) Deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in

#### whole or in part; (d) Imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group; (e)  Forcibly transferring children of the group to another group.

#### *Article III*

#### The following acts shall be punishable: (a) Genocide; (b) Conspiracy to commit genocide; (c) Direct and public incitement to commit genocide; (d) Attempt to commit genocide; (e) Complicity in genocide.

#### *Article IV* Persons committing genocide or any of the other acts enumerated in article III shall be punished, whether they are constitutionally responsible rulers, public officials or private individuals.

#### *Article V* The Contracting Parties undertake to enact, in accordance with their respective Constitutions, the necessary legislation to give effect to the provisions of the present Convention, and, in particular, to provide effective penalties for persons guilty of genocide or any of the other acts enumerated in article III.

#### This text and the awareness of humanity on which it is based should be the indispensable basis for everyone, including those who still have some doubts in — or even believe that they have arguments to object to — considering whether all the actions carried out by the State of Israel against the Palestinian people fall fully within the definition of “the crime of genocide.”

#### —

#### *THE FIRST TIME I heard about Eyal Weizman was in 2017, while I was writing the book Palestinian Refugees in International Law with Lex Takkenberg.*

#### At that time I was living with my family in Indonesia, but I spent long periods in the Middle East, especially in Jordan and Palestine, doing archival research and talking to people who could help me put together all the elements I was collecting to reconstruct from a legal point of view almost eighty years of the forced exodus of Palestinians from their homeland. Although it is a purely legal and technical book, I was very concerned that the history of what has been done to Palestinian people not be lost. It was essential for me to make it clear to the readers of that text how *politics had determined certain legal implications: for example, in some cases, in the non-application of the law.*

#### In this search for greater understanding and useful tools for me and for those who would one day read that text, I spent many afternoons in the office of Dr. Anis Kassim in Amman. He is a great lawyer and man of culture who is the author of very important legal analyses on the Palestinian question, and for many years was also the director of a *scientific publication on international law, The Palestine Yearbook of International Law.*

#### The ritual of our sessions was to greet all the lawyers present in the studio and then take our seats around the table, while Kassim moved a mountain of stuff from his desk full of books and files, made room, brought biscuits and tea, and then began to speak. I have always loved his calm, elegant voice, which guided me through ravines of history of which he himself had been the protagonist, such as the peace process. It was during one of these *conversations that he asked me: “But have you read Hollow Land, by Eyal Weizman?”*

#### I noticed that some of those present frowned at hearing that Israeli name, but knowing Kassim well enough I was sure that he would never exclude an author from his readings just because he is an Israeli. As a matter of fact, it was he who a few years earlier had recommended that I read a series of books by the Israeli historian Avi Shlaim, to whom years later I would be bound by a relationship of friendship and deep esteem.

#### *That afternoon “Dr. Anis” — as we all call him, as a sign of respect — spoke to me at length about Hollow Land, which I read shortly afterward and found to be a powerful and necessary book to understanding what* happened in Palestine, starting from the fact that the systematic, human, political destruction of a people begins first of all with the creation of an empty land.

#### A forensic architect, Eyal uses architectural tools and digital technologies to reconstruct past events related to crimes, disasters, or human rights violations. As the founder and director of the research group Forensic Architecture, Eyal has been committed to revealing, through spatial analysis, the miserable conditions imposed on *Palestinians by the Israeli occupation. Hollow Land traces the history of the Israeli occupation in Palestine between* 1967 and 2007.

#### This very technical study of events, which I believed I knew well from a legal historical point of view,

#### introduced me to new elements of a specifically geographical matrix, but also focused on the experience of a people and therefore on the unfolding of history in people’s daily lives. All this has helped my understanding of violence in Palestine through the fragmentation of law, which paradoxically exacerbates — rather than resolves — geographical fragmentation.

#### *In Hollow Land, it is evident that Israel has used architecture and geography as tools of power to consolidate its* control over the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Urban space and the landscape have been modified to favor Israel’s military and political domination. Israeli colonies in the West Bank were strategically designed so that colonization would create territorial fragmentation. The management of infrastructure and mobility, through a system of roads, checkpoints, and separation walls, have been increasingly restricting the freedom of movement of Palestinians in every respect for decades. At the same time, the transportation infrastructure continues to guarantee safe and rapid access to Israeli settlers, under the vigilant and “neutral” eyes of the international community.

#### *A concept that was crucial for me in reading Hollow Land is “vertical politics”: a fully three-dimensional use of* space, which demonstrates unequivocally how the Israeli occupation is not limited only to horizontal borders but also addresses the control of airspace, the subsoil — for example, through tunnels and aqueducts — and the height of buildings.

#### Thanks to his studies, his many interests, and what I would later discover to be a polyhedric personality, Eyal recounts many things, but the gist of the book is how Israel has managed to box in the Palestinians politically by putting in place a geographical chaos “structured” to the Palestinians’ disadvantage. According to him, practically anyone can be an accomplice to this system (voluntarily or voluntarily), unless he distances himself from it very rigorously:

#### The spatial organization of the Occupied Territories is a reflection not only of an ordered process of planning and implementation, but, and increasingly so, of ‘structured chaos,’ in which the — often deliberate — selective absence of government intervention promotes an unregulated process of violent dispossession. The actors operating within this frontier — young settlers, the Israeli military, the cellular network provider and other capitalist corporations, human rights and political activists, armed resistance, humanitarian and legal experts, government ministries, foreign governments, ‘supportive’ communities overseas, state planners, the media, the Israeli High Court of Justice — although with differences and contradictions of their aims, all play their part in the diffused and anarchic, albeit collective authorship of its spaces.

#### One of the most brilliant ideas in his book is the invitation to open our eyes to the risk of the “humanitarian paradox”: that humanitarian interventions may unwittingly end up supporting the military occupation rather than opposing it. Eyal believes that by correcting the consequences of certain decisions taken by the occupying force, these interventions could help rid Israel of its responsibilities, including legal responsibilities, allowing it to divert resources to other objectives, while making the occupation more tolerable in the eyes of public opinion. Starting from this assumption, we arrive at the concept that anyone operating, in any capacity, in such a serious situation must respect his own integrity even far beyond the boundaries of the profession he is called upon to carry out in a given context. For example, as Rony Brauman of Doctors Without Borders has said, it is essential that humanitarian organizations — which sometimes gain access to areas and information that are closed to others, including journalists — use their privileged access to report and denounce the injustices observed, while maintaining independence and impartiality in their activities. According to Brauman, any health worker “goes into the field with medical instruments and comes back with an eyewitness account.” The worker’s task is therefore not only to treat those who are sick but also “to bear witness to the truth of the injustices committed and point out the political responsibility.”

#### —

#### EYAL AND I FIRST MET in person in London, where I had gone for a conference. After publishing my report on Palestinian self-determination for the United Nations, I contacted him because of the great affinity I found between our ways of analyzing the materiality and immateriality of Israel’s ongoing colonial project of displacement and replacement of the Palestinian population in the occupied territory. His was a spatial point of view, mine a legal one. We met at his home on a cold morning, in the company of some of his most trusted collaborators. One thing he said that struck me most in the course of that conversation involved his relationship with Israel. “I’ll only go back when I can have a Palestinian passport,” he told me, leaving me stunned. That meeting marked the start of a fruitful collaboration that gradually turned into a precious and increasingly close friendship.

#### In February 2025, Eyal and I found ourselves side by side again in Berlin. During my visit, we should have been able to discuss the effects of Israeli military operations and the policies that have led to the devastation of life in Gaza. However, two of our speeches were canceled or sabotaged due to political pressure on universities and sponsoring organizations, throwing a truly worrying light on the decline of academic freedom in Germany.

#### Nevertheless, in the context of the increasing intimidation of those persisting on keeping the debate open, Eyal and I agreed that we should commit ourselves to being a light of hope, together with those Germans who do not bow to oppression and the many Jews and Palestinians in Germany who are facing an unprecedented repression in Europe. Despite the adversity and the climate of fear, our conferences were held thanks to the determination of all the people involved, even if in makeshift places and with a strong police presence.

#### Eyal explained a concept of home from the perspective of architecture that touched me deeply: that for Palestinians, for generations now, the home is “something you leave, not the place where you stay.” Very similar to what I often say about genocide by means of settler colonialism or ethnic cleansing: for Indigenous peoples, the land *is what you are, not where you live.*

#### Settler colonialism, Eyal explained, is a process that operates through a dual dynamic: construction and destruction. On the one hand, outposts, infrastructure, colonies are built; on the other hand, the conditions that make life possible for the colonized population are systematically destroyed.

#### The conference that we were supposed to give the next day at the University of Berlin — but which the German authorities forced us to move at the last moment to a location with a much smaller seating capacity — had precisely this title: “Living Conditions Calculated to Destroy.” Referring to Article II (c) of the Convention on Genocide, which prohibits imposing on a human group “conditions of life intended to cause its physical destruction in whole or in part,” Eyal added on that day: “We could say that calculating the living conditions of others is in and of itself an implicit concept in settler colonialism.”

#### This type of colonialism, according to his analysis, acts in two opposite ways: on the one hand, by improving conditions in the occupied territory to encourage the arrival of new settlers and increase the demographic weight of the Israelis; on the other, by destroying, in countless ways, the living conditions of the Palestinian population.

#### “The Gaza Strip,” Eyal said, “is nothing more than the result of an engineering effort aimed at destroying the living conditions within it. It is a long experiment in which living conditions are degraded to the point of forcing the population to leave.” And he was not only referring to the state of siege of the last twenty years or the genocide we have been witnessing since October 2023 but in general to the spatial and political configuration of the Gaza Strip since its creation in 1948. Gaza, according to him, has been shaped as a space where life is made increasingly unsustainable by a system that the American scholar Sara Roy has defined as one of “de-development”: progressive cuts in water, electricity, and infrastructure construction, after having created for decades the conditions to decimate and pollute the subsoil, making the aquifer unsustainable, impoverishing economic conditions, and weakening hospitals and scientific research. All this within a ghetto, because since 1948 Gaza has always de facto been a ghetto, as Eyal reminded us. Over time, the growth of the population and its unwillingness to be bent to the idea of voluntary migration — which Israel, even through the United Nations, has tried in vain to promote for decades — have led Israelis to consider drastic measures to reduce the “demographic threat” that Gaza poses to them. While the West Bank is less densely populated and there are still many ways to take care of — or avoid taking care of — its local population, Gaza is one of the most densely populated places in the world. Or, rather, it was before the genocide.

#### “In the last twenty years, living conditions in Gaza have been calculated so meticulously that even calories have been modulated,” says Eyal, explaining that Israel has decided how much and what food to let in, establishing the quantities based on the minimum necessary standard by age and gender. During this time, the Palestinians have also received water and electricity supplies “according to a level defined as ‘humanitarian minimum.’ “

#### It is striking how in the meantime the Israeli state has instead improved the living conditions in Israel’s areas adjacent to Gaza, to entice Israelis to settle there, by providing subsidies, infrastructure, and water transfers from the north to the south of historic Palestine. “It was not easy to convince new settlers to come and live near Gaza,” said Eyal — who calls “settlers” anyone who was not originally from Gaza and went to live in historic Palestine (now Israel). To that end it was essential to “calculate living conditions” in the opposite direction.

#### All forms of oppression against the Palestinians — ethnic cleansing, permanent occupation, apartheid, genocide — are in fact aspects of the same colonial system. And on this Eyal added an unforgettable sentence: “When certain mechanisms for calculating the living conditions of a people are already active, the moment you decide to exterminate that people, it is enough to reinforce those mechanisms and take them to their extreme consequences.”

#### The same conclusion was reached, before the organization directed by Eyal drew up a real “cartography of the *genocide” in Gaza (the interactive platform A Cartography of Genocide dates back to 2024), by other Israeli* historians such as Ilan Pappé, who delved into the concept of ethnic cleansing in the context of the Nakba, and Raz

#### Segal, who described the current reality in Gaza as a paradigmatic example of “explicit genocide, for all to see, without any shame.” Genocide, according to Eyal, does not start from scratch, it does not consist of a sudden escalation, but is grafted onto preexisting structures and mechanisms. This is true in the case of Israeli actions on Palestine, as well as in other situations and contexts confronted by Eyal in his work as an analyst and scholar. One such example is the genocide committed in Guatemala by the government and armed forces during the early 1980s against the indigenous Mayan populations accused of supporting the left-wing rebels, or the genocide of the Nama and Herero in Namibia, when between 1904 and 1908 the German colonial forces responded to the revolt against colonial oppression with a campaign of extermination by means of deportation, concentration camps, starvation, and disease.

#### In both cases, Eyal says he found the same pattern, based on the destruction of the territory and living conditions as a means of extermination. “Violence is not only inflicted directly on human beings but also on the environment that supports them: hospitals, schools, communities, places of worship.”

#### The genocide of which Eyal speaks is a sort of archetypal model of the elimination of the Other. It is the massacre of a body by all possible means, including those of spatial destruction.

#### If bullets are enough to kill a body, much more is needed to kill a people: Every means must be used to ensure that the collective body is emptied, annihilated, even if it continues to move.

#### I imagine it as a series of continual electric shocks that, by dint of repeated strikes, extinguishes life in its very essence. Just look at the conditions of the Native Americans or of many of the First Nations people of Australia. While in nearby New Zealand, the Māori have been colonized and occupied, but their lives as a people, although restricted and not totally protected, have neither been suffocated nor completely destroyed. But for many other Indigenous peoples this is the reality. This is what is happening to the people of Palestine in their own land, just as it happened to the Jews of Europe a century ago.

#### After years of discrimination and persecution, racial laws were introduced, expulsion from civil life, extreme ghettoization, hunger, disease. Then — since the number of Jews in Europe continued to be high — at the command of unscrupulous criminals, the final solution was reached amid the almost complete silence of their contemporaries.

#### It was that unprecedented horror on European soil, that mechanized extermination on an industrial scale, that led the world to say “never again” and to define genocide as a crime.

#### —

#### TODAY IN PALESTINE, the genocide that was ordered in the aftermath of the attack launched by Hamas on October 7th clearly appears as a systematic action with the intention of destroying a people through a series of military operations that have indiscriminately affected civilians, causing death and devastation everywhere. Israeli forces, with a lethal arsenal, have razed entire cities, destroying homes, schools, hospitals, and the very networks that sustain daily life. The wounds inflicted on the Palestinian population are evident, with tens of thousands of deaths, including more than twenty thousand children, and hundreds of thousands wounded. The real figures are likely to be horrendously higher than the current official ones, but all of the million children of Gaza have been struck in body or at least in soul, silenced by indiscriminate violence that spares nothing.

#### From October 2023 onward, life in Gaza has become a succession of bombings and massacres, a context in which access to basic resources, such as water and medicine, has been deliberately impeded, pushing the population toward hunger, despair, and death. The words used to demonize the Palestinians — “human animals,” “there are no innocent civilians,” “not even children are innocent” — accompany a policy of violence and impunity that echoes an ignoble past that we Europeans, more than anyone else, should not have forgotten.

#### I will say it bluntly: To deny the seriousness of these actions is to close our eyes to a crime in progress. A crime that would call for the urgent mobilization of the international community, which unfortunately has not yet taken place to a sufficient degree, because today as yesterday, before a genocide can be stopped, it must be seen.

#### Genocide can be recognized by its victims: a people targeted as such. For decades, the Palestinians have been treated as an uncomfortable and unwelcome presence, even in what little land they have left — Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem — where they should have been able to build the state that they have longed for and that the international community claims to support. Instead, Israel has continued to reign with an iron fist and to drive the Palestinians out of their homes, in order to claim that land the “exclusive sovereignty of the Jewish people,” a concept that, if you think about it, was already absurd a hundred years ago, given that the land in question has never been inhabited only by Jews but was a welcoming jumble of different cultures, religions, and peoples of which the Jews constituted an integrated minority. It appears even more absurd in light of the current international legal framework, which does not tolerate discrimination of any kind, including that of religion or “race,” this horrendous word that has done so much harm to humanity in the last five hundred years.

#### The ongoing tragedy in Palestine has been the chronicle of a genocide in evolution, unfortunately. Genocide analysts have long warned of the precursor signs, just like people such as Eyal have been doing: summary killings, arbitrary arrests, racial segregation. Conditions calculated specifically to bring a people to destruction.

#### But all of this has been systematically ignored, if not normalized, over time. The expansion of the Israeli colonies — carried out under the pretense of endless and inconclusive negotiations — has revealed just how illusory the idea of a peace is without rights. But all of this goes unnoticed because in the meantime the history of Palestine that gets told is completely different.

#### Italy is a perfect example of how public opinion has been progressively manipulated by politics — increasingly more aligned with the successive center-right governments in Israel (even the so-called Italian “left” with many leaders of the Democratic Party actively involved in the defense of Israeli interests) — and as a direct consequence of the indications of political leaders, by the mass media.

#### After September 11, 2001, with the advent of the global war on terror, the resistance of those who defend what is left of their land has been subjected to a blanket condemnation. So the Palestinians have been labeled as terrorists *ante litteram, without a trial and without appeal, and it appears that, as such, they must be eliminated. The idea that,* finding themselves in a position of oppression and subjugation, the Palestinians have a right to defend themselves from that oppression and to claim their right to effective self-determination seems to have disappeared from Italian public discourse. So, then, are our Italian partisan resistance leaders, including the former president of the Republic Sandro Pertini, Nuto Revelli, Carla Capponi, and many others whom we honor for their role in founding the Republic, to be considered terrorists as well?

#### —

#### ON A WARM WINTER MORNING in Berlin, in the second year of the genocide of the Palestinian people, in front of a crowd of demoralized students and policemen in riot gear, Eyal closed his speech with a final warning: “In this case, reconstruction would not be a remedy for destruction but rather its continuation: It would be used to complete what the genocide failed to accomplish.”

#### I share with Eyal the dismay at President Trump’s proposal to rebuild Gaza as a Mediterranean Riviera, after having “cleansed” it of its inhabitants. A total absurdity, illegal and immoral. On closer inspection, it fits perfectly into the terms of ethnic cleansing or, rather, with the incitement to forced transfer, a crime recognized by international law, that with the latest declarations of the US administration has made its entry for the first time into the foreign policy of the United States. Forced transfers and further expropriations, in the context of this genocide, would reinforce the complicity of other countries with respect to the crimes that Israel has already committed in these last decades and aggravated exponentially in recent months, worsening even more the crisis that threatens to destroy the Palestinian people.

#### But the very fact that, while Eyal and I were discussing these issues, the backdrop of our conversation was dotted with police vans, officers in riot gear, and threats of arrest against me, reveals to us that the whole system in which we live has already been seriously compromised.

#### We are all called upon to be ready to bring our contribution, our testimony, and, as far as we can, our active commitment so that the horrors of the past and present cease to be the frame of our daily lives.

# MALAK

#### *Where is home for a refugee?*

#### When I travel I always take too much with me…Analysing that, I concluded that I had a secret but ineradicable fear of not returning. — EDWARD W. SAID, “On Writing a Memoir”

#### BETWEEN THE END OF the British Mandate in 1948 and the first years following the birth of the State of Israel, seven hundred and fifty thousand Palestinians were forced to leave their homes as a result of harassment, massacres, extreme violence, and the systematic destruction of their villages. This is what the Palestinians call the Nakba.

#### During the Nakba large areas of land were taken from or abandoned under duress by Palestinians. At first, they fled as news spread of the violence committed by the Jewish militias Irgun, Haganah, and Lehi. Then they were expelled at gunpoint, either on foot or in trucks organized by Israeli militias. Thus, in a short time, about five hundred Palestinian villages and localities were destroyed or depopulated. Historians, including Israeli ones such as Ilan Pappé, Benny Morris, and Avi Shlaim, speak of several dozen massacres with summary executions, rapes, and other crimes against the elderly, men, women, and children — such as those in Tantura and Deir Yassin — which accelerated the depopulation of historic Palestine. The destroyed villages were not simply abandoned; many were deliberately demolished, and the land was often repurposed to build new Jewish communities or for other projects within the new State of Israel.

#### Salman Abu Sitta, the founder and president of the London-based Palestine Land Society, which is dedicated to documenting Palestinian land and people, and many other historians and scholars of the Nakba have attested to how land abandoned by Palestinians was subsequently occupied and used by the new State of Israel. Abu Sitta, in particular, has conducted many research studies aimed at mapping pre-1948 Palestinian localities and analyzing the possibilities of return for refugees. He argues that the right of return is not only just but absolutely feasible.

#### For the hundreds of thousands of Palestinians who have been sealed off in the Gaza Strip since 1948, the Jews who occupied their lands are nothing but colonists, colonists who from the first days of the life of the State of Israel have defended with gunfire the lands taken from the rightful owners. The kibbutzim, the agricultural communities, which many abroad saw simply as the flagship of the great socialist model of the newborn Jewish state, were used by the settlers as defensive outposts.

#### This painful history has been passed down among the Palestinians from generation to generation, and it is useful to recall that the dispossession of the Palestinians had already begun well before 1948, during the three decades of British colonial presence in disguise (1920–1948). The British almost uninterruptedly favored the waves of migration that led many Jews escaping persecution in Europe to settle in Palestine and build a new life in the land of “their ancestors.” But that land was already inhabited, and to the Zionist leadership of the time it was clear from the beginning that the existing population would have to be driven out.

#### How could you fail to teach this history or expect people to simply forget it? Imagine the cruelty of asking Armenians not to talk about the violence they suffered and the great theft of their lives, land, and culture during the genocide committed by the Ottomans, and the same is true of the Indigenous peoples of Australia, America, and so many other theaters of genocide in history.

#### Yet, when I was working as a lawyer for the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) and in the years that followed, I often had the feeling that the American administrations *expected the agency to carry out a process of pacification of the Palestinians. Whatever abuse had been committed* in the past against their grandparents, their lands, their lives, the Palestinian people, starting in 1948, were supposed to love the new State of Israel, and certainly not challenge it and its policies.

#### When I arrived in Jerusalem in 2010, one of my tasks was to follow an audit of the agency’s human rights

#### program and the curricula in use at UNRWA schools. This audit was commissioned by the United States, which at that time had always been the largest contributor to

#### the agency’s funding. I prepared what was needed for the three auditors who had arrived from the United States to conduct their own examination of school materials to ensure that there was nothing that could “incite terrorism, anti-Semitism, and violence.” Nothing ever emerged regarding “anti-Israel messages, including anti-Semitic ones,” but for years now these programs have still been constantly under attack, accused by the Israeli government and its allies of containing anti-Semitic messaging.

#### Although UNRWA, under a memorandum of understanding signed with Israel in 1967, has always dealt with some five million Palestinian refugees in the occupied territories, relieving Israel — as the occupying power — of this burden, things have changed since the peace process initiated by the Madrid Conference in 1991.

#### Before the Madrid Conference, the discussion around the refugee issue had almost ceased. But, in the context of the peace process, Palestinians and others began to reflect on what peace and the two-state solution would entail for refugees. A copious production of estimates, historical reconstructions, legal analyses, statistical and economic calculations reopened the refugee question and it became a thorn in the side of Israel, which had considered the question closed, dead, and buried.

#### During a workshop in 2017, a well-known Israeli professor from the Hebrew University said to me, nonchalantly, “It happened a long time ago, who thinks about it anymore!”

#### Israel does not see the Palestinians, does not listen to them, and, even more seriously, does not “hear” them. For most Israelis who speak publicly, but also for many members of the Jewish diaspora, there is only one point of view: Israel’s. How Israel experiences history, how much pain it has endured, the special context in which it moves.

#### Nowadays, many intellectuals, while declaring themselves moderate and opposed to the occupation, focus only on condemning the violence of Hamas, while remaining silent on the impressive numbers of Palestinian casualties and the wanton destruction caused by the Israeli army after October 7, 2023. They repeat accusations that have never been verified, such as alleged mass rape and beheaded babies, but they avoid acknowledging the ferocity suffered by the Palestinian population.

#### —

#### BUT LET’S GO BACK TO 2010. To prepare for my audit I had the opportunity to visit for the first time the entire territory commonly known as the Gaza Strip and to return there several times in the following months. During one of those visits, a school hosted in its atrium an exhibition of paintings made by the children. Some of the works struck me deeply: They were not on paper, like almost all the others, but on canvas, and they demonstrated a mastery and beauty that I would not have expected in that context.

#### “Who made these paintings?” I asked the teachers. “A sixth-grade girl. She’s very good, isn’t she?” “I would like to have one of her paintings: this one,” I said, pointing to an image of two little girls with round

#### faces and eyes as cerulean as the sky behind them, with a large potbellied dove flying by. “I would also like to meet her, is it possible?”

#### So, that afternoon fifteen years ago, I met Malak Mattar, who was then an eleven-year-old girl with a chubby face framed by two braids of thick black hair. I remember her as beautiful and very shy; she didn’t speak English but, through her teachers, she told me sweetly that she couldn’t sell me the painting I liked so much: First of all, because it belonged to the school. Second, because she didn’t know how to propose a price. She would have to ask if she could accept money, but her uncle, a well-known painter from Gaza, who had taught her to paint, was not there.

#### Years later, I was doing an online search for an image to use for a poster advertising a lecture, when I came upon a painting of white doves flying around human figures with large eyes and soft faces, and I had an illumination. “Is this work Palestinian?” I asked.

#### Someone confirmed to me: “Yes, it’s Palestinian.” “More specifically, it’s from Gaza, isn’t it?” “Yes, the painter is from Gaza. Her name is Malak Mattar.” I had no doubts: It could only have been her, that

#### little girl I had met briefly in one of the UNRWA schools. I wrote to her immediately and at that point I had decided: We absolutely had to have one of her works for the

#### poster of our event, and so it was. It was a conference organized to commemorate the twentieth anniversary of the death of Edward Said, a great Palestinian intellectual and author, who had been an academic at Columbia University. The conference was held in London on October 3, 2023, a few days before the event that would forever change the lives of Palestinians and Israelis, and certainly of all the inhabitants of the Gaza Strip, including Malak and her family.

#### From that moment on, we have always stayed in touch. However, several years had to pass between our first meeting and the next one, which did not take place in Gaza

#### but in London, at the end of 2024, on the occasion of the conference at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, where I spoke alongside Ghassan Abu Sitta. That evening, I immediately recognized Malak in the audience, and after the conference we were finally able to hug each other.

#### She told me that she had left Gaza the day before October 7th and then moved to London, where she had been admitted to the master’s program in fine arts at Central Saint Martins, one of the world’s leading schools of visual arts. Her parents and two brothers, however, had remained in Gaza and were trying to find refuge in Egypt. It would take months before they managed to leave Gaza under very difficult conditions, after having miraculously survived the bombings.

#### “At first,” she explained to me, “part of my family decided to stay in the north. They thought: ‘This land is ours and we will save it. We must protect it from colonization, so we will stay here. Let them kill us, if they want, but we won’t leave.’ For many people, including my family, the decision to leave or remain has always dragged with it a strong trauma from the past: After the Nakba of 1948, those who left their lands could no longer return.”

#### Then, one morning, something happened that convinced them to flee the neighborhood of Rimal, where they lived: The secondary school where her mother taught was bombed a few minutes after she had left, while she was still in the car on her way home. So they moved, finding refuge farther north: first in a neighborhood called Al-Karama, then near the Al-Shifa Hospital. And during all this the family had to separate: the men in one place, the women and children in another. A crazy situation. A few days later they decided to head south. The air-raid sirens were more frequent, a sea of people were leaving their homes, and there was increased pressure for people from the north to move to the south.

#### “My family went to Deir al-Balah and lived at my aunt’s house for five months. It was a nightmare for me: I had just arrived in London and with all that moving around I could never get in touch with them. I had no news, I didn’t know how they were, I didn’t even know if they were alive or dead. I constantly tried to call them, but the phones weren’t working and all I got was music on the other end of the line. I went from enthusiasm for my new path at Saint Martins, which would allow me to grow as an artist, to the anguish of not knowing if the people closest to me were safe.”

#### —

#### THAT EVENING, after the London event, Malak and I were only able to exchange a few words and she didn’t finish her story until many months later: In March 2025, as I was completing the drafting of this book in Italian, I had come back to London. I managed to plan a more intimate dinner, and finally Malak was able to tell me the second part of this complicated and painful story. “And anyway, much less painful than many others,” she said immediately after sitting down at the table, even before choosing what to eat. “In the family of my friend Ahmed, for example, everyone has died in recent months. He has no one left.”

#### But Malak’s family managed to save themselves. “After trying in every possible way, we realized that the only way was to raise enough money to bribe the Egyptians, that is, a lot of money. Five thousand dollars for each person, a total of twenty thousand. Fortunately, they were able to recover their savings and leave Palestine to take refuge in Egypt. Finally, on the day of the evacuation, I went to Egypt and was able to see them again. They were traumatized, shocked, and even physically injured: When the building in front of theirs was bombed, the windowpanes exploded on my sister. But she herself told me that the most terrifying moments were those of the journey from Deir al-Balah to the border, littered with the bodies of people killed and left there, along the way. They prayed the whole time, but when they finally arrived in Egypt, they felt overwhelmed by some sort of guilt for having survived. My mother was beside herself. She kept telling me, ‘How could I leave so many people behind? Especially those who hosted me. And my friends, my relatives, my things…’ Even now she can’t get over it.”

#### Then another battle began — this time legal. The British government had refused the family visas to join Malak in London and they had to file a lawsuit to have the decision overturned. “We attended countless hearings, and the lawyers kept telling me: ‘Malak, you’re fighting a battle that you’re probably going to lose.’ But I said to myself, ‘Well, at least we’ll fight it.’ “

#### Their appeal, Malak says, was based on demonstrating how important it was for her to have her family by her side. The request was supported by the testimony of various experts: psychologists, sociologists, and other professionals. The main obstacle was the idea that her loved ones might be “a security threat,” and at each hearing some of the opposing lawyers would refer to them as dangerous people.

#### It was necessary to show that they all loved art, theater…As if, implicitly, those who were not cultured enough to love paintings and opera did not deserve this opportunity.

#### After endless months they won. In fact, in the first weeks of 2025, visas were issued, technically on the basis of family reunification, and her family eventually joined Malak in London. At that point in the story, she picked up her fork and with a sigh began to eat.

#### “Both of my parents grew up in Gaza as refugees, after my mother’s and my father’s families were forcibly displaced from their villages in 1948: My father comes from Al-Jura, while my mother comes from Al-Batani al-Sharqi, of which by now there is almost nothing left. But even if they are places that I have never been able to visit, I seem to know them well because my grandparents have always talked about them a lot. Since I was a child, I have developed a strong sense of belonging to the towns where my roots are, and of course the relationship I have with Gaza is quite complex.”

#### The villages Malak told me about were erased from the map of history with the creation of the State of Israel, but the land, the remains of the houses, the graves of the ancestors of the Palestinian families displaced in 1948 are still there, in Israel.

#### “So you don’t feel like Gaza is your home?” I asked her. “Well,” she replied with a very eloquent smile. “Actually, yes. I am a refugee, it is not there that the story of my

#### family took place, but it is there that I grew up and it is there that I began to learn the language of art thanks to my uncle Mohammed Musallam, who is an internationally renowned artist and who has also worked as an art teacher in Gaza. And so, yes, to answer your question, I could tell you that Gaza is not my home, but today I would choose it as my home. Even more so now, perhaps, that the neighborhood where I grew up has been practically razed to the ground and lives only in our memory. My best memories are in Gaza and, despite everything, for me it is a place where you can dream. When I was fifteen, I was invited to do an exhibition in Bristol. Of course I was very happy, and I went to my father and asked him: ‘Dad! Can I go? Will they give me permission? These people say that they will pay for everything, they want me to go there and talk a little about my painting.’ But he replied: ‘Do you think Israel will allow you to go abroad for an exhibition, when it does not even give permission to leave to cancer patients, who are stuck here dying without medicine?’ His words hurt me a lot, but that didn’t stop me from continuing to paint, dream, and have ambitions in life. And I felt the same thing in all my friends. Each of us had the drive to achieve something.”

#### This is a feature that has always struck me about the Palestinians. Even under a military dictatorship and a real siege — the one that Gaza has suffered in every way since 2007 — under the military (and not only military) blockade, under the occupation, in truly difficult living conditions, they have managed to preserve that drive, that love for life that shines through in every word that Malak spoke to me.

#### —

#### AFTER SHE GRADUATED from high school and won a scholarship to pursue her art in Turkey, it took Malak a whole year to obtain the necessary permits to leave. From there she could have continued her studies in France or the United Kingdom, but both countries refused her a visa.

#### In her first year outside Palestine, she was denied entry to almost every country. The idea of freedom that she had cultivated for so long had shattered against reality. She thought that once she got out of Gaza, she would finally be free, with wings to fly wherever she wanted. But it didn’t go that way. During her time in Turkey, she realized that it is not enough to leave Gaza if the whole world continues to see the Palestinians as a threat.

#### “In any case,” she told me, raising her head, her eyes brighter, “it took quite a few attempts, but now I live here and I’m traveling so much that there is only one blank page left on my passport. Even this, for me, is resistance!” she concluded, laughing. “It’s silly, isn’t it?”

#### “I don’t think so,” I told her. I smiled too, but I wanted to cry thinking of Malak’s vicissitudes and then of the stamps on my children’s passports.

#### “It’s important for me to be able to say to the settlers, ‘You know what? I travel around the world to present my art!’ This is the spirit with which I grew up as a woman and as an artist in Gaza. Just think that at my first solo exhibition I exhibited a large painting on corruption, on the dynamics of power, and an old professor came to me and said: ‘Your painting is interesting, but you are a young woman, wouldn’t it be better to paint flowers, vases, something nice, and leave politics to men?’ Perhaps it was precisely this kind of comment that, instead of discouraging me, spurred me to go beyond other people’s expectations and to do everything I could to ensure that our voices resonated and could be heard. Indeed, these episodes were fundamental stages in my artistic career.”

#### The really difficult challenges, Malak told me, were quite different: The art shop where she used to buy supplies was bombed and no longer exists; the gallery in which she dreamed of exhibiting her works has been destroyed; many of the friends who frequented her house to talk and paint together have been killed. This is the reality of those who make art in Gaza: to live and create under occupation.

#### Her eyes on fire, she told me that when she was fourteen or fifteen, she had received a commission from the United States, from Tennessee: a painting of a Christmas tree. But when it was time to send it, she had been asked at the post office, “Is it a political work?”

#### Any artist living in Gaza always had to deal with a form of censorship on what they could or could not paint, on what symbols they could or could not include in their works. If an artwork was considered political, the military would confiscate it.

#### At that point I asked her how difficult it had been to become an artist under occupation. “Very much so,” she replied seriously. “It was unbelievably difficult. Do you know why they hate us and want

#### to destroy any aspect of art? Because art is hope. That’s why they killed Refaat Alareer,[\*] who gave hope to so many with his poems. The most shocking reality that the occupation has to face is that we speak with the language of art, which is the most powerful language against all forms of dehumanization: Being able to reach other people with a poem or a painting is the best way to sweep away all stereotypes. That’s why I really think that art is dangerous,” she concluded with a smile.

#### After eating, we went for a walk and crossed one of the many gardens that dot the center of London. I looked at Malak’s lunar face, very sweet but marked and hardened by violence, by oppression, while she told

#### me that even there in London many things are very difficult for her. For example, now she is looking for a house that can accommodate the whole family when her parents manage to join her, but the rents are too expensive and, with her scholarship, it’s really complex. Theirs is a wonderful scenario, because they are all alive, especially when compared to the constant anguish that Malak felt before her family managed to get to Egypt, when she knew that they had no food, that they were under a rain of bombs, and that they risked death every moment. Yet, she told me that every time they could talk on the phone, her father only asked her: “So, what are you painting these days?”

#### At first, Malak did not understand: “But what does it matter, Dad?” Then he explained it to her: “You are there for a reason, Malak. You have to paint our lives, our struggle, all that

#### we are going through. You are an artist, so you are our voice.” Those words, she told me, she will never forget. Hearing the survivor of a genocide ask her to give voice,

#### through painting, to what her people were experiencing, was an enormous responsibility for her, and what an honor. It was from there that the idea of a monumental work took shape: a painting of almost sixteen by six feet in which *she tried to convey everything she could not say in words. It came to be known as “the Guernica of Gaza,” even though its real title is No Words. It is a work that was born from the heart of the ongoing genocide and is entirely in* black and white, because, as she explained in an interview, “only black can reflect reality, a horrible reality that silences us.” Malak no longer sees the colors of her homeland.

#### On the walls, graffiti shouts in Arabic and English: “Gaza will live forever” and “Gaza will persecute you.” In the canvas you can see animals feeding on the corpses left to rot. In the center, a distraught man rides a donkey, his mouth wide open with pain, shock, shame. Around him, bodies and rubble: women, men, children. The composition is dense with raw details, with a violence that saturates the space. Houses, schools, mosques, cultural centers: Everything has been destroyed. No one speaks anymore in that work.

#### Malak has painted silence. She has painted the disappearance of journalists, artists, poets, intellectuals. A work that freezes the blood in your veins, Malak knows that.

#### But her art is pure expression, without filters, both when she sees the world in black and white, and when she uses colors in her own unique way, as in the painting that illustrates the cover of this book and from which we have *drawn inspiration for the title: When the World Sleeps.*

#### As we say goodbye, hugging each other, Malak tells me with a sad but pungent smile: “Apparently, people are interested in seeing the pain of Gaza painted. But there is not enough paint to tell it all.”
