* this page.

# GABOR

#### *Why is it so important to preserve the memory of a people?*

#### Neytiri: “Sky People can’t learn, you can’t see.” Jake: “Then teach me to see!” *— AVATAR*

#### “A MONTH BEFORE the liberation of Budapest, while we were walking down the street, my mother entrusted me to a total stranger, because she no longer felt certain that she could guarantee my survival. The Jews were again being deported and killed by the Hungarian Nazis. She had no idea when it would be our turn, and so that day she put me in the arms of a stranger she met on the street.”

#### This is a fundamental memory in the life story of Gabor Maté, a doctor and psychotherapist of Canadian nationality and Hungarian origin. Today Gabor deals with trauma and healing, pivoting on his own pain to give hope to people by saying things that are extremely sensible, precious, always with great simplicity. During an event in which we were debating the situation in Palestine, I heard him say in no uncertain terms, but in a voice as quiet as a caress: “You have to be really ignorant not to know, not to understand, not to see colonialism in Palestine, or to deny that the Palestinians are the oppressed and the Israelis the oppressors.” There is something wrong, Gabor also believes, in those who fail to see how Judaism, his religion, is being exploited in the name of an ethno-nationalism that is based on the premise of a discriminatory ideology.

#### And this for me makes him a person who is no longer just a therapist of the individual but of the collectivity. I think that’s also why many people listen to him. Trauma, according to Gabor, is not so much what happens to an individual externally but what happens internally in response to a painful event. An intimate wound is generated that sooner or later will inevitably manifest itself externally, potentially harming a person’s emotional, psychological, and relational abilities forever. However, if the person can develop awareness and compassion, they can start a healing process.

#### Disconnection from self and others, which Gabor describes as an inevitable consequence of any trauma, does not only affect the individual. A person may feel isolated, distrustful, and alienated, and eventually somaticize that emotional suffering. But the same feeling can emerge from historical traumas as well and generate shared experiences that affect families, entire communities or peoples, influencing collective bonds and identities.

#### Indeed, as he points out, the transmission of trauma — especially when it occurs through a lack of emotional regulation — can also be interpreted in an intergenerational or collective perspective. If the adults of a society carry with them painful experiences that have left deep marks, their trauma has the power to be handed down culturally to new generations. The invisible scars of ancestors can affect the way young people perceive themselves and the world, perpetuating a cycle of suffering and disconnection that requires conscious and compassionate work, if it is to be interrupted.

#### Trauma, according to Gabor, “changes one’s perception of the world.” When whole groups internalize a view of life influenced by their trauma, by their fear, this feeds a continuous

#### sense of threat and mistrust in their collective view of the outside world. It is not difficult to imagine the importance of such dynamics for populations that have experienced oppression, wars, persecution, exile, and extermination. That is the eternal point of contact between Jews and Palestinians.

#### —

#### THE IDEA THAT TRAUMA is central to the collective experience of Jews as well as Palestinians is a theme explored by *scholars such as Amos Goldberg and Bashir Bashir. In the text they coedited, The Holocaust and the Nakba:*

#### *Between History and Trauma, Goldberg and Bashir highlight how the collective pain, loss, and bewilderment* common to these events — beyond the dramatic differences between them — have marked the identities and memories of both peoples. Thus, in the passage from one generation to the next, they have become central elements of their history, shaping not only past experiences but also current relations and struggles for dignity and justice. The act of guarding the memory is fundamental, precisely because — as Gabor explains in one of his most touching *books, The Myth of Normal — trauma does not simply consist in what has happened, on a personal and collective level, but above all, precisely in what happens and continues to happen inside people in response to that experience.* This is especially true when the trauma touches on something very painful: for example, the genocide of the Jews during the Holocaust, and the ongoing genocide of the Palestinians in Gaza.

#### According to Gabor, every authentic healing requires the courage to look our emotional pain in the face. The typical convictions of those who have suffered a trauma, such as the classic “There is something wrong with me,” are not just negative thoughts but something that continues to live in our neurophysiology, creating entire sets of interconnected mental processes. When one tries to avoid the memory of pain — by denying it, or by unconsciously hiding it under guilt, self-sabotage, or self-loathing — one effectively prevents the healing process from getting underway. Cultivating emotional memory, on the contrary, is an act of restoring the truth to oneself or to an entire population that has been wounded and outraged. Only by recognizing the wound can one begin to heal it.

#### Some time ago, an Israeli colleague made me realize that the Jews, and not only those living in Israel, have had many opportunities to face and soothe their collective trauma, the result of centuries of persecution culminating in one of the most horrendous genocides in history. This opportunity has materialized in moments of collective compassion and pain expressed through days of remembrance, museums, and memorials around the world. In schools — or at least in schools in Europe, where the Holocaust was committed — the history of the genocide of the Jews is taught with seriousness and respect, offering new generations the opportunity to confront and reflect on that painful past.

#### Of course, it is interesting to note how little is said about the genocide of the Roma and Sinti — the Porrajmos, which in the Romani language means “great devouring,” or Samudaripen, “killing of all” — which also took place during the Second World War mainly at the hands of the Nazi regime. The extermination affected hundreds of thousands of people belonging to these communities who in many parts of Europe are still discriminated against today. The Palestinians are also still denied this opportunity. They have never been able to close the circle of their past, to process the collective grief of the loss of the land, homes, and community life they had until 1948. Not only have their rights and legitimate demands for justice for all their past suffering not been recognized; the injustices they continue to suffer today are often made invisible and are misunderstood, both by Israel and by most of the Western political system.

#### The genocide currently taking place in Gaza is proof of this. In the prevailing debate in the West, it seems that one cannot talk about the violence that the Palestinians experience every day without first having to consider Israel and its right to defense, even when this right is claimed by the occupier on the very little land that the Palestinians have left, and therefore illegitimately. Of course, like any member country of the United Nations, Israel can invoke the right to self-defense enshrined in Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations, when the conditions are met: that is, when it is attacked by another state or when there is the authorization of the UN Security Council. Israel’s use of force in Gaza and the rest of occupied Palestine is illegitimate. As the Court of Justice reminds us, Israel cannot attack militarily the population it occupies. Pure logic that is expressed in law. (But does the right to defend oneself also apply to Palestinians, yes or no?)

#### Moreover, it seems that one cannot talk about the current situation in Palestine without starting from the horror of October 7, 2023, almost as though decades of unspeakable violence committed by Israel against Palestinians before that date — as well as the pain suffered by Israeli civilians on other occasions, such as the wave of suicide attacks during the second intifada — count for nothing any longer. This selective reading of history leaves entire generations in a state of continuous trauma. Their trauma is renewed every day, the value of their suffering is denied, and the intensification of the violence itself persists.

#### The almost total lack of understanding for the rights of the Palestinians often makes them invisible, in life and in death, forced into an inevitable subordination to the logic and claims of Israel, a state that, day after day, swallows up more and more of the land of another people. Meanwhile, Israel unfailingly manages to make other people discuss its sacrosanct right to exist. It, and it alone. Wherever it wants, as it wishes, by any means it deems appropriate.

#### The contemporary world has demonstrated this a thousand times: What colonialism does is not only to impose its rule on a people, annihilating any possible future, but also to complete the work by sweeping away its memory. Destroying or minimizing the memory and pain of a genocide, or other atrocities, means adding a further barrier to prevent those affected by that trauma from achieving any possible form of healing.

#### I find it almost cathartic that to speak of these topics in strong and clear words there is someone like Gabor, who, as a Jew, has also experienced the effects of a historical and personal trauma that marked him emotionally for his entire life. Gabor now lives in Canada, as part of a “colonial society” on a land that was inhabited by other peoples before Europeans came to settle there, imposing their political power and forcing the Indigenous peoples to culturally assimilate their language and canons.

#### Not only have the Indigenous peoples been prevented from having the right to self-determination during centuries of colonization but they are still being prevented from preserving their collective and cultural memory. A genocide, in the broadest sense, also consists of this.

#### —

#### THE LAST TIME I WENT TO CANADA, at the end of October 2024, I already knew Gabor by reputation, but he was not there, and we had not yet met. At the time, I was under a lot of stress from family problems. On the other side of the world, my mother, who had been ill for years, was facing a difficult period. I was emotionally and physically exhausted, and as often happens to me in moments of overload, I got a very strong back pain, accompanied by migraines and nausea. I remember spending the whole car trip between Ottawa and Toronto trying to meditate, to restore oxygen and calm to my back through mental exercise, but the energy available to me was very little. It was under these conditions that, the following day, I went to meet a delegation of academics from the Centre for Indigenous Studies at the University of Toronto.

#### In Europe or in Italy, few seem to know that Canada was the scene of a massive genocide of the Native populations.

#### From the mid-nineteenth century until the 1990s, Canadian governments implemented systematic policies and practices to sterilize Indigenous populations or forcibly assimilate them into the dominant culture. Assimilation took place mainly through the system of residential schools, designed to separate children from their families, forcing them to adopt the European language and values. Adoption by nonindigenous families served to sever the link with their roots, whether they were Inuit, Métis, or First Nations. Many of those children suffered mistreatment, physical and sexual abuse, and died as a result of inhumane living conditions. Recent investigations have unearthed mass graves and testimonies that highlight the horror of these genocidal policies. This process has had a devastating impact on Indigenous communities, leading to the loss of languages, cultures, and identities, and has left deep wounds that continue to affect them. In today’s Canada, the genocide is recognized, and there is a process of reconciliation underway. However, true justice for the Indigenous people of this part of Turtle Island (the name by which many Indigenous ethnic groups, including the Iroquois and Anishinaabe, call North America) is still far away. As the UN Special Rapporteur for Palestine, I felt that it was my duty, in North America, Australia, and New Zealand, to meet with representatives of Indigenous communities.

#### And so that day at the University of Toronto, there were twenty people gathered around a table in addition to me and my collaborator. For a few moments, there was some embarrassment: I was not part of that group and I was unsure how to start the conversation and what procedure to follow. How do you say hello? Who is responsible for breaking the ice? However, the state of indecision did not last long, because the connection that was established immediately, the shared energy and the mutual openness, transformed that meeting into an unforgettable experience of community and compassion.

#### These scholars recited their welcome for me in the Indigenous languages: an invocation with words of gratitude addressed first of all to nature, recognizing the elements: water, earth, fire, air. It is a way of being in the world that marks a non-anthropocentric horizon, where man is a thread in the vast fabric of existence, not its fulcrum. A way of being in the world that gives us back forgotten proportions, returns us to an ancient wisdom with its magical symbolism: a revelation that this historical moment has the power to whisper long-dormant truths to us.

#### A way of being in the world that invites us to see. Opening the meeting, one of the Indigenous scholars, who is also a musician, began to sing a song that was also

#### ancestral, powerful, progressively more intense, one of those songs that shakes you up inside. And there, in that university classroom, it almost seemed as if the windows were rattling. The song was so awesome, so full of meaning, that at one point I was almost afraid; but it was a sacred fear, because we were no longer in a simple classroom: The singer’s voice had taken us to another space, another time.

#### Already at that moment, listening to the singing, I was distracted from my pain. It was as if for a moment besides me, with my suffering body, there was also something else, bigger, that was crossing through me. Like a river. Then they started passing tobacco to each other, everyone took some and let it rest in the palm of their hand. Later, they explained to me that this is used to absorb pain. A leader had passed away and that gesture helped them to concentrate, to enter a space of deep connection before talking to others. They held that ball of dried leaves in their

#### hands, charged it with intention, and only then did they start telling their stories. Hard, pungent stories. Many descended from mixed families: because, if not them, one or both parents had been taken from their homes and assigned to schools or adoptive families of white Canadians. Children taken away from their parents to break their lineage, to annihilate cultural transmission, to erase their identity.

#### Yet, one by one, those people — as well as the Indigenous communities to which they belong — are taking back the space to live their own identity. This process of liberation with a view to a reaffirmation of identity, culture, and politics was not born today, but it seems to be pulsating with a new force. And this made me reflect broadly on what is happening to all of us.

#### For some time now, I have sensed a growing feeling of renewal almost everywhere, as if the seeds of a revolution were germinating, preparing to rise up against political dissatisfaction. As happens in a sick body, when antibodies are activated to ensure that healthy cells come to the aid of those having difficulty in fighting diseases, the seeds of resistance, which react and mobilize in the face of injustice, in some countries, especially in the West, are the antibodies of a healthy society. There is also this momentum among various peoples of the Earth, and the solidarity of Indigenous peoples and different nations in the world with Palestine confirms this. Unfortunately, the crust to be scratched is thick. Ancient.

#### That day the scholars told me that the university complex we were in stands on a river that is sacred to them. “This cement is suffocating him,” they said. “They destroyed the trees, they took them away from us, but we still hear their voice.” They expressed themselves with an acute awareness, and it was as if the earth spoke through them.

#### Among the academics sitting around that table there were some who particularly struck me. A woman in her thirties told us that she had been adopted by a Zionist Jewish family, which caused her a double heartbreak, a laceration of identity that is not easily bridged. Another Native woman, small but with an imposing presence, was *sitting next to me. She told us that she had been a hidden child, that is, a child who had been hidden so as not to be* taken from her family of origin. In fact, she spoke perfectly the language of its people, which others must recover to make it their own. Like her, all the people present in that room shared a very strong bond with the earth, as well as a wound, deep and alive: a trauma that they carry inside and that they can only heal by committing themselves to preserving its memory.

#### —

#### SOMETIMES IT SEEMS TO ME that it is difficult for many people in Western countries to understand settler colonialism and what it entails. Most of the textbooks Western children study in school, for example, speak in neutral — if not heroic — terms of the acts of violent colonialism on which the Greek and Roman civilizations were founded, wiping out entire peoples and erasing the memory of their cultures, of their native languages, of all their knowledge. These cultural eliminations are taken for granted, not considered worthy of attention. The same is true of the most recent colonialism, the one that began with the three caravels led by the Genoese captain Christopher Columbus: an event, often romanticized as the “discovery of America,” which instead marked the beginning of an era of colonization and exploitation that led to the death of tens of millions of Indigenous peoples throughout the American continent. These historical events have often been neglected but they have had devasting and enduring consequences.

#### So it is no wonder that most people in the West have trouble understanding what it means for a people to be destroyed and a collective body dismembered and abandoned without recognition, without treatment, causing internal wounds, traumas that are incarnated and that can rebound in the pain of many generations to come, as Gabor explains. At the same time, new awareness is blossoming today, accompanied by concrete commitments. As in Canada and other countries, studies of Indigenous cultures and movements are being introduced or consolidated that cultivate memory, to mend and heal these deep wounds.

#### —

#### JUST A FEW WEEKS BEFORE GOING TO CANADA, I held a public event in one of the bookstores of the independent Busboys and Poets chain, between Fourteenth Street and V Street NW in Washington, DC: spaces that have always hosted rebellious voices, African American literature, resistance texts, and which constitute real places of countertrend compared to the world of lobbyists that populate the streets of the US capital. During the years I was living in DC, after leaving Palestine, this was one of my favorite refuges, where I attended meetings, discussions, and book presentations, and indulged myself with reading and a cup of coffee on rainy or snowy days with my infant daughter, Leila, who traveled everywhere with me in her stroller.

#### The event at the Busboys and Poets was introduced by Hope, a woman of the Piscataway people, one of the many Indigenous peoples exterminated by Western settlers in the process of forming what is now the United States.

#### She introduced herself as Firestarter, “she who lights the fire,” and brought us the offerings of her people and a greeting in the Lenape language, which she then translated for us. The Piscataway dialect has been lost, but the Lenape language shares common roots. This poem is by Nora Thompson Dean — her Lenape name was Weènchipahkihëlèxkwe, “woman who touches the leaves”—who was among the last fluent speakers of the southern Unami dialect and dedicated her life to documenting, teaching, and transmitting the spiritual and cultural traditions of her people, collaborating with scholars and institutions to preserve them for future generations.

#### *Kuxëna Kishelëmienk, wanishi tili nkàski nipain yushe tali, ok wèmi weltëk kéku ènta milian, wanishi, mpi òk yu ènta kishux pèchi òxekamakuna yushe xkwithakamika Milinèn weltëk tëmakàn tìlìch kàski ikalìchi pèchi pètawsinèn yushe ènta xkwithakamika. Punelìntàmainèn wèmi ènta ahchanilan òk ènta ahchanaptunhe. Wanìshi Nuxati, wètënëmai winëweokàn.*

#### *Na në lekèch.*

#### Our Father who created us, Thank you that I can be here in this place, and for all the good things that you have given me,

#### thank you for the water and for the sun that shines on us on this Earth. Give us a good path, so that we can continue to live longer here on this Earth. Forgive us when

#### we do what is wrong and when we say something wrong. Thank you, dear Father, and accept this plea from me.

#### Amen

#### It was very emotional to be welcomed like this, and it also seemed instructive to the hundreds of people who had come to listen to the debate. That is precisely what we must do: take every opportunity to learn to see better, to understand, to preserve and honor the memory of what has disappeared, by fighting alongside those who resist, to help us to heal the wounds of the offended peoples.

#### The union of different struggles for self-determination, still unfinished, is a path that is built with so many acts, practical and symbolic, of rupture with the past, that we can learn to make part of our daily life every time we have the opportunity.

#### As I asked in my opening remarks at the event hosted by Busboys and Poets, how is it possible that for decades, we have gathered in North America to talk about Palestine, without ever involving the Native peoples who have lived — and still live — a colonial and genocidal experience in these lands?

#### So, a few days after that meeting in the bookshop, when I found myself presenting my report to the United Nations, I began my speech like this: “We are meeting today on the land of the Piscataway Nation, which still belongs to them.” And I made the salute to the land that I had learned from Hope.

#### I was amazed at how little importance was given to this incipit of my speech. It was not particularly important for anyone to note that in that beautiful building where the official meetings of the United Nations are held, with its many floors and its imposing glass-and-steel facades that reflect the sky and the surrounding city, someone said: “Today we find ourselves on a land that belonged to a people — the Native Americans — who were victims of genocide, committed by one of the permanent members of the Security Council.” In those rooms pulsated a palpable contrast between the presumed elegance of power that is expressed through overbuilding, and the land below, which lies forgotten, marked by stratifications of history, suffering, and struggles.

#### *No one is free until everyone is free. All of them. All those who have been made invisible on this Earth; all the* peoples whose memory, traditions, and culture have been reduced to folklore; all those who still have the realization of freedom from oppression and need only as a horizon and not as a present. In America there are now museums about Native Americans, such as the National Museum of the American Indian in DC, where traditional clothes and the reconstruction of tents are on display along with the typical covers made of feathers and wax reproductions of scenes of life at the time when the tribes lived their lives freely, immersed in nature and surrounded by bison. As for the story of the extermination of the vast majority of Native Americans, however, very little can be deduced from the legends that accompany the various historical images. It almost seems that the Native Americans became extinct on their own, and not because of a series of devastating policies and actions of aggression undertaken by the European colonies that settled in the “New World” from the sixteenth century onward. Then, in the seventeenth century, the strongholds established by the colonists and the progressive expansion of their dominions for the exploitation of natural resources led to various conflicts with the Indigenous populations, who were often forced to cede their lands. Wars and the spread of European infectious diseases, against which the Native populations had no

#### defenses, contributed to a dramatic demographic decline. These factors were exacerbated by policies of famine and forced transfer, such as the infamous Trail of Tears in the 1830s, which lead to the evacuation and death of many Cherokee and other tribes.

#### Although many tribes are now federally recognized, life on the reservations remains very difficult. After having gone through centuries of violence and the destruction of hundreds of tribes, Native communities still face serious problems today: Access to natural resources is very limited and the US government has never officially recognized the genocide — or rather, the genocides — suffered by Native peoples.

#### The lack of historical justice leaves the descendants of survivors in a fragile condition, facing daily challenges such as poverty, unemployment, and difficulty in accessing essential services.

#### In Canada there is a little more evolution than in the United States, since at least there the genocide is recognized. In all public events it is customary to state that we are on land belonging to Native peoples who have never renounced their land and their culture. Homage is paid to them, to their ancestors, and to their leaders, past, present, and future, but care must be taken that this recognition is not only performative, and that there is a real commitment to eradicate discrimination against the Indigenous people, and that tribute is not paid in public but then the policies of subtraction of land and resources continue, as happens in Canada, but also in Australia and New Zealand — and in Palestine.

#### —

#### WHEN I THINK OF HOPE’S INTRODUCTION to our meeting at Busboys and Poets, I fear what might happen in Palestine if the plan of the current Israeli government, supported by the Trump administration, were to be effectively carried out. Forty years from now, someone may be in a place once known as Palestine, but in a university lecture hall named after Donald Trump, offering tribute “to the Palestinians, the ancient inhabitants of this land,” when all that remains of Palestine will be ruins.

#### This is why it is so important to fight together to understand, know, and preserve the memory of our collective history and defend those who remain.

#### This is why human rights perform an almost therapeutic balancing function: They remind us that we too are human, despite the fact that we may find ourselves on the side of power. We know well that, by nature, human beings are vulnerable, complex, fractured. And this fragility is inevitably also reflected in the colonizer, in whom it is often possible to find a bit of the drama of the colonized. How can we forget the tragedy that struck Ireland in the mid-nineteenth century, when in just under five years some one million Irish were killed by hunger, typhus, and cholera, while almost two million were forced to emigrate? Today, 20 percent of the white American population is among the descendants of those migrants, and this tells us that while the Irish were trying to rebuild their lives in America, they in turn contributed, knowingly or unknowingly, to the colonial system that existed in North America.

#### —

#### *I REMEMBER WHEN I saw Avatar for the first time, while living in Jerusalem. I came away with a very clear thought:* “What a turning point for Palestine, this film!” In that story there was everything: the invasion, the extraction of resources, the connection with the land, the resistance, the anchor of spirituality for the oppressed people.

#### Outside the theater, I was struck that so many Israelis were coming out crying. It took me a while to understand, listening and chatting with fellow moviegoers, that they were not crying because of what I had seen but because they too felt part of the Na’vi people. They identified with the persecuted, with those who were driven from their land by an invincible and superhuman military force.

#### This made me aware that, by virtue of the persecutions suffered for centuries in Europe and Russia, many Israelis carry with them a certain type of memory of pain, just like the one Gabor talks about: a form of emotional dissociation that can also be unconscious, but which still leaves its traces. Whether it is real or projected, it remains in the body, in the language, in the imagination. For me, understanding this complexity makes the whole situation we are experiencing much less banal.

#### *When people are called upon to commit to human rights, I think they must do so from a human, radical point of* view, but also a radically open mind, where there can certainly be right and wrong acts without the need to separate *the “good” people from the “bad” people. Therefore, it is possible to embrace everyone as human beings. Everyone.*

#### There is something profoundly distorted in those who fail to recognize the humanity of the Other. For many Israelis, this means not being able or willing to see Palestinians as human beings. And the same is true

#### for those among the Palestinians who struggle to recognize the humanity of the Israelis. Fortunately, although they are still not enough, there are Israeli citizens and Jews in the diaspora who are

#### fighting for Palestinian rights. This is precisely the meaning of the motto “decolonize your mind,” which means breaking down boundaries and barriers, doing our best to free ourselves, on both sides, from the superstructures that prevent us from staying in touch with what is most human and true that we have in common.

#### *“The great mother doesn’t take anyone’s side,” says Neytiri in Avatar. “She only protects the equilibrium of* life.”

#### To preserve the humanity of others, to commit ourselves to continuing to see their uniqueness without normalizing or flattening them, is in itself a contribution to the fight against genocide. All colonizers and all instruments operate not only by killing people materially but also by erasing the identity of a people.

#### What was the sense of the numbers that were tattooed on prisoners’ arms in concentration camps, if not this? Within that space their name was no longer meaningful, and part of the struggle for survival consisted in the precious act of being able to remember who they were and who they had been, preserving the sense of what is highest in human beings even in the face of something that demonstrates the opposite.

#### Cordelia Edvardson, deported at the age of fifteen to Theresienstadt and then to Auschwitz with the number A3709, for decades was the correspondent from Jerusalem for one of Sweden’s leading newspapers, as well as one of the first Jewish voices to denounce the atrocities committed by the State of Israel against the Palestinian people. *She wrote about her concentration camp experience in the book Brȁant barn sȍker, sig till elden (Burned Child Seeks the Fire, Beacon Press, 1998). Her stories evoking the memories of a young girl, little more than a child, show* very clearly how fundamental it was for her to cling to culture, knowledge, poetry to continue to see herself as a human being in the true and noble sense of this term. So the story of Demeter and Persephone — the princess who, like the seed, enters the shadows of the earth and then emerges at the right time with her flower and her fruit — is not only a beautiful myth but a promise of rebirth that nourishes the heart, reminding us of who we are, who we can be.

#### We Are Not Numbers, the organization of emerging Palestinian writers, was also born from the awareness that victims of war and extermination are exposed to many risks, including that of losing their identity under avalanches of statistical data and death counts. In places like Gaza, such periods have always been cyclical. The victims end up no longer having faces, stories, names; they become numbers in the war bulletins to which, day after day, people seem to become accustomed.

#### In 2015, in a Gaza already scarred by siege, the poet Refaat Alareer, who always believed in the power of the word as a form of resistance and care, wanted to overturn this logic by teaching literature and poetry and helping many young people in Gaza through the power of creative writing. Along with other activists, writers, and organizations, Refaat was very committed to supporting We Are Not Numbers, with the aim of restoring the dignity of narrative to the victims and survivors of every Israeli crime in Gaza. Through writing workshops, many Palestinian children were able to tell their personal stories, their dreams, what they had lost, and that part of hope that remained, to affirm themselves as complete human beings, beyond the labels and numbers of the news.

#### Refaat was killed in an Israeli bombing on December 6, 2023, along with his brother, sister, and four children. The last video that remains of this professor who loved Shakespeare, who had learned Hebrew and kept the need to rehumanize Israelis as a cornerstone of his mission to his friends and students, lasts less than a minute. Refaat is visibly upset and struggles to hold back his tears, but he manages to keep his voice firm and clear as he says: “We are aware that the situation is very bleak, without hope, with no way out. If there is no water, if we cannot get out of Gaza, what should we do? Throw ourselves into the sea and drown? Commit mass suicide? Is this what Israel wants? Well, we won’t. The other day I was saying to some of my friends: I am an academic, probably the most dangerous object I keep at home is a felt-tip pen. But if the Israelis invade us, if they go house to house to slaughter us, I will use that felt-tip pen, I will throw it at them, even if it is the last thing I can do in my life. That’s how we all feel: in a state of absolute helplessness, with nothing left to lose.” He was forty-four years old.

#### Today we can commemorate him by spreading, each of us in our own way, the knowledge of what is happening to the Palestinian people, because knowledge is crucial and memory is indispensable in every healing process, as Gabor teaches us.

#### We can remember Refaat with an excerpt from the preface to a book in which he collected the stories of many *Palestinian boys and girls, which is entitled Gaza Writes Back. Not “Strikes Back,” not “Fights Back,” but Writes Back. Atrocities suffered can also be reacted to with the weapon of a story, or a felt-tip pen.*

#### Gaza writes back because storytelling helps construct Palestinian national identity and unity. Gaza writes back because there is a Palestine that needs to be rescued, at least textually for the time being. Gaza tells stories because Palestine is at a short story’s span. Gaza narrates so that people might not forget. Gaza writes back because the power of imagination is a creative way of constructing a new reality. Gaza writes back because writing is a national obligation, a duty to

#### humanity, and a moral responsibility.

#### ALL PALESTINIANS, and not only Palestinians, love to remember Refaat with white kites, a tribute to his poem “If I Must Die”:

#### *If I must die, you must live to tell my story to sell my things to buy a piece of cloth and some strings, (make it white with a long tail) so that a child, somewhere in Gaza while looking heaven in the eye awaiting his dad who left in a blaze — and bid no one farewell not even to his flesh not even to himself — sees the kite, my kite you made, flying up above and thinks for a moment an angel is there bringing back love. If I must die, make it bring hope make it be a tale.*

# MAX

#### *It takes two to tango.*

#### And if I fall, let me fall graciously. And if I rise, let me rise gracefully.

#### AT THE BEGINNING OF THIS BOOK I said that I had chosen ten people as the focal point for my stories, since from each of them I learned something essential about Palestine. The first is Hind; the second is Abu Hassan; the third is George; the fourth is Alon; the fifth is Ingrid; the sixth is Ghassan; the seventh is Eyal; the eighth is Malak; the ninth is Gabor.

#### The tenth is Max. My life partner, the person with whom I set foot for the first time in Palestine and the one with whom, three years later, I decided to leave Palestine. But Palestine is like that: You can also choose to leave it, but for those who have been there, have seen it and experienced it, it will not be the one who leaves you. My life is proof of this.

#### In the early days, when we moved to Jerusalem, Max and I traveled a lot, we kept moving in search of understanding that land and, paradoxically, it was as if we did not see its confines. Turning on the trail of historic Palestine, in that initial period we were in Nazareth, we visited Galilee, the coastal area, from Haifa to Jaffa, and then the south, the desert. All of this is now part of the State of Israel. Moving in that land, we learned to familiarize ourselves with its wounds. Evident wounds, carved in stone. On Sundays we went for walks in the forest around the city, on the hills surrounding Jerusalem, which are also now part of Israel. The forest under which the village of Ein Karem is located, with its square stone houses surrounded by citrus and jasmine trees. On those walks we got to know better many friends who stayed with us for a long part of their lives, and there we began to understand what the Palestinians meant when they said: “Even the stones here tell our story.” Walking in the forest, for example, we often happened to come across ruins of houses, fragments of masonry. They were the remains of Arab villages that were depopulated and destroyed in 1948 during the Nakba, and on which carpets of trees were planted. Many are the gift of the Jews of the diaspora to the State of Israel, which is projected into the world as a beacon, a hearth, for all Jews.

#### We discovered that land little by little, and some time after we had taken up residence in East Jerusalem, protests began in Sheikh Jarrah, right in the area where we lived, on a hill in a part of the city that was as beautiful as it was devastated. But all of East Jerusalem is a disaster, with the Palestinians paying very high taxes, and in return they receive minimal services; waste collection and electricity amount to only 13 percent of what they pay; we also paid a very high municipal tax. Many Palestinian families, like our friend George’s, lived around and in front of us, and many were literally driven from their homes before our eyes. Meanwhile, the settlers arrived, supported by organizations such as Ateret Cohanim, Ir David Foundation, Israel Land Fund, who started real legal battles against the Palestinian resident kings, presenting property titles of dubious authenticity dating back to the Ottoman Empire. And yet the Israeli courts have accepted those deeds, allowing the eviction of Palestinians who, having nowhere else to go, ended up in the houses built by the United Nations Relief and Work Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), on land that from 1949 to 1967 was administered by the Jordanians. We witnessed some dramatic scenes: families chased away even in the middle of the night by the police who threw out kitchen utensils, tables, beds. Some Israelis came to protest, but there were very few. The Palestinians, for their part, did not want simple protests but concrete actions, especially on the part of Jewish Israelis: those who vote. From those who have rights in Israel and cannot think that it is enough to limit themselves to protesting once a week with tambourines and banners, in Sheikh Jarrah. This was openly said by the people of Lecce who refused to join those protests in 2010. Thus, we too had found ourselves involved in the roar of the demonstrations, in which Max actively participated (my work with the United Nations prevented me from doing so). And that’s how Max met so many pacifists in Tel

#### Aviv, some of whom we remained friends with, even if it has now become impossible to see them again. After years of knowing each other and talking about many things, it was there in Jerusalem that I saw Max’s

#### political spirit fully emerge and be put into practice. I was struck by this aspect of him, because he proved to be someone who throws himself into things in the first person, with his refined intellect, as an upright thinker, first of all. He felt the same intolerance toward injustice as I did, in fact he often went with the Israelis of Ta’ayush, an organization that deals with interposition between settlers and Palestinians in the West Bank, physically accompanying the Palestinians in their daily activities — such as cultivating the land or taking the animals out to pasture — in order to protect them from aggression, document any abuse, and act as a deterrent to violence. Often, on Fridays, he joined them, or took part in the protests in Ni’lin and Bil’in. One day he returned from a visit to an olive grove with a basket full of black rubber balls. I had never seen anything like it: They were tear gas canisters, which the Israeli army had thrown at the protesters. “Christmas is approaching. Let’s decorate the tree,” he said with his usual sarcasm.

#### Max could write a book about the years we spent in Jerusalem, about his experience with the Israeli peaceful resistance movement. He saw in that movement the essential germ of something destined to travel for a while on two separate and parallel binaries, one for the Palestinians and one for the Israelis, who would still have a separate piece of road to go before merging. For many Israelis, the privilege to be renounced in order to welcome the Palestinians as a free people is too high.

#### I remember beautiful moments of life in Jerusalem. We had so many landmarks in town: our favorite falafel place; the Educational Bookshop, where Max had met George and even now the owners remember my husband, because he used to hold Zoom meetings upstairs and when he spoke you could only hear his voice! Yet the period in Jerusalem was very heavy for me. It cost me a lot to live immersed in apartheid. Jerusalem, as well as the rest of the Cisjordan, is a dystopian city.

#### Every time someone came to visit, we ended up retracing the ordeal of the occupation. Where did we take them, our guests? Certainly not Tel Aviv or Nazareth. No, we took them to see the epicenter of the occupation: Jerusalem, the Old City and the part cut off from the wall, Bethlehem scarred by the wall, Hebron invaded by violent settlers, the Bedouins displaced everywhere from the Jordan Valley, and then Nablus, Jenin, Tulkarem, the Balata camp. How many of our friends and relatives who have come to visit us have changed their minds about Israel and Palestine? There were those who came with opinions that were lined up a priori, in defense of Israel to the bitter end and without any sympathy for the Palestinians, who they saw as troublemakers and “terrorists.” No one returned to Italy with the same opinion toward Israel. Some of our friends have had hysterical reactions: “But what do I care about coming to Hebron?” “I didn’t come here to see these monsters!” “Why do you take me to where all these soldiers are?” “I am afraid, in the midst of all these armed people! I’m scared! You are not normal!”

#### After a couple of similar scenes, at a certain point we reduced a little the traffic of people we were taking around the nerve centers of the occupation. But Max and I continued to visit Palestine. We have found our niches of relief, even in the middle of the ongoing colonization. For example, Sebastia, a small village perched in the hills of the West Bank, a few kilometers from Nablus. Upon arriving, a landscape dotted with Roman columns, remains of temples, an amphitheater hidden among the olive trees, a crusader basilica now in ruins, and in the center of the village, among the stone houses, what according to tradition should be the tomb of John the Baptist opens up before us. That magical place was our refuge, with the Roman ruins and the Old City largely recovered by an Italian Palestinian couple, both architects, who had made it the first form of widespread hospitality that Max and I had seen. I remember the guesthouse and the house where mosaic courses were held, immersed in the heart of the small village. The Palestinian residents could not do much, because the whole area was under the control of the Israelis, who did not allow either development or recovery plans, but the part of the village managed by the Palestinians had been transformed into a network of cozy houses, a vanguard of the entrepreneurial resistance. There we made our last trip before leaving Palestine. I was five months pregnant with Leila.

#### Now, when I think of Sebastia, my heart tightens, because the Israelis are destroying it. I also remember the Israeli offensive in the Gaza Strip in 2014, in which two thousand people died, including

#### more than five hundred children. We were in Washington, DC. I spent hours with Leila clutched to my chest, reading the news that arrived from Gaza. How many UNRWA colleagues killed, how much destruction! It seemed to us an unimaginable thing at the time. And in those days it was Max who urged me to say yes to the proposal that my former colleague Lex Takkenberg had been to making me for two years: to write a book on Palestinian refugees with him. “Don’t worry,” Max told me. “If you find the funding, great. If not, never mind. Dedicate yourself to something that is useful. Because it’s really important to understand the Palestinian refugee issue better.”

#### I was full of doubts, but that’s when I said to myself, “You know what? Let me think about it for a moment. Actually, I don’t know how to write a book, but I will understand it, I will learn how to do it.”

#### At that time Max supported me a lot, and also during the preparation of the book, when, with my somewhat

#### obsessive-compulsive nature, I felt like I could no longer let go of that creature that grew up with my children, occupying so much time, space, and enormous amount of mental energy. Much of that book was written between DC and Indonesia. Our friends joked: “It is easier to see Francesca without her children than without her computer.”

#### I must admit that I have never been very good at constructing borders between my work and my private life, and the barriers totally collapsed when I began my term as UN Special Rapporteur in 2022. In the beginning it was very difficult for our family life. Until then, even though I had a time-consuming job, I had always taken care of raising the children — from getting them ready for school to getting them into their pajamas — of the house and the common chores, shopping and vacations. Suddenly, I was no longer able to take care of very much, apart from myself. The first summer that we spent in Sicily, I devoted to the preparation of my report on self-determination, taking refuge to write on the terrace of the Lido dei Ciclopi while Max and the kids went swimming and enjoyed the attention of friends and relatives; the second summer was very much the same, with interviews of the Palestinian children while preparing the report on childhood in Palestine.

#### And then came October 7th, which took away the world as we saw it and lived it before, completely and suddenly. For the first time we were able to take three days of vacation with the children at a resort near Tunis, after the delivery of my report on minors. I had just returned from London, where I had given a lecture on the twentieth anniversary of Edward Said’s death. I remember that chilling morning, when we were woken up by incessant phone calls that forced us to get out of bed and fiddle with the remote control to connect to Al Jazeera. In front of the television, at six in the morning, trying to understand what had happened, both of us were speechless.

#### “But what did they do? How many people…how many children have they killed?” Of those first hours I remember the shock in the absence of full understanding of what was happening, the fear for what was and would be, the pleas for Max to take the children out of the room. At nine o’clock I had regained control of the situation, I was on the phone nonstop and had begun to respond to journalists’ requests. The first sentences spoken in those days, which I still hear echoing heavily within me, were: “I hope that the world will be able to embrace Israelis and Palestinians in a spirit of compassion and common sense. May they both find themselves in this moment of acute pain and understanding of the other’s trauma.” No one on the political spectrum has welcomed them, unfortunately.

#### Meanwhile, Max and I continued to experience everything together, including what concerned Palestine. During this last year and a half — the era of the genocide — Max has changed again, putting himself completely

#### at the helm of the family and becoming my number one support. It’s true, at the beginning I would get some digs like “Look, I have a job too, eh,” or “You’re never there anyway,” in the face of my absences from school activities for the children, for example. Over time, however, it has changed a lot. Sometimes he gets angry because I work too much, because I never put limits on anything or anyone. But he always supports me. Even when he thinks my tweets are too provocative. In fact, it is always Max who tells me: “Go at them with your stiletto, because when you are brutally honest people love you even more.”

#### So I am grateful to him for his support. And I also thank him for his work in economic analysis and for what he has written about Palestine. I do not

#### forget that, in one of the last reports that my predecessor, Michael Lynk, wrote for the United Nations, in 2021, when he did not even know that I existed, he was strongly critical of the World Bank for helping to normalize the Israeli occupation. He added, however, that the only World Bank report worth keeping was the one on the costs of employment in the West Bank for the Palestinian economy, which was the first one Max had worked on when he was hired by the World Bank in 2012.

#### Thank you, Max, because you are always full of ideas. Thank you because you are good and generous, and because it would make no sense for me to talk about Palestine without you.

#### Thank you for the tears you have collected in recent years, and for those you have helped me not to shed, with your strength and incendiary irony. Thank you for supporting me in these burdensome years, always encouraging me to persevere. Even in the face of the horror of death, which although physically distant has blown oppressively on our lives, tearing our nights apart for long months. Thank you for the many times you have helped me to transform sadness and anger into determination, allowing me to act incisively, without ever backing down. Thank you for helping me to see, understand, and begin to expose to others the mafia nature of the system against which we fight together, in order to build a present of which we do not have to be ashamed, and to not mortgage further the future of our children and other children, who are always children.

# CONCLUSION

#### *The habit of hope.*

#### Upright I walk… Head high I walk An olive branch in my hand, My coffin on my shoulder …. I walk and I walk My heart is a red moon, My heart is an orchard With boxthorn and basil My lips a sky raining Fire at times, love always. An olive branch in my hand, My coffin on my shoulder …. I walk and I walk — SAMIH AL-QASIM, “Upright I Walk”

#### IT IS WHEN THE WORLD SLEEPS that monsters are generated. We already have many monsters among us. First among them, our indifference.

#### —

#### AS MARIAME KABA, an African American educator and activist, says, hope is a discipline. And I would like to add that hope can, and should, also become a predisposition, a habit: something that we consider indispensable and to which we are so attached that we cannot do without it, beyond any logic or reasoning.

#### Even if doing so is not always as easy as saying it.

#### —

#### FEBRUARY 2025. I returned home, to Tunis, after a difficult experience in Germany. Between the fear of being arrested and separated from my family for who knows how long, and the awareness of the seriousness of what was happening in Europe, I felt an inner agitation that I don’t think I had ever felt before. I felt like I was in a state of post-traumatic stress, and maybe I was. The fact is that my nerves were on edge, I was spouting off for everything, I found myself arguing with my children, raising my voice for trivial things. I was not myself. My own family looked at me without seeing me, without finding me.

#### Then something very special happened. While my husband had taken the children out for a walk and I continued to pace around the house like a caged lion trying to regain my composure, a small book caught my attention as I *walked past the bookcase in my bedroom. Peace Is Every Step, by the Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh.*

#### Without even realizing it, I began to leaf through the book and it struck me like lightning, as if suddenly those pages had begun to speak to me. If they were to read it, many of my friends probably would not understand my enthusiasm, since Nhat Hanh uses such essential language that it could perhaps be misunderstood as simplistic. Instead, those words hit the mark precisely because they were so clear and spoke to me of something that at that *moment was both unfeasible and necessary: the idea of bringing back within me that peace for which I fight every day. It reminded me that, if you want to achieve change, first of all you have to be change, and that you cannot* change anything if you do not change yourself in some way; that you cannot work for peace in the world if you do

#### not first of all have inner peace, if you are not a true peacemaker. This is a concept that is quite familiar to me and even dear, at least in theory. In fact, reading that book, I was reminded of a speech I had made in 2023 at the opening of the Peace March in Assisi, where I had been invited by the peacemakers and had said more or less this: “If we don’t start with ourselves, what are we left with? Peace is built with peace, not thinking about war, so we *have to change the way we live and see things. Why are children taught conflict management instead of restoring peace? Why must conflicts be managed rather than avoided? What has happened to diplomacy? Where has it gone?”*

#### But bringing peace into our everyday lives, making that hope our habit, is the greatest of challenges, and in this effort, the little book that providentially caught my attention on that difficult day explains that there is and there cannot be any distinction between our politics and our living in this world.

#### Thich Nhat Hanh’s words made me reflect very deeply. With how much anger, with how much violence was I stamping my feet on the earth that supports me? For the first time in too many days, I remembered my yoga practice and took a truly deep breath. I let myself fall back into the sofa, I squeezed my eyes closed for a moment, and then I started reading again.

#### When I was in Vietnam, so many of our villages were being bombed. Along with my monastic brothers and sisters, I had to decide what to do. Should we continue to practice in our monasteries, or should we leave the meditation halls in order to help the people who were suffering under the bombs? After careful reflection, we decided to do both — to go out to help people and to do so in mindfulness. We called it engaged Buddhism. Mindfulness must be engaged. Once there is seeing, there must be acting. Otherwise, what is the use of seeing?

#### We must be aware of the real problems of the world. Then, with mindfulness, we will know what to do and what not to do to be of help. If we maintain awareness of our breathing and continue to practice smiling, even in difficult situations, many people, animals, and plants will benefit from our way of doing things. Are you massaging our Mother Earth every time your foot touches her? Are you planting seeds of joy and peace? I try to do do that with every step, and I know that our Mother Earth is most appreciative. Peace is every step. Shall we continue our journey?

#### *PEACE IS ALSO MINDFULNESS: being aware of what you are doing at any given moment. When we eat, when we* move, when we think, when we are with our children. How many times do we lose presence, in every action of our day? How many times do we hurry unnecessarily or let ourselves be distracted by something that seems more important than what we are doing? These are the questions that little book brought me back to, inviting me to give myself time for a few breaths without gasping, bringing my attention to the air that enters and leaves my body.

#### At that moment I remembered an evening a few years ago, when I was in Rome to participate in a conference. At that time — it was December 2023 — the genocide was already underway and in response to the externalization of my fear, I said: “One day there will be peace in Palestine, but at what price? I am terrified of what will come next, because, with all the pain and suffering that is being done to those in the West Bank and Gaza, I dare not imagine the violence that could be unleashed against the Israelis.” A man from the audience raised his hand and asked to speak.

#### It was Wasim Dabash, an Italian Palestinian professor of history at Sapienza University in Rome, who replied to me: “No. There will be no violence. If all this stops, when it stops, if there is no more violence, there will be no more violence. Because we Palestinians are not sustained by a thirst for revenge but for justice. From 1948 to today we have tried, as it was before, to return to Palestine, and to live in peace. And it is clear that there were reactions to oppression, actions of resistance, when the cup was overflowing. But most Palestinians have never taken part in violent actions against Israelis. For almost all of us, being religious does not mean being bigoted, it means having God inside, that is, the love of life, honoring both what remains and what is gone as something that must be brought into this life, and not as something for which one may want to die.”

#### For me it was a very important revelation, which allowed me to understand that even there, at that conference, without realizing it, I had brought my Western lens, which is accustomed to thinking in terms of the law of retaliation. The words of that wise teacher, however, reassured me and also taught me something important about the meaning of hope.

#### —

#### SOMETHING THAT I HOPE I have also transmitted to those who have read this book is the idea that each of us can become a spokesperson and bearer of that hope, learning day after day to adopt it as a posture, a good habit that we

#### can no longer do without. *You can be a journalist, a baker, or a lawyer, it doesn’t matter what you do but how you do it, how you conduct*

#### yourself. Because — as Thich Nhat Hanh writes — what is the use of seeing, if not acting? So I hope that anyone who reads these pages, now that they have met the people who helped me open my eyes to

#### see more clearly and to act for Palestine, will take with them the idea that they can be light, always, in any corner of the Earth.

#### *Francesca Albanese, March 2025*

# ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

#### THANKS THEN to all the beautiful souls I have met over the years, too many for me to name them all: I take you with me. Thanks also to my team of tireless “peacebuilders”: Sara Troian has given herself body and soul to my mandate for two years, the first, so uncertain but so fundamental. I love you Sara, and I’m happy to be able to do wonderful things elsewhere. To my closest collaborators, those without whom much of what is seen outside would not be possible: Melissa O’Donnell, a pillar for me since the fatal months in which the genocide began; Amal Loubani, whose patience and sweetness are second only to her stubborn dedication to work; and last but not least Teresa Rasella, who is everything that cannot be missing in a guardian angel. To the three of you I say: I don’t have all the words to thank you. Only, let’s move on, the road is still long.

#### To the researchers, to the university colleagues, among whom Nicola Perugini of the University of Edinburgh and Luigi Daniele of the University of Nottingham, for your inspiration and constant support.

#### Thank you to Palestinian civil society, under occupation and in the diaspora — there are too many of you, but I thank you all — and, in Israel, to Amos Goldberg and Itay Epshtain. Daniel Levy is no longer in Israel, but for me he represents the best part of it.

#### I thank my extended family of friends, especially those in Tunis, who have supported me and my loved ones so much in these complex months: Marija Maya Nikolić and Budimir Buda Milić, Iman Simon, Ahmed Shihab Eldin, Vittoria Capresi, Stefano Cozzani, Manal Warde, and Tunisian friends, precious defenders of human rights.

#### All those I met on the street, those with whom the road began, from my beloved Ariano onward: Mamma Libera, my brother Giuseppe, and my sister Lella. To my mother goes the greatest thanks for everything she gave me, for all the small seeds she planted in me, teaching me to be independent, the basis necessary to be free.

#### My children, Leila and Giordano, with the wonder in their hearts that is typical of my experience of being their mother, and not without regret for how much weight I have placed on their little shoulders in recent years of absence and torment induced by the genocide, which I have not always been able to keep locked away in my office.

#### And finally, Angela Lombardo, Marina Mercuriali, Marianna Loy, Adele Iannone, and Studio Littera, who helped this creature that you now hold in your hands to come into the world, and without whose questions, advice, and patient care this book so dear to me would never have seen the light of day.
